Source: Blockchain land transfers: Technology, promises, and perils
Abstract: The blockchain's apparent immutability has attracted significant interest on whether it may be relied on for registering and transferring land. Proponents of blockchain-based land systems point toward data security, automated transacting, and improved accessibility as key benefits; critics raise concerns over structural vulnerabilities, such as majority attacks, and inconsistencies with existing legal frameworks. The literature, however, tends to conceptualise blockchain as one monolithic data structure invariably built on the same mechanisms powering Bitcoin. This paper seeks to situate the debate on a closer understanding of the range of blockchain implementations possible. To this end, we provide a detailed technological survey of established and emerging blockchain technologies, clarifying that different consensus mechanisms, permissioning schemes, and other use-based customisations, are possible. We then re-evaluate the promises and perils of blockchain land transfers in this light, focusing on the English conveyancing system, and illustrate how different implementations involve different advantages and limitations. However, the features necessary to avoid key vulnerabilities also diminish the marginal advantages of using blockchains over traditional electronic databases. Thus, we conclude that blockchains, even properly understood, remain unsuitable for land transfers.
Methods: Narrative legal-technical article with a detailed technological survey of blockchain implementations and an applied analysis of English conveyancing and land registration. It compares public, private, and hybrid blockchain models against digitised land registries rather than using an empirical study design.
Results: Different blockchain implementations have different consensus, permissioning, and security trade-offs, but the features needed to avoid key vulnerabilities also erode the advantages over electronic databases. The paper argues that private blockchains are the only feasible model for land registries, yet their main benefits can already be achieved by digitised land registries.
Conclusions: Blockchains remain unsuitable for land transfers because their benefits are outweighed by vulnerabilities, implementation costs, and poor fit with land law. A digitised land registry is presented as the better modernization path, with the caveat that equitable interests and legal reform remain unresolved issues.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual legal-technology analysis and technological survey, focused on blockchain land transfers and the English conveyancing system. Highest maturity discussed is a private blockchain as a feasible model, but the paper concludes it remains unsuitable and argues digitised land registries are preferable.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, supported by a detailed technological survey of blockchain implementations and an application to the English conveyancing system. No empirical experiments are reported; the evidence is qualitative and conceptual.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: The paper surveys Bitcoin and Ethereum-style blockchains, including public permissionless chains, private permissioned chains, hybrid/consortium models, smart contracts, and sidechains. It discusses PoW, PoS (including Ethereum Casper), and BFT consensus, and concludes that a private blockchain would be the only feasible model for land registries.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: The paper discusses blockchain-based land registries as public, private, or hybrid systems, with blockchain used as data storage and consensus-enabled transaction validation. It mentions smart contracts on Ethereum, sidechains, P2P exchange platforms, integration of government data into digital land addresses, and identity via public/private keys; no implementation details or deployment stack are given.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land registration and conveyancing for registered land, focusing on blockchain or digitised land registries in the English system. The use case is transfer of title and related land records, including ownership, encumbrances, and equitable interests.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses cryptographic hash functions, public key cryptography, consensus mechanisms (POW, POS, BFT), permissioning, and private/public keys to secure records and verify participants. Threats discussed include tampering, majority/51% attacks, identity fraud, key theft or loss, and fraud; AI is mentioned only as a possible future addition.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to interoperability standards such as LADM/ISO 19152, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, GIS, or legacy cadastral database integration.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: English conveyancing law would need amendment to recognize blockchain transactions, including formalities under the Law of Property Act 1925 and the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989. The Land Registrar, certified conveyancers, notaries, and the registry retain key roles; the paper favors a private or hybrid permissioned model with possible sanctions and indemnity for defects.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: England-focused land registration; blockchain land registries had been explored in Sweden, Georgia, Ukraine, Dubai, Brazil, and Ghana. Barriers include 51% attacks, high computational and electricity costs, slow transaction rates, key loss, legal incompatibility, need for legislative reform, and limited added value over digitised registries.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Performance criteria discussed are security, transaction speed, fraud reduction, data transparency, accessibility, and compatibility with land registration law. The paper argues private blockchain could improve security, but its advantages over digitised land registries are marginal; no empirical benchmarks or measurements are reported.

Source: Blockchain in real estate: Recent developments and empirical applications
Abstract: The real estate sector is often presented as an exemplary field that benefits from practical blockchain applications. The general hypothesis is that, in theory, blockchain could solve some significant challenges the real estate sector is facing, such as nontransparency, inefficiencies, fraud and corruption, high costs, and trust issues. However, the literature focuses on blockchain's theoretical benefits, challenges, or concepts. This research aims to understand the recent developments in the blockchain literature, specifically in the real estate sector, and to understand the current real-world applications by collecting empirical evidence from blockchain studies. The systematic literature review identified 262 relevant documents, after which a thematic content analysis was performed. Conceptual blockchain literature was identified to propose blockchain benefits for the real estate sector in four categories: land administration, real estate transactions, tokenization, and real estate management. The thematic content analysis also identified 26 empirical applications, of which all except one were related to land administration. Although the conceptual and theoretical blockchain literature presents blockchain as a disruptive and transformative technology for the real estate sector, the empirical applications suggest that blockchain adoption materializes more in hybrid, smaller-scale settings, where blockchain is merely an add-on layer to existing systems. Overall, most of the conceptual blockchain benefits remain empirically unconfirmed. On the other hand, the empirical applications suggest that blockchain could, for example, increase efficiency, reduce time, and provide verifiability, transparency, and automation, even in smaller-scale, hybrid settings. In addition, the applications indicate that blockchain could, in some cases, help reduce fraud and increase security and trust compared with centralized digital solutions. Finally, the empirical insights emphasize the role of political will, regulatory framework, availability of reliable digital data, publicâ€“private partnerships, and educational aspects in blockchain applications.
Methods: Systematic literature review of 262 English peer-reviewed documents (plus some reports, theses, and magazine articles) from Scopus, ProQuest, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, using PRISMA and thematic content analysis in ATLAS.ti.
Results: Four conceptual categories emerged: land administration, transactions, tokenization, and real estate management; 26 empirical applications were identified, almost all in land administration. Empirical cases suggested blockchain mainly works as a hybrid, small-scale add-on and can improve efficiency, transparency, verifiability, and sometimes trust, while many theoretical benefits remain unconfirmed.
Conclusions: Blockchain has potential in real estate, but current evidence supports mainly hybrid, limited applications rather than disruptive transformation. Key caveats are scarce empirical data, limited scaling, and strong dependence on regulation, political will, reliable data, and institutional context.
Study Classification and Maturity: Systematic literature review with thematic content analysis of 262 documents and 26 empirical applications. Highest demonstrated maturity is small-scale, hybrid, early-stage pilot or limited production deployment, not full operational transformation.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Systematic literature review of 262 documents with PRISMA and thematic content analysis; 26 empirical applications were identified and 12 had empirical evaluations. Evidence is both quantitative and qualitative.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: The paper does not specify one platform or consensus mechanism overall; it describes mostly hybrid, smaller-scale applications where blockchain is an add-on layer to existing systems. One example used a permissioned blockchain with a limited number of nodes, and another mentions KSI Blockchain securing Estoniaâ€™s property registry.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Most applications use a hybrid approach, with blockchain as an add-on layer integrated with existing databases or registries rather than replacing them. Some implementations store hashes on-chain and keep original data off-chain; smart contracts and existing digital identity solutions are also mentioned.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Real estate blockchain applications, mainly land administration and land/title registration, with some focus on real estate transactions, tokenization, and real estate management. Empirical cases were mostly hybrid, small-scale systems using blockchain as an add-on layer to existing registries.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Blockchain is described as using cryptography, verifiable and virtually unchangeable blocks, and secure peer-to-peer records. The paper reports coverage of tampering, fraud, corruption, and cyber threats; one application used KSI Blockchain to secure critical data and another noted cryptographic protection and information security requirements.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to interoperability standards such as LADM/ISO 19152, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, GIS, or legacy cadastral database integration.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Blockchain adoption was constrained by legal uncertainties, regulatory frameworks, and the validity of electronic signatures; in Sweden, production was blocked because electronic signatures were not yet valid in real estate transactions. Publicâ€“private partnerships, governmental support, and political will were central, and governments retained a key role in hybrid land administration models.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Blockchain adoption in real estate is mostly hybrid, small-scale, and concentrated in land administration; 26 empirical applications were identified, with 12 empirically evaluated. Main barriers were implementation complexity, legal and regulatory uncertainty, lack of reliable digitized data, scaling challenges, resistance among stakeholders, limited blockchain expertise, and the need for governmental support and publicâ€“private partnerships.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Empirical applications suggested increased efficiency, reduced time, verifiability, transparency, automation, and sometimes lower fraud and higher security/trust; cost effects were mixed and no implementation cost assessments were available. Key gaps were limited empirical evidence, scarce technical details, few production deployments, underrepresentation of real estate management/transactions, and unclear economic viability.

Source: User-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance in blockchain adoption for land administration systems: A systematic literature review
Abstract: Blockchain technology has emerged as a disruptive force with the potential to support the securitisation of tenure in land administration systems (LAS). Like in every new and emerging technologies, â€˜trust and acceptanceâ€™ play significant roles in stakeholdersâ€™ intention to either embrace or reject the adoption of blockchain technology in LAS. While previous research on the topic has placed considerable attention on the potential of adopting blockchain for improving LAS, limited attention has been placed on understanding the user-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance. To address this gap, this study conducted a systematic literature review on the user-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance influencing blockchain technology adoption for LAS. The analysis employs two complementary theoretical frameworks: the Multilevel Trust (MLT) framework to categorize trust factors, and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) to guide the analysis of acceptance factors. The results categorize the key factors influencing stakeholders' trust into three dimensions: trust in technology (data privacy and control, security), trust in administrative processes (traceability and transparency), and trust in institutions (regulation and legal compliance), while performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions emerge as the key factors that influence stakeholdersâ€™ acceptance. Drawing upon these findings, a conceptual framework was developed to illustrate the interrelationship between the trust and acceptance factors influencing stakeholdersâ€™ intention to either embrace or reject the adoption of blockchain for LAS. This research contributes to the literature on emerging technology adoption for LAS, which may help land administration stakeholders take suitable measures to address stakeholder concerns and thereby promote blockchain technology adoption.
Methods: Systematic literature review using PRISMA, with 68 peer-reviewed articles selected from 1,520 records in Scopus, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and ProQuest. Analysis was guided by the MLT and UTAUT frameworks and used structured data extraction in Excel.
Results: Trust factors clustered into three dimensions: trust in technology (data privacy and control, security), trust in administrative processes (traceability and transparency), and trust in institutions (regulation and legal compliance). Acceptance was driven by performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions.
Conclusions: Trust is the cornerstone of acceptance in blockchain-based LAS, and the study proposes a conceptual framework linking trust and acceptance to adoption intentions. The main limitation is that the evidence base is limited, so future survey-based empirical studies are needed to validate the factors and framework.
Study Classification and Maturity: Systematic literature review of blockchain adoption for land administration systems, using MLT and UTAUT to develop a conceptual framework. Highest maturity is conceptual framework/proposal; no operational deployment is reported.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Systematic literature review (SLR) following PRISMA; 68 peer-reviewed articles were included from 1,520 retrieved records. Evidence is qualitative synthesis of reviewed studies, with citation frequencies recorded for key factors.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Permissioned and public/private blockchain architectures are discussed, including consortium and hybrid models; the paper does not evaluate a single platform or consensus protocol. Examples include a private blockchain in Swedenâ€™s pilot and a public blockchain for Georgiaâ€™s land registry, with smart contracts and cryptographic mechanisms noted.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: The paper is a systematic literature review, not an implemented system. It describes blockchain-based LAS concepts such as public/private and permissioned/permissionless blockchains, smart contracts, secure digital identity services, zero-knowledge proofs, homomorphic encryption, role-based access control, and hybrid blockchain models.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Blockchain adoption for land administration systems (LAS), especially land registration, property/ownership records, and land transaction management. The review focuses on trust and acceptance factors for using blockchain to secure tenure and improve transparency, traceability, and legal compliance.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Blockchain security relies on cryptographic hashing, consensus algorithms, encryption, access control, and secure digital identity services. Threats covered include tampering, unauthorized access, fraud, identity theft, 51% attacks, smart-contract vulnerabilities, cyberattacks, and double-spending; ZKPs, homomorphic encryption, role-based access control, hybrid blockchains, and multifactor authentication are proposed mitigations.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to interoperability standards such as LADM/ISO 19152, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, GIS, or legacy cadastral database integration.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Blockchain-based LAS is discussed as requiring clear legal frameworks, regulatory compliance, data protection rules, and institutional support. The paper notes unresolved issues such as legal validity of blockchain records, right to be forgotten, data ownership, liability, and compatibility with existing LAS processes.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Adoption is still exploratory; blockchain-based LAS has been piloted in Georgia, Cyprus, the UAE, and Sweden. Main barriers include privacy and security concerns, regulatory and legal compliance, fragmented or weak regulations, infrastructure and technical expertise gaps, compatibility issues, bureaucratic delays, and the need for stakeholder coordination and consensus.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Performance was framed mainly as acceptance criteria: performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions. Key research gaps were the underexplored user-centric trust/acceptance dimensions in blockchain-based LAS and the lack of empirical validation of the proposed framework.

Source: Reducing clientsâ€™ influence in property valuation: An exploration of a blockchain-based solution
Abstract: Clients' influence remains a significant issue in the property valuation industry, particularly in emerging countries like Nigeria, where existing solutions have proven ineffective. This study, therefore, considers blockchain technology as a medium for delivering information transparency and explores the application of a blockchain-based tool for reducing clients' influence in property valuation. Specifically, this study is pioneering in proposing, developing, and testing a blockchain-based solution for reducing client influence in property valuation, suggesting a promising avenue for increasing transparency in the process. This study involves several stages. Firstly, propchain, a blockchain-based mobile application, was developed and deployed on the Hyperledger Fabric Network, a permissioned blockchain network. The efficacy of the proposed solution was qualitatively tested by a single-round focus group held with valuers, bankers, and a loan customer who used the application to simulate a property valuation exercise for a mortgage. The findings suggest that blockchain technology could be a viable tool for reducing client influence in property valuations. However, specific challenges in the Nigerian context, such as data access, information verification, and stakeholder trust, present significant obstacles. These issues highlight the need for robust institutional support systems to enhance the efficacy of blockchain solutions in this domain. This study supports Levy and Schuck's (2005) assertion that increased information transparency can reduce client influence. Nevertheless, our research indicates that the successful implementation of blockchain in property valuation will require overcoming systemic barriers unique to the Nigerian environment. The implication of key findings is also discussed.
Methods: Design science plus qualitative methods: a blockchain-based mobile app (Propchain) was built on Hyperledger Fabric, deployed on AWS, and tested in a simulated mortgage valuation exercise. A single-round Zoom focus group with five participants (two valuers, two bankers, one client) was transcribed and thematically analyzed in NVivo 12.
Results: Five themes emerged: blockchain as useful for reducing client influence, ease of use, changing the valuation process, limitations/challenges, and adoption mechanisms. Participants generally viewed Propchain positively, but noted gaps in data access, stakeholder trust, regulatory support, and database integration.
Conclusions: Propchain shows strong potential to improve transparency and reduce client influence in property valuation, but it cannot eliminate the problem in Nigeria because of institutional and data-system gaps. Key limitations were no performance/scalability test, dummy data, and only one focus group round.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical design-science study with qualitative validation; a blockchain-based mobile application (Propchain) was developed, deployed, and tested in a single-round focus group simulation. Highest maturity demonstrated was proof-of-concept/prototype, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Design science was used to develop Propchain on Hyperledger Fabric, then a single-round Zoom focus group with five participants simulated a mortgage valuation to qualitatively assess usefulness, ease of use, and ability to reduce client influence. No performance or scalability testing was done; evidence was qualitative.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Propchain was developed on the Hyperledger Fabric Network, a permissioned blockchain. It used one Certificate Authority, one ordering service, two organizations, and two peer nodes; smart contracts were written in Java, and uploaded files were stored on AWS S3.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Propchain was built on Hyperledger Fabric using the client SDK, with one Certificate Authority, one orderer, two organisations, and two peer nodes. Java chaincode automated enrolment and report submission; the network was deployed on AWS EC2 and linked to an AWS S3 bucket for uploaded files and documents.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Property valuation in Nigeria, using a blockchain-based mobile application (Propchain) on Hyperledger Fabric to increase information transparency and reduce client influence in mortgage-related valuation exercises.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses Hyperledger Fabric permissioned blockchain, Certificate Authority authentication, smart contracts, hashed transaction records, and immutable timestamped blocks. It aims to reduce tampering, unauthorized access, report revision, and client influence; the paper also notes risks from hacking, misleading information, and weak data verification.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Propchain was built on Hyperledger Fabric and deployed with an Android app, AWS EC2, AWS S3, Java chaincode, and Hyperledger Fabric SDK. It mentions integrating with a valuation workflow and existing property databases, but no formal standards such as LADM, ISO 19152, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE are cited or implemented.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Blockchain may support transparency, but the paper says its success in Nigeria depends on stronger legal and regulatory support, institutional capacity, stakeholder trust, and monitoring systems. It notes unresolved issues around land registry/database access, compliance checks, and the role of ESVARBON and government.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Nigeria; propchain was developed and deployed on Hyperledger Fabric, then piloted in a single-round focus group with valuers, bankers, and a loan customer. Barriers included lack of property databases, data access and verification problems, stakeholder trust, legal/regulatory support, institutional capacity, security concerns, and scalability/performance not yet evaluated.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: No technical performance evaluation was done; the blockchain network was not assessed for performance or scalability. The study used qualitative focus-group criteria: usefulness, ease of use, impact on valuation workflow, confidence in reducing client influence, and barriers; gaps included missing databases, legal/regulatory support, trust, and real-life testing.

Source: Tokenizing the city: NFTs as tools for equitable urban governance and community-led planning
Abstract: Applying NFTs to urban planning offers revolutionary potential but raises serious equity concerns. Although NFTs are linked to digital art speculation, their underlying technology, decentralized ownership, smart contracts, and tamper-proof records could transform participatory planning, land-use management, and community asset stewardship. This article discusses how NFTs could decentralize planning power by enabling tokenized community land trusts, zoning-compliance automation, and neighborhood DAOs (Decentralized Autonomous Organizations). However, they also pose dangers, such as digital exclusion, environmental degradation from energy-hungry blockchains, and capture by technocratic elites. Mitigation is needed through hybrid digital-physical participation systems, public sector-led blockchain infrastructure, and equity-sensitive token design if these tools are to benefit the public interest. The article proposes a staged implementation approach, beginning with controlled pilots (e.g., NFT-tracked community benefit agreements) before scaling up to more advanced applications such as dynamic zoning regimes. Lastly, ethical use of NFTs in planning demands visionary public-sector leadership to avert the entrenchment of existing inequalities in the name of innovation. Planners must critically engage with this emerging technology not as eager consumers but as stewards shaping its trajectory toward more equitable, open, and democratic urban futures. The question is not whether NFTs will influence cities, but who will determine that influence and to what ends.
Methods: Critical interpretive review of literature at the intersection of blockchain governance, urban planning, and digital equity, synthesizing conceptual frameworks and limited pilot evidence. The paper also uses scenario planning with heuristic prototypes and failure-mode analysis.
Results: NFTs are presented as potentially useful for participatory planning, community land trusts, zoning compliance, and decentralized local governance, but they also create risks of digital exclusion, environmental burden, and technocratic capture. The paper identifies phased pilots, hybrid digital-physical participation, and public-sector blockchain infrastructure as key mitigations.
Conclusions: NFTs could support more equitable urban governance only if implemented through strong public-sector guardrails, equity-sensitive design, and staged pilots. Key limitations are digital divides, environmental impacts, governance capture, and the risk of speculative or extractive deployment.
Study Classification and Maturity: Critical interpretive review / conceptual article synthesizing emerging literature and limited pilot evidence. Highest demonstrated maturity is conceptual and phased-implementation proposal, with illustrative pilots only; not validated for citywide deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Critical interpretive review synthesizing conceptual frameworks and limited pilot evidence. It uses scenario planning and illustrative municipal pilots, but reports no formal empirical benchmarking or quantitative evaluation of the proposed NFT applications.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Uses public blockchains for NFT-based governance, with options including Layer-2 rollups (Arbitrum, Optimism), permissioned public-sector sidechains, and public-sector-operated ledgers. Consensus mechanisms discussed include proof-of-work, proof-of-stake, proof-of-authority, and delegated proof-of-stake; NFTs store pointers to off-chain metadata in IPFS or hybrid cloud-blockchain repositories.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: NFTs are blockchain-based certificates with smart contracts; planning records are stored off-chain in IPFS or hybrid cloud-blockchain repositories, while the NFT stores a URI pointer. Integration with land registries, zoning maps, and permit databases requires custom APIs and middleware, with bi-directional synchronization to the official cadastre.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Urban planning and land-use governance using NFTs/blockchain for participatory planning, community land trusts, zoning compliance, community benefit agreements, and tokenized land-use or real-estate rights.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: NFTs use blockchain-based ownership, tamper-proof records, and smart contracts to verify authenticity, enforce zoning or benefit agreements, and support auditable records. Threats discussed include tampering, digital exclusion, data privacy risk, governance capture, speculation, and environmental harm.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Municipal land registries, zoning maps, and permit databases in Oracle, PostgreSQL, and Esri ArcGIS must synchronize bidirectionally with official cadastre records via custom APIs and middleware. The paper also recommends open-source standards, self-hosted IPFS clusters, and public technical appendices, but cites no specific LADM, ISO 19152, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE implementation.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Legal compatibility is framed as needing bi-directional synchronization with official cadastre systems, legal recognition of on-chain records as prima facie evidence, and legislation to reconcile blockchain immutability with public records law, error correction, and the right to be forgotten. Public-sector leadership, procurement reform, auditability, and regulatory sandboxes are emphasized.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Interoperability with legacy planning systems, volatile gas fees, data privacy, limited municipal technical expertise, procurement constraints, and legal tension with public records and due process are key barriers. The paper is a critical interpretive review focused on urban planning, with staged pilots proposed and examples from Seoul, Barcelona, Dubai, Vienna, and Pittsburgh; it is not reporting an operational deployment.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Key criteria are equity, accessibility, sustainability, interoperability, privacy, transparency, and cost. Reported figures include nearly 40% of low-income urban households lacking stable broadband and zoning smart-contract execution costs of $10â€“$150, with Layer-2 rollups reducing fees by 90â€“95%; the paper notes more evidence is needed on effectiveness, corruption reduction, and citywide deployment.

Source: Application-layer integrity protection and temporal administrative control for centralized state registries: Implementation and evaluation
Abstract: Centralized state registries risk unauthorized database-layer modification and misuse of privileged access outside authorized working hours. We present a service-layer architecture combining temporal role-based access control (TRBAC)-inspired per-request restriction of privileged writes, deterministic record verification using a hash-based message authentication code with SHA-256 (HMAC-SHA-256) and an external secret, and optional hash-linked audit evidence. The Spring Boot/MySQL implementation was evaluated using single-thread and 1â€“32-worker benchmarks, a paired diagnostic experiment, and automated tampering and temporal-control tests. In the single-thread benchmark, FINGERPRINT, CHECKPOINT (K = 100), and STRICT incurred 174.9â€“200.3%, 68.6â€“77.2%, and 215.0â€“237.3% median overhead relative to STANDARD. HMAC_COMPUTE added 1.21â€“1.26 ms per successful update (59.1â€“60.4% overhead), isolating the required database re-read and 23-field HMAC computation. Under concurrency, FINGERPRINT reached 934.2 updates per second at 32 workers, CHECKPOINT peaked at 686.6 at four workers, and STRICT remained synchronization-bound near 300 before declining to 265.9 at 32 workers. Automated validation confirmed reproducible data_hash recomputation, configured CHECKPOINT batch persistence, exposure of the tested direct SQL modification of freq.nominal through a fingerprint mismatch when its normalized representation changed, detection of modification of retained checkpoint evidence, and per-request off-hours authority downgrade with conditional authentication restoration. The results define a tested operating envelope: unchained per-write evidence with FINGERPRINT, batched hash-linked evidence with CHECKPOINT, and a per-write global chain with STRICT, with distinct performance and synchronization costs. Same-database verification establishes retained-state consistency but not independent completeness or freshness after coordinated suffix removal or restoration of an older consistent snapshot.
Methods: Spring Boot/MySQL service-layer architecture with TRBAC-inspired per-request temporal control, HMAC-SHA-256 record fingerprinting over a fixed 23-field canonical serialization, and optional CHECKPOINT/STRICT hash-linked audit evidence. Evaluated with single-thread and 1â€“32-worker benchmarks, a paired diagnostic isolation test, and automated tampering and temporal-control validation.
Results: Single-thread overhead was 174.9â€“200.3% for FINGERPRINT, 68.6â€“77.2% for CHECKPOINT (K=100), and 215.0â€“237.3% for STRICT; HMAC_COMPUTE added 1.21â€“1.26 ms per update (59.1â€“60.4%). Under concurrency, FINGERPRINT reached 934.2 TPS at 32 workers, CHECKPOINT peaked at 686.6 TPS at 4 workers, and STRICT declined to 265.9 TPS at 32 workers; tests confirmed tamper detection and temporal downgrade.
Conclusions: The architecture is deployable for centralized registries and provides configurable integrity assurance with temporal access restriction, but at measurable performance and synchronization cost. Same-database verification shows retained-state consistency only, not independent completeness or freshness after suffix removal or rollback; trusted server time and protected application secrets are key assumptions.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical implementation and evaluation study of a centralized registry security architecture. Highest demonstrated maturity is tested Spring Boot/MySQL prototype with automated validation and benchmark evaluation, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Spring Boot/MySQL implementation evaluated with single-thread and 1â€“32-worker benchmarks, a paired diagnostic experiment, and automated tampering and temporal-control tests. Evidence is quantitative and qualitative, including overhead percentages, TPS, and validation of checkpoint persistence, tamper detection, and request-time authority downgrade.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: No blockchain platform or consensus mechanism is used. The architecture is a centralized service-layer design implemented in Spring Boot/MySQL, with optional hash-linked audit evidence and no distributed-ledger infrastructure.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Spring Boot service layer with MySQL backend. TRBAC per-request filtering, HMAC-SHA-256 fingerprinting with an external secret, and optional checkpoint/strict hash-chained audit evidence are coordinated in the application layer; registry tables use MyISAM and integrity tables use InnoDB.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Centralized state registries in e-government, specifically a radio-frequency management registry with land-ownership-style legal records and database integrity protection for update verification, tamper detection, and temporal access control.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Temporal role-based access control restricts privileged writes outside working hours; HMAC-SHA-256 with an external secret provides record verification, and optional checkpoint chaining provides hash-linked audit evidence. It addresses unauthorized database-layer tampering, off-hours privileged misuse, audit-evidence manipulation, and key-compromise assumptions.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to LADM/ISO 19152, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, GIS, legacy cadastral databases, or other interoperability standards integration.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Centralized state registries are described as legally binding systems used for regulatory enforcement and legal decision-making. The paper notes governance and accountability challenges for blockchain in public-sector registries, and reports formal transfer and acceptance by the responsible state authority with installation, staff instruction, and six months of support.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Target setting was a centralized state radio frequency management registry in a developing-country public administration context. Barriers included insider misuse, direct database-layer tampering, off-hours privileged access, same-database completeness/freshness limits, checkpoint crash/restart loss up to K âˆ’ 1 pending events, and performance overhead under concurrency; the implementation was formally transferred and accepted by the responsible state authority.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Single-thread median overhead was 174.9â€“200.3% for FINGERPRINT, 68.6â€“77.2% for CHECKPOINT (K=100), and 215.0â€“237.3% for STRICT; HMAC_COMPUTE added 1.21â€“1.26 ms per update. Gaps: same-database verification does not ensure completeness/freshness after suffix removal or rollback, CHECKPOINT recovery after crash was not validated, and broader multi-node/mixed-workload scalability remains untested.

Source: Improving implementation of the Blockchain technology in real estate registration
Abstract: Difficulties are caused by the introduction of the Blockchain in the field of registration of rights to real estate and real estate turnover since this requires the establishment of a balance between public and private interests. The article proposes a set of measures, the implementation of which would improve the implementation of the Blockchain technology to modernize the registration of rights to real estate and real estate turnover. The main hypothesis of the study is the assumption that the wider use of the Blockchain will increase the reliability of the register of real estate rights and make the circulation of real estate more secure. During the research were used the comparative legal research method, the method of legal modeling, the method of economic analysis of law. The article identified and characterized the vectors of modernization of real estate registration using the Blockchain have been identified and characterized. The regional aspect of introducing Blockchain technology for registering rights to real estate and improving legal regulation has been considered. The use of virtual reality and augmented reality technology for real estate accounting has been proposed, through the creation of a virtual real estate registry. The possibility of using online arbitration when challenging the right to real estate, which is registered using Blockchain technology, has been argued. The main directions of legal regulation of Smart factory and Digital Enterprise have been proposed.
Methods: Comparative legal research, legal modeling, and economic analysis of law were used, with an interdisciplinary and systematic approach. The paper also draws on comparative examples from multiple countries and pilot blockchain registration experiments.
Results: Four implementation directions were identified: transfer of transaction workflow to blockchain, blockchain-based title registries, real estate tokenization, and a virtual real estate registry using VR/AR. The paper also argues for gradual regional rollout, use of regulatory sandboxes, and online arbitration for disputes.
Conclusions: Blockchain can simplify real estate registration and increase indisputability only if the deposit principle is fully implemented and contestation remains exceptional. Limitations include the need for gradual pilot-based deployment and further empirical validation, especially for the post-implementation phase.

Source: BERE: Ensuring immutability and transparency with blockchain in real estate appraisal industry
Abstract: Real estate appraisal plays a pivotal role in various financial transactions and regulatory processes, necessitating the assurance of unalterable and transparent Real Estate Appraisal rePorts (REA_Ps). Authorized appraisal experts employ diverse methodologies to ascertain the market value of real estate properties, contributing to critical decisions in property transactions, loans, taxation, insurance, financial reporting, and lease calculations. The standardized format and jurisdiction-compliant methodologies used in official REA_Ps emphasize the need for their preservation in an unaltered state. Despite the importance of official REA_Ps, the potential for unauthorized alterations poses a significant challenge when stored in centralized databases. With its inherent tamper-proof nature, Blockchain (BC) technology emerges as an ideal solution to safeguard integrity of the REA_Ps. This study proposes a Blockchain-Enhanced Real Estate appraisal management framework, BERE , to ensure the immutability of REA_Ps and enhance appraisal process transparency. The proposed BERE framework fosters trust among stakeholders in the real estate appraisal sector. By securely storing REA_Ps authored by on-field appraisal experts on the BC, the method prevents unauthorized modifications and ensures the confidentiality of private data. Simulations employ a variety of measures, such as BC size, transaction verification time, CPU usage, and message overhead on transaction generation, to assess system performance. The results indicate that the BERE framework successfully maintains the accuracy and reliability of REA_Ps. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study showcasing a practical application of BC technology to demonstrate its ability to transform the appraisal process and inspire trust in the accuracy of REA_Ps.

Results: Simulations showed BERE maintained REA_P accuracy and reliability, with blockchain size ranging from 0.84 to 58.61 MB, transaction verification peaks around 3.2 s to 15.5 s, and message overhead reaching 243,000 to 450,000 messages. The experiments found largely linear scaling with node count and transaction rate, with minor deviations from variable report size.
Conclusions: BERE is presented as the first comprehensive practical blockchain application for real estate appraisal, improving immutability, transparency, privacy, and trust. Limitations include privacy concerns from blockchain transparency and practical memory/runtime constraints in large-scale simulation; future work will explore advanced consensus and cryptography.

Source: A systematic review of the institutional success factors for blockchain-based land administration
Abstract: The land administration systems have witnessed many innovative technologies in the attempt to revolutionalize the task of recording land and property rights. One such revolution is the transition toward blockchain-based land administration. Like most technologies, blockchain-based land administration projects are not immune to failures, early adopters have encountered challenges, and several pilot cases have failed. Institutional factors have proven to be issues that can hinder the successful adoption of technological innovations such as blockchain-based land administration. This study identifies and analyses institutional success factors for adopting blockchain-based land administration. A systematic literature review of 37 studies resulted in the extraction of 18 related institutional factors critical to adopting blockchain-based land administration projects. Using Scott's three-pillar framework, the factors were divided into three dimensions: regulatory, organisational and cultural environment. Despite the popular opinion that the regulatory environment is integral to adopting blockchain-based land administration, our review suggests that a mutual co-existence and interplay between all the factors is key to the success of blockchain-based land projects. This study concludes that the adoption of blockchain-based land projects can be enhanced by understanding the institutional factors necessary to adopt blockchain-based land administration.

Results: The review extracted 18 institutional success factors, with government support, political stability, public-private partnership, public trust, stakeholder expertise, collaboration, and regulatory clarity most emphasized.
Conclusions: Blockchain-based land administration succeeds through the combined fit of regulatory, organizational, and cultural-cognitive support, not regulation alone. Source: A Blockchain-based Land Title Management System for Bangladesh
Abstract: Bangladesh is a small country with a large population. Its increasingly developing economy further makes land a lucrative source of fixed capital. On the other hand, land titling is a cumbersome and lengthy process, where different government bodies process different sets of documents, and bureaucratic loopholes encourage fraudulent activities by organized people. As a result, the current model suffers from good governance. In this paper, we propose a Blockchain-based solution that offers data synchronization and transparency, ease of access, immutable records management, a faster and cheaper solution. Considering the technological knowledge and capacity of the people and the government, we introduced a phase by phase Blockchain adoption model that starts with a public Blockchain ledger and later gradually incorporates two levels of Hybrid Blockchain. We provide detailed smart contracts design of the public Blockchain and implement a prototype system using Ethereum. Our experimental setup uses local and live Ethereum test networks to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed system. Our analysis shows that the proposed model reduces the number of required travels, the overall cost of information processing as well as provide easy access to vital information. As a result, Blockchain adoption can improve the land title digitization effort of Bangladesh.
Methods: Phase-by-phase blockchain adoption proposal for Bangladesh land titling, with a public Ethereum smart-contract prototype built in Solidity and tested on Ganache CLI and Ropsten.
Results: The prototype reduced travel, processing cost, and time for ROR handover; operations took only a few minutes and were cheaper than the current months-long manual process.
Conclusions: A phased hybrid blockchain could improve transparency, synchronization, accessibility, and immutable record management for Bangladesh land titling. The authors note future government policy, capacity-building, PKI management, and security work are still needed.

Source: Does the extent of time in drought affect the rate of farm ownership change in a local government area? A sixteen-year assessment of rural land ownership change in New South Wales, Australia
Abstract: Droughts are significant catalysts of financial and emotional hardship for farming communities. However, does the extent of time an area has been in drought impact upon the rate at which agricultural land changes hands? Does it encourage more land to change ownership, as stressed farmers depart at faster rates, or does its negative impacts on farm production dampen demand for rural land? This study addresses this question through a unique, longitudinal (2004â€“2020) dataset of property transactions in 96 rural Local Government Areas (LGAs) in New South Wales, Australia. We measure the proportion of time each LGA has been in drought during the previous 1, 2, 5 and 10 years, and correlate this against the rate of agricultural land ownership change. Results indicate that in the short-term (<5 years), the proportion of time in drought is not a major influence on the extent of agricultural land ownership change. However, over a 10-year timespan, there is a statistically significant negative correlation between the two for non-irrigated agricultural land, grazing land and land owned by individuals (as opposed to companies). These findings suggest these agricultural land markets are sensitive to the long-term effects of drought. The take-home message seems to be that the persistence of drought saps the vitality of these agricultural land markets, leaving farmers with reduced prospects to capitalise on their land assets. This finding has resonance given that climate change models suggest an intensification of the frequency and severity of drought in much of rural NSW.
Methods: Longitudinal observational study using 96 rural NSW LGAs and 2004â€“2020 parcel-transfer data. A geodatabase was built from land registry, cadastre, land-use, and Combined Drought Indicator datasets, then analyzed with 36 univariate linear regressions.
Results: No significant short-term effect (<5 years) was found, but 10-year drought exposure was negatively associated with ownership change in the total sample and several agricultural subsets. Effects were strongest for non-irrigated land, grazing land, and individually owned agricultural land, explaining about 4â€“5% of variation.
Conclusions: Drought acts as a long-term inhibitor of agricultural land ownership change in rural NSW, especially for non-irrigated and grazing land. The authors argue the geodatabase approach can be extended to other longitudinal land-market relationships beyond 2020.

Source: Enhancing smart city infrastructure with a geospatial blockchain-based addressing system

The second goal is very important for creating standardized information services in an international context, where land administration domain semantics have to be shared between countries (in order to enable needed translations). This paper presents an overview of the core cadastral domain model and its developments over the last 4 years. The model has been developed in a set of versions, which were each time adjusted based on the discussions at workshops with international experts and the experience from case studies in several countries of the world (Netherlands, El Salvador, Bolivia, Denmark, Sweden, Portugal, Greece, Australia, Nepal, Egypt, Iceland, and several African and Arab countries). Important conditions during the design of the model were and still are: should cover the common aspects of cadastral registrations all over the world, should be based on the conceptual framework of Cadastre 2014, should follow the international ISO and OGC standards, and at the same time the model should be as simple as possible in order to be useful in practise. Besides presenting the CCDM itself this paper represents an important new wave in geo-information standardization: after the domain independent basic geo-information standards (current series of ISO and OGC standards), the new standards based on specific domains will now be developed. Due to historical differences between countries (and regions) similar domains, such as the cadastral domain, may be modeled differently and therefore non-trivial harmonisation has to be done first. The presented CCDM is a result of this harmonisation and one of the first presented examples of semantic geo-information domain standards. Besides the three well-known concepts, Parcel, Person and Right, at the class level the model also includes immovables such as Building and OtherRegisterObject (geometry of easement, like a right of way, protected region, legal space around utility object, etc.) and the following concepts: SourceDocument such as SurveyDocument or LegalDocument (e.g. deed or title), Responsibilities, Restrictions (defined as Rights by other Person than the one having the ownership Right) and Mortgages. At the attribute level of the model the following aspects are included: SalePrize, UseCode, TaxAmount, Interest, Ranking, Share, Measurements, QualityLabel, LegalSize, EstimatedSize, ComputedSize, TransformationParams, PointCode, and several different date/times. The heart of the model is based on the three classes: (1) RegisterObject (including all kinds of immovables and movables), (2) RRR (right, restriction, responsibility), and (3) Person (natural, non-natural and group). The model supports the temporal aspects of the involved classes and offers several levels of Parcel fuzziness: Parcel (full topology), SpaghettiParcel (only geometry), PointParcel (single point), and TextParcel (no coordinate, just a description). The geometry and topology (2D and 3D) are based on the OGC and ISO/TC211 standard classes. The model is specified in UML class diagrams and it is indicated how this UML model can be converted into and XML schema, which can then be used for actual data exchange in our networked society (interoperability). Abstract: Smart contracts are programs that execute autonomously on blockchains.
