Source: The Legal Nature of Smart Contracts in a Perspective of Jordanian Civil Legislation
Abstract: This legal research explores the jurisprudential aspects of smart contracts in the context of Jordanian civil legislation. Smart contracts, which are digital programs based on blockchain technology, have emerged as a disruptive force with the potential to revolutionize traditional contractual relations. They autonomously execute binding agreements by adhering to pre-programmed instructions when specific conditions are met, thereby obviating the need for intermediaries. The growing global prominence of smart contracts makes their compatibility with and implications for the legal framework in Jordan an imperative subject of inquiry. Nevertheless, the integration of smart contracts into the existing legal framework presents distinctive challenges, especially within the milieu of Jordanian civil legislation. This research paper aims to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the stance of Jordanian civil legislation regarding smart contracts. Abstract: The Smart Manufacturing paradigm requires support by smart supply chains with capabilities of self-organizing and self-optimizing capabilities to accommodate uncertainties. Source: Large-scale acquisitions of communal land in the Global South: Assessing the risks and formulating policy recommendations
Abstract: This article conceptualises and empirically assesses the socioeconomic and environmental risks of large-scale land acquisitions (LSLAs) for communal lands in the Global South. These risks include the displacement of local communities due to the insufficient formal recognition of communal land and exclusive and corrupt negotiations with investors who frequently exploit the legal pluralism inherent in these tenure systems. Furthermore, LSLAs often imply the loss of important ecological and socioeconomic functions that communal land holds for local communities across the world. These risks are in particular severe for already marginalised groups such as women, pastoralists and forest-dependent communities. Our empirical analysis focusses on spatial data of LSLAs and communal lands in three countries with varying degrees of communal land recognition. In the case of Colombia, where communal lands are relatively well documented and protected, we identify overlaps and conflicts arising from deficient consultation processes, primarily linked to extractive industries. Similarly, Cambodia formalises communal lands, but the actual extent of collective titles remains limited, and prevalent social forestry schemes in the region provide only restricted land rights. This leaves local communities with far less and also less well protected land facing LSLAs. The Democratic Republic of the Congo with almost no effective safeguards to protect communal lands is surely the most problematic case, as our analysis suggests potential overlaps of LSLAs with close to one million hectares of communal land. Increasing the compliance of land policies with global frameworks but also exploiting upcoming due diligence regulations will be key mitigating the risks of LSLAs for communal land.
Methods: Narrative review plus spatial empirical analysis of LSLA and communal land data. Uses LandMark and Land Matrix geospatial datasets to calculate overlaps and proximity buffers (1, 10, 20 km) for Colombia, Cambodia, and the DRC.
Results: Colombia had 53,369 ha of overlap and 297,986 ha within 20 km; Cambodia had 43,150 ha overlap and about 1.7 million ha within 20 km; the DRC had up to close to 1 million ha of potential overlap, with 6.85 million ha within 20 km.
Conclusions: LSLAs pose severe socioeconomic and environmental risks to communal lands, especially where recognition and consultation are weak. Formalization and stronger VGGT/HREDD-aligned policies can reduce risk, but implementation and on-the-ground practice remain the main barrier.

Source: Digitalizing land administration: The geographies and temporalities of infrastructural promise
Abstract: Blockchain technology has been explored recently for digitalizing land administration in different parts of the world. It has been viewed as contributing to formalization of property rights in the Global South, and enhancing coordination of real estate markets in the Global North. It investigates the broader embeddedness of blockchain-based land registries in non-digital infrastructural modalities and the peopled infrastructures of informal networks. It argues that the abstraction of blockchain may obscure the complex layering of formal and informal, institutionalized and grassroots texture of property rights and claims to land. Results: The three cases show very different blockchain roles: Ghana remains largely planned/piloted, Georgia has published 1.5 million land titles on-chain, and Sweden has trialled blockchain since 2017 with expected faster conveyancing and lower costs. Across cases, blockchain is most effective where pre-existing digital infrastructure and legal support are strong.

Source: Attribute-based encryption for fine-grained access control of encrypted data
Abstract: As more sensitive data is shared and stored by third-party sites on the Internet, there will be a need to encrypt data stored at these sites. One drawback of encrypting data, is that it can be selectively shared only at a coarse-grained level (i.e., giving another party your private key). We develop a new cryptosystem for fine-grained sharing of encrypted data that we call Key-Policy Attribute-Based Encryption (KP-ABE). In our cryptosystem, ciphertexts are labeled with sets of attributes and private keys are associated with access structures that control which ciphertexts a user is able to decrypt. We demonstrate the applicability of our construction to sharing of audit-log information and broadcast encryption. Our construction supports delegation of private keys which subsumesHierarchical Identity-Based Encryption (HIBE). Copyright 2006 ACM.
Methods: New cryptosystem proposal: Key-Policy Attribute-Based Encryption (KP-ABE), where ciphertexts carry attribute sets and private keys encode access structures. The abstract gives no formal evaluation method.
Results: KP-ABE enables fine-grained decryption control, supports delegation of private keys, and subsumes Hierarchical Identity-Based Encryption (HIBE). It is presented as applicable to audit-log sharing and broadcast encryption.
Conclusions: The work concludes that attribute-based encryption can provide fine-grained access control for encrypted data stored on third-party sites. It argues this is better suited than coarse private-key sharing for sensitive Internet data.

Source: Blockchain for the future of sustainable supply chain management in Industry 4.0
Abstract: The objective of this study is to provide an overview of Blockchain technology and Industry 4.0 for advancing supply chains towards sustainability. First, extracted from the existing literature, we evaluate the capabilities of Industry 4.0 for sustainability under three main topics of (1) Internet of things (IoT)-enabled energy management in smart factories; (2) smart logistics and transportation; and (3) smart business models. We expand beyond Industry 4.0 with unfolding the capabilities that Blockchain offers for increasing sustainability, under four main areas: (1) design of incentive mechanisms and tokenization to promote consumer green behavior; (2) enhance visibility across the entire product lifecycle; (3) increase systems efficiency while decreasing development and operational costs; and (4) foster sustainability monitoring and reporting performance across supply chain networks. Furthermore, Blockchain technology capabilities for contributing to social and environmental sustainability, research gaps, adversary effects of Blockchain, and future research directions are discussed.
Methods: Narrative literature review using a standard four-step review method: define the unit of analysis, classify context, collect literature, and evaluate/interpret publications. Sources were journal articles, full conference papers, and books from Engineering Village, Inspec, Compendex, Knovel, NTIS, and GeoRef (1990â€“2019).
Results: The review identifies three Industry 4.0 sustainability themes (IoT energy management, green logistics/transportation, and new business models) and four blockchain sustainability capabilities (green-behavior incentives, product lifecycle visibility, lower costs/greater efficiency, and sustainability reporting). It also highlights research gaps and adverse effects of blockchain, especially scalability, energy use, and regulatory issues.
Conclusions: Blockchain and Industry 4.0 can support circular-economy and sustainability goals, but blockchain remains immature and its benefits depend on the underlying business model and governance. Future work should address performance indicators, data analytics, design strategies, case studies, and workforce issues.

Abstract: This study aims to investigate the barriers to the adoption of Blockchain Technology (BT) within the field of Construction Supply Chain Management (CSCM) by unravelling their interrelationships. In doing so, a Pythagorean fuzzy-set-based DEMATEL method to assess these barriers in a complex environment is proposed. The results of the study suggest that â€œmarket-based risksâ€, â€œhigh costs for maintaining sustainabilityâ€, and â€œusage in the underground economyâ€ are the most influential barriers to the adoption of BT in CSCM. Furthermore, the study identifies that â€œinadequate knowledge/employee trainingâ€, â€œcontractual riskâ€, and â€œscalability issuesâ€ play a pivotal role within the CSCM system. The reliability and validation of the obtained results were also shown using sensitivity analysis and the focus-group-discussion approach. The findings of this study provide valuable insights for stakeholders in the construction industry to design and implement effective measures to overcome the identified barriers to the adoption of BT in CSCM. By addressing these barriers, stakeholders can facilitate the adoption of BT, leading to more efficient and effective construction supply chain management practices.

Source: User-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance in blockchain adoption for land administration systems: A systematic literature review
Abstract: Blockchain technology has emerged as a disruptive force with the potential to support the securitisation of tenure in land administration systems (LAS). While previous research on the topic has placed considerable attention on the potential of adopting blockchain for improving LAS, limited attention has been placed on understanding the user-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance. To address this gap, this study conducted a systematic literature review on the user-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance influencing blockchain technology adoption for LAS. The analysis employs two complementary theoretical frameworks: the Multilevel Trust (MLT) framework to categorize trust factors, and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) to guide the analysis of acceptance factors. The results categorize the key factors influencing stakeholders' trust into three dimensions: trust in technology (data privacy and control, security), trust in administrative processes (traceability and transparency), and trust in institutions (regulation and legal compliance), while performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions emerge as the key factors that influence stakeholdersâ€™ acceptance. Drawing upon these findings, a conceptual framework was developed to illustrate the interrelationship between the trust and acceptance factors influencing stakeholdersâ€™ intention to either embrace or reject the adoption of blockchain for LAS. This research contributes to the literature on emerging technology adoption for LAS, which may help land administration stakeholders take suitable measures to address stakeholder concerns and thereby promote blockchain technology adoption.
Methods: Systematic literature review of 68 peer-reviewed articles selected from 1,520 records using PRISMA. Analysis was organized with the Multilevel Trust framework and UTAUT, with data extracted in Excel from abstracts and full texts.
Results: Trust factors clustered into trust in technology, institutions, and administrative processes, led by data privacy and control, security, traceability and transparency, and regulation/legal compliance. Acceptance was driven by performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions.

Source: Data-Availability-Aware Hybrid Storage Optimization in Permissioned Blockchains: A Multi-Objective Metaheuristic Approach
Abstract: Modern permissioned blockchain systems increasingly adopt hybrid data architectures in which critical metadata are anchored on-chain, while large or sensitive payloads are stored off-chain using infrastructures such as IPFS and cloud services. Although this paradigm improves scalability and cost efficiency, it introduces a coupled design challenge where latency, operational cost, and security must be balanced simultaneously. Existing Layer-2 and data-availability approaches primarily focus on throughput and verification, leaving data placement decisions in enterprise permissioned environments insufficiently explored. This paper formulates hybrid on-chain, IPFS, and cloud data placement as a multi-objective optimization problem that jointly encodes storage location, transaction execution mode, and key blockchain parameters, aiming to minimize latency and cost while maximizing integrity and resilience. To explore this high-dimensional design space without costly physical deployment, a digital-twin-based evaluation framework is proposed to approximate the performance, cost, and security behavior of a Fabric-class permissioned blockchain integrated with IPFS and cloud storage. The optimization problem is solved using NSGA-II, yielding a Pareto front that reveals fundamental trade-offs among hybrid configurations. The results demonstrate that hash-anchored off-chain storage consistently outperforms purely on-chain and purely off-chain strategies by reducing latency and cost while preserving strong integrity and replication guarantees. The proposed framework provides practical decision support for data-availability-aware permissioned blockchains in domains such as supply chains, healthcare, and disaster response.
Methods: Multi-objective optimization of hybrid on-chain, IPFS, and cloud data placement using NSGA-II. A digital-twin framework approximates the performance, cost, and security behavior of a Fabric-class permissioned blockchain.
Results: NSGA-II produced a Pareto front showing trade-offs among hybrid configurations. Hash-anchored off-chain storage outperformed purely on-chain and purely off-chain strategies by reducing latency and cost while preserving integrity and replication guarantees.
Conclusions: Data-availability-aware hybrid storage can improve permissioned blockchain design by balancing latency, cost, integrity, and resilience. The framework is positioned as decision support for enterprise deployments in supply chains, healthcare, and disaster response.

Source: Tokenizing the city: NFTs as tools for equitable urban governance and community-led planning
Abstract: Applying NFTs to urban planning offers revolutionary potential but raises serious equity concerns. Although NFTs are linked to digital art speculation, their underlying technology, decentralized ownership, smart contracts, and tamper-proof records could transform participatory planning, land-use management, and community asset stewardship. This article discusses how NFTs could decentralize planning power by enabling tokenized community land trusts, zoning-compliance automation, and neighborhood DAOs (Decentralized Autonomous Organizations). However, they also pose dangers, such as digital exclusion, environmental degradation from energy-hungry blockchains, and capture by technocratic elites. Mitigation is needed through hybrid digital-physical participation systems, public sector-led blockchain infrastructure, and equity-sensitive token design if these tools are to benefit the public interest. The article proposes a staged implementation approach, beginning with controlled pilots (e.g., NFT-tracked community benefit agreements) before scaling up to more advanced applications such as dynamic zoning regimes. Lastly, ethical use of NFTs in planning demands visionary public-sector leadership to avert the entrenchment of existing inequalities in the name of innovation. Planners must critically engage with this emerging technology not as eager consumers but as stewards shaping its trajectory toward more equitable, open, and democratic urban futures. The question is not whether NFTs will influence cities, but who will determine that influence and to what ends.

Source: Blockchain-Based Secure Cloud Data Management: A Novel Approach for Data Privacy and Integrity
Abstract: Due to its potential to increase trust, security, and transparency across numerous industries, decentralized apps and smart contracts are growing in popularity. A network of peer-to-peer computers called Inter Planetary File System (IPFS) enables decentralized content exchange and storage. As smart contracts allow for the automated and safe execution of established rules and logic, they can improve IPFS functionality when implemented on blockchain networks. This study compares the support for smart contracts on IPFS provided by various blockchain networks. The comparison comprises Polkadot, Binance Smart Chain, Solana, and Ethereum. When utilized to deploy and carry out smart contracts over IPFS, these networksâ€™ scalability, security, and transaction costs are the main subjects of the study. Despite having higher transaction costs, more established networks like Ethereum and Solana provide greater degrees of security and scalability. Although it has cheaper transaction costs than Ethereum and Solana, Binance Smart Chain is less secure. Although less mature and more sophisticated than Polkadot, it can handle numerous parallel chains and offers greater compatibility with other the use of blockchains.

Source: Application-layer integrity protection and temporal administrative control for centralized state registries: Implementation and evaluation
Abstract: Centralized state registries risk unauthorized database-layer modification and misuse of privileged access outside authorized working hours. We present a service-layer architecture combining temporal role-based access control (TRBAC)-inspired per-request restriction of privileged writes, deterministic record verification using a hash-based message authentication code with SHA-256 (HMAC-SHA-256) and an external secret, and optional hash-linked audit evidence. The Spring Boot/MySQL implementation was evaluated using single-thread and 1â€“32-worker benchmarks, a paired diagnostic experiment, and automated tampering and temporal-control tests. In the single-thread benchmark, FINGERPRINT, CHECKPOINT (K = 100), and STRICT incurred 174.9â€“200.3%, 68.6â€“77.2%, and 215.0â€“237.3% median overhead relative to STANDARD. HMAC_COMPUTE added 1.21â€“1.26 ms per successful update (59.1â€“60.4% overhead), isolating the required database re-read and 23-field HMAC computation. Under concurrency, FINGERPRINT reached 934.2 updates per second at 32 workers, CHECKPOINT peaked at 686.6 at four workers, and STRICT remained synchronization-bound near 300 before declining to 265.9 at 32 workers. Automated validation confirmed reproducible data_hash recomputation, configured CHECKPOINT batch persistence, exposure of the tested direct SQL modification of freq.nominal through a fingerprint mismatch when its normalized representation changed, detection of modification of retained checkpoint evidence, and per-request off-hours authority downgrade with conditional authentication restoration. The results define a tested operating envelope: unchained per-write evidence with FINGERPRINT, batched hash-linked evidence with CHECKPOINT, and a per-write global chain with STRICT, with distinct performance and synchronization costs. Same-database verification establishes retained-state consistency but not independent completeness or freshness after coordinated suffix removal or restoration of an older consistent snapshot.
Methods: Spring Boot/MySQL service-layer architecture combining TRBAC-inspired per-request temporal restriction, HMAC-SHA-256 record verification, and optional checkpoint-based audit evidence. Evaluated with single-thread and 1â€“32-worker benchmarks, diagnostic isolation, automated tampering tests, and temporal-control tests.
Results: FINGERPRINT incurred 174.9â€“200.3% median overhead, CHECKPOINT 68.6â€“77.2%, and STRICT 215.0â€“237.3% versus STANDARD; HMAC_COMPUTE added 1.21â€“1.26 ms per update. Under concurrency, FINGERPRINT reached 934.2 TPS at 32 workers, CHECKPOINT peaked at 686.6 TPS at 4 workers, and STRICT declined to 265.9 TPS at 32 workers.
Conclusions: The architecture provides deployable integrity assurance and temporal administrative control in centralized registries without blockchain. Same-database verification confirms retained-state consistency, but not independent completeness or freshness after suffix removal or older snapshot restoration.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical implementation-and-evaluation study of a prototype service-layer registry security architecture. Highest maturity demonstrated is controlled single-node test deployment with automated validation and institutional handover/acceptance, not operational production rollout.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation used benchmarks, paired diagnostic isolation, live-database integration tests, tampering tests, and focused request-filter tests. Evidence was quantitative (TPS, overhead, ms) and functional (successful/failed verification, checkpoint persistence, authority downgrade/restoration).

A service layer coordinates registry updates, server-side TRBAC filtering, HMAC generation, event logging, strict-chain state, and checkpoint batching.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Centralized state registries for legally binding records, especially radio-frequency allocation; the worked schema uses owner, site, and frequency records. The system protects registry updates and detects tampering in administrative record management.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses TRBAC-inspired per-request temporal downgrade, HMAC-SHA-256 with an external secret, optional hash chaining/checkpoints, and record re-reading for verification. Targets unauthorized database-layer modification, off-hours privileged misuse, audit-evidence manipulation, deletion/rollback, and key-compromise assumptions.

Source: Security risk and response analysis of typical application architecture of information and communication blockchain
Abstract: As the role of blockchain technology in various industries becomes more and more important, the technical limitations of its consensus mechanism, private key management and smart contracts are gradually emerging. However, security events such as blockchain platform applications are emerging one after another. As a new round of transformative power in the network era, it combines the blockchain with existing technologies to generate new formats and new models. Technology applications and existing cybersecurity regulatory policies have brought new challenges. This paper analyzes the typical application architecture of blockchain technology, and analyzes the security risks of blockchain application architecture from key layers such as storage layer, protocol layer, extension layer, and application layer. This article combines the DOC mechanism with IOT application scenarios to propose a blockchain-based confidential IOT service model (Beekeeper 1.0) that supports first-order homomorphic multiplication, and a blockchain-based confidential IOT service model that supports high-order homomorphic multiplication (Beekeeper 2.0), Beekeeper 2.0 significantly improves Beekeeper 1.0 in server capabilities, verification efficiency, verification key length, and device work diversity. This article finds that the chain code call delay basically increases with the increase in the transaction sending rate. When the transaction sending rate reaches 300TPS, the chain code calling delay only increases a little, and when the transaction sending rate reaches 300TPS, the success rate of the transaction on the chain increases. Finally, the average blockchain access delay increases with the increase in the transaction sending rate. The blockchain access delay is affected by less throughput, and the transaction success rate is stable at 98%.

Conclusions: Blockchain application architectures face rising security risks from consensus, private key management, smart contracts, and layered system design. The proposed Beekeeper models are presented as responses to confidential IoT security and efficiency needs.

Source: Asynchronous Tiered Federated Learning Storage Scheme Based on Blockchain and IPFS
Abstract: As is known, centralized federated learning faces risks of a single point of failure and privacy breaches, and blockchain-based federated learning frameworks can address these challenges to a certain extent in recent works. However, malicious clients may still illegally access the blockchain to upload malicious data or steal on-chain data. In addition, blockchain-based federated training suffers from a heavy storage burden and excessive network communication overhead. To address these issues, we propose an asynchronous, tiered federated learning storage scheme based on blockchain and IPFS. It manages the execution of federated learning tasks through smart contracts deployed on the blockchain, decentralizing the entire training process. Additionally, the scheme employs a secure and efficient blockchain-based asynchronous tiered architecture, integrating attribute-based access control technology for resource exchange between the clients and the blockchain network. It dynamically manages access control policies during training and adopts a hybrid data storage strategy combining blockchain and IPFS. Experiments with multiple sets of image classification tasks are conducted, indicating that the storage strategy used in this scheme saves nearly 50 percent of the communication overhead and significantly reduces the on-chain storage burden compared to the traditional blockchain-only storage strategy. In terms of training effectiveness, it maintains similar accuracy as centralized training and minimizes the probability of being attacked.
Methods: Proposed asynchronous tiered federated learning storage scheme using blockchain and IPFS, with smart contracts and attribute-based access control; evaluated on multiple image classification tasks.
Results: Storage strategy saves nearly 50% of communication overhead and significantly reduces on-chain storage burden versus blockchain-only storage. It maintains similar accuracy to centralized training and lowers attack probability.
Conclusions: The hybrid blockchain-IPFS design addresses storage and communication overhead while preserving training accuracy and improving security. It targets privacy and malicious-client risks in federated learning.

Source: Improving implementation of the Blockchain technology in real estate registration
Abstract: Difficulties are caused by the introduction of the Blockchain in the field of registration of rights to real estate and real estate turnover since this requires the establishment of a balance between public and private interests. The article proposes a set of measures, the implementation of which would improve the implementation of the Blockchain technology to modernize the registration of rights to real estate and real estate turnover. The article identified and characterized the vectors of modernization of real estate registration using the Blockchain have been identified and characterized. Source: BERE: Ensuring immutability and transparency with blockchain in real estate appraisal industry
Abstract: Real estate appraisal plays a pivotal role in various financial transactions and regulatory processes, necessitating the assurance of unalterable and transparent Real Estate Appraisal rePorts (REA_Ps). Authorized appraisal experts employ diverse methodologies to ascertain the market value of real estate properties, contributing to critical decisions in property transactions, loans, taxation, insurance, financial reporting, and lease calculations. The standardized format and jurisdiction-compliant methodologies used in official REA_Ps emphasize the need for their preservation in an unaltered state. Despite the importance of official REA_Ps, the potential for unauthorized alterations poses a significant challenge when stored in centralized databases. With its inherent tamper-proof nature, Blockchain (BC) technology emerges as an ideal solution to safeguard integrity of the REA_Ps. This study proposes a Blockchain-Enhanced Real Estate appraisal management framework, BERE , to ensure the immutability of REA_Ps and enhance appraisal process transparency. The proposed BERE framework fosters trust among stakeholders in the real estate appraisal sector. By securely storing REA_Ps authored by on-field appraisal experts on the BC, the method prevents unauthorized modifications and ensures the confidentiality of private data. Simulations employ a variety of measures, such as BC size, transaction verification time, CPU usage, and message overhead on transaction generation, to assess system performance. The results indicate that the BERE framework successfully maintains the accuracy and reliability of REA_Ps. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study showcasing a practical application of BC technology to demonstrate its ability to transform the appraisal process and inspire trust in the accuracy of REA_Ps.

Source: A survey on Ethereum pseudonymity: Techniques, challenges, and future directions
Abstract: Blockchain technology has emerged as a transformative force in various sectors, including finance, healthcare, supply chains, and intellectual property management. Beyond Bitcoin's role as a decentralized payment system, Ethereum represents a notable application of blockchain, featuring Smart Contract functionality that enables the development and execution of decentralized applications (DApps). A key feature of Ethereum, and public blockchains in general, is pseudonymity, typically achieved by using public keys as pseudonyms for users. Despite implementing several privacy-preserving techniques, the public recording of user activities on the blockchain allows various deanonymization methods that can profile users, reveal sensitive information, and potentially re-identify them. Most blockchains, such as Bitcoin, Litecoin, and Cardano, employ the Unspent Transaction Output (UTXO) model for accounting, which focuses on individual transactions and is susceptible to various deanonymization techniques. In contrast, Ethereum uses an account-based transaction model, integrating the concepts of accounts and wallets at the protocol level. This makes most UTXO-based deanonymization techniques ineffective for Ethereum. However, alternative methods with the potential to deanonymize Ethereum users have been proposed and developed. Privacy preservation techniques have been used to counteract deanonymization attempts; however, the challenges related to these techniques, their effectiveness and efficiency, and the trade-off between usability and protection levels remain areas for further exploration. This survey presents a comprehensive analysis of state-of-the-art privacy preservation along with deanonymization techniques in the blockchain and Ethereum ecosystems. This survey examines the intrinsic mechanisms supporting pseudonymity in Ethereum, providing a detailed assessment of the advantages and disadvantages of privacy preservation techniques, and suggests potential countermeasures against those deanonymization methods. It also discusses the implications arising from the intersection of DApps and data protection legislation, which is vital for ensuring the coexistence and advancement of groundbreaking blockchain capabilities and protecting user data.
Methods: Narrative survey of Ethereum pseudonymity, privacy-preserving techniques, deanonymization methods, and GDPR-related compliance issues. No formal search strategy or empirical study design is described.
Results: Identifies address clustering, transaction graph analysis, timing analysis, and off-chain data linkage as major deanonymization approaches on Ethereum. Reviews mixers, zk-SNARKs, SMPC, ABE, HE, differential privacy, and layer-2/off-chain methods as countermeasures, each with privacyâ€“scalability trade-offs.
Conclusions: Privacy on Ethereum requires balancing transparency, scalability, and GDPR compliance. Future work should focus on ZKP, HE, SMPC, rollups, cross-chain privacy frameworks, and better smart-contract privacy and legal guidance.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual/narrative survey and literature review on Ethereum privacy and deanonymization. Maturity is at the review and future-directions stage, with proposed countermeasures and no new system implementation.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Evidence is synthesized from prior literature, examples, and comparative discussion rather than new experiments. No quantitative benchmarking or prototype evaluation is reported.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Ethereum public permissionless blockchain with account-based transaction model, smart contracts, and EVM. Consensus is described generically as majority consensus, with PoW, PoS, DPoS, PoA, and PoH mentioned as common mechanisms.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Ethereum uses accounts, wallets, smart contracts written in Solidity, and the EVM. The paper also discusses mixers, ZKPs, SMPC, IPFS/Storj, off-chain storage, layer-2 rollups, state channels, and Plasma as complementary components.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: General blockchain and Ethereum DApps, with examples from finance, healthcare, supply chains, digital identity, NFTs, decentralized storage, and smart-city/location data. No single cadastral or land-registry use case is addressed.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Covers digital signatures, hash-linked blocks, Merkle trees, cryptographic keys, ZKPs, SMPC, ABE, HE, differential privacy, mixers, and ring signatures. Threats include deanonymization, privacy leakage, tampering, DDoS, Sybil, eclipse, 51% attacks, wallet attacks, and smart-contract vulnerabilities.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Discusses cross-chain interoperability, Layer-2 interactions, and data transfers across blockchains, but no formal standards such as LADM, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE are used. Mentions GDPR compliance and off-chain/on-chain coordination rather than schema-level standard integration.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Focuses on GDPR compliance, data controllers/processors, right to erasure, data minimization, and cross-border transfer rules. Proposes off-chain storage, encryption, privacy-by-design, and decentralized compliance mechanisms, but governance roles in DApps remain unresolved.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Main barriers are privacy leakage, scalability costs, gas fees, computational overhead, interoperability issues, and regulatory conflict with GDPR. Context is Ethereum and permissionless blockchains, with examples and countermeasures remaining largely conceptual.

Source: Trust and Transparency in IoT: The Role of Federated Learning and Blockchain
Abstract: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has transformed domains such as smart homes, healthcare, and industrial automation, while increasing concerns about security, privacy, and trust. Due to their decentralized structure and large-scale data generation, IoT systems are highly vulnerable to cyber threats, making transparency essential. This survey highlights Federated Learning (FL) and Blockchain as effective solutions. FL enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data, preserving privacy by exchanging only aggregated updates. Blockchain provides a distributed and immutable ledger that ensures transparent, verifiable, and tamper-resistant records. Together, they create a complementary framework where FL supports privacy-preserving intelligence and Blockchain ensures trust. The survey reviews their integration in IoT applications, examines existing research, and identifies key challenges such as scalability, computational overhead, and regulatory issues. It also outlines future research directions to support the development of secure, efficient, and trustworthy IoT systems. Furthermore, the work also surveys the system models, and experimental studies.
Methods: Narrative survey of peer-reviewed FL and blockchain research in IoT, organized into FL, blockchain, integration, discussion, and future work sections. No formal search strategy or systematic review protocol is described.
Results: The paper synthesizes that FL preserves privacy by keeping raw IoT data local, while blockchain adds immutable, auditable trust for model updates and device identities. It highlights recurring challenges of scalability, computational overhead, latency, and regulatory compliance, and summarizes reported defenses with high attack-detection/accuracy results in selected studies.
Conclusions: FL and blockchain are presented as complementary for trustworthy, privacy-preserving IoT, but efficient consensus, incentive/reputation design, adversarial robustness, and privacy-preserving compliance remain unresolved. Main limitations are the prototype/simulation gap and heterogeneity of IoT devices.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual/narrative survey with synthesis of academic system models, conceptual frameworks, and experimental studies. Highest maturity discussed is prototype/testbed and simulation; the paper states it does not cover large-scale industrial deployments or operational systems.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Literature-based review and critical synthesis, with comparisons of selected quantitative studies and their reported metrics. Evidence includes simulation-based results, some prototype/testbed-style validations, and qualitative discussion; no new experiment is performed.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain is described as a decentralized immutable ledger with smart contracts and consensus; specific platforms are not named for the main framework. The discussion mentions PoW, PoS, PoA, DAG-based ledgers, sharding, and permissioned/hybrid architectures for IoT.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: IoT devices collect data locally, FL performs local training and FedAvg aggregation, and blockchain stores device identities, validated updates, and global model records. Smart contracts, cryptographic signatures, secure aggregation, and off-chain storage are used to verify, log, and control exchange.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: IoT data across smart homes, healthcare, smart cities, smart farming, industrial IoT, autonomous vehicles, and supply chains. The focus is on privacy-preserving learning, secure data exchange, device authentication, provenance, and auditable model-update logging.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Mechanisms include hashing, cryptographic links, digital signatures, PKI-style keys/certificates, encryption, access control, smart contracts, secure aggregation, differential privacy, secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, and zero-knowledge proofs. Threats covered include tampering, unauthorized access, identity fraud, data/model poisoning, Sybil attacks, inference attacks, key/privacy leakage, and single points of failure.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Interoperability is discussed mainly through generic gateways/bridges and standards such as IEEE P2413, IEEE P2958, and W3C VC. These are proposed for cross-domain identity, trust, and secure data exchange, but no detailed implementation or version-specific integration is described.

Governance is discussed through decentralized authentication, smart-contract enforcement, permissioned/off-chain designs, and reputation or approval mechanisms, but no concrete legal implementation is established.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Main barriers are scalability, computational overhead, latency, energy use, heterogeneity, interoperability, privacy/regulatory conflict, and communication bottlenecks. The target context is IoT and FL-Blockchain systems, with the paper emphasizing simulation/testbed evidence rather than operational deployment.

Gaps include limited real-world validation, sparse latency/energy evaluation, weak coverage of collusion/backdoor attacks, and insufficient cross-domain scalability testing.

Source: Traceability for privacy: A foundational pillar for an effective and competitive EU digital rulebook
Abstract: The European Union has established a comprehensive digital rulebook (GDPR, DSA, DMA, DGA, Data Act, AI Act), to develop a digital single market that respects fundamental rights. An investigation into this legal framework, however, reveals significant barriers to its effectiveness, including inconsistent enforcement, "gold-plating," and a burdensome compliance landscape for SMEs. This paper's analysis establishes that a standardized, interoperable, and privacy-preserving traceability layer is a critical infrastructural prerequisite to bridge the gap between legal principles and technical enforceability. Traceability, defined as the ability to document the data lifecycle and link processing to a verifiable legal basis, provides the necessary foundation for accountability, a gap in the institutional enforcement system. This paper conducts a legal-technical analysis, first establishing through a systematic review that traceability is a foundational requirement across the EU digital rulebook. Second, it compares technical architectures based on blockchains, attestations (OTrace) and cryptographic claims (W3C Verifiable Credentials). The analysis concludes that while public blockchains present GDPR compliance paradoxes and require workarounds, a careful merger of OTrace and VCs, and an operational framework synthesizing the EU Digital Identity Wallet and Data Governance Act data intermediaries offers a pragmatic, legally-aligned solution to the current institutional deficit. Finally, it connects this "EU-Trace" model to the EuroStack's strategic vision, concluding that a risk-based mandate for traceability can mitigate the negative effects of regulatory fragmentation by harmonizing the mechanism of compliance, thereby enhancing competitiveness for a transparent, accountable digital Europe.
Methods: Legal-technical analysis with a systematic review of the EU digital rulebook, plus a comparative assessment of blockchain, attestation (OTrace), and W3C Verifiable Credentials architectures. Uses a hypothetical multi-actor AI-health data supply chain as the evaluation scenario.
Results: Traceability is argued to be a foundational requirement across GDPR, DMA, DSA, DGA, Data Act, and AI Act. The comparative analysis finds public blockchains poorly fit for GDPR compliance, while a hybrid of Verifiable Credentials and attestation-based logging is the strongest overall fit.
Conclusions: EU-Trace is proposed as a risk-based, privacy-preserving traceability layer to improve accountability, interoperability, and competitiveness in the EU digital rulebook. The paper recommends formal recognition of traceability, standardized VC vocabularies, and further research on governance and AI lifecycle use.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual/legal-technical comparative paper proposing the EU-Trace architecture. Maturity is at design/prototype concept level, not implemented or field-tested.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is by legal analysis and comparative architecture assessment, using regulatory requirements from EU law as criteria. Evidence is qualitative and conceptual, with no experimental implementation or quantitative benchmarking.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain is treated as a candidate traceability architecture, mainly public/permissionless versus private/permissioned consortium chains. It is described as a decentralized distributed ledger with cryptographic consensus, but public chains are judged unsuitable and workarounds rely on off-chain storage and on-chain hashes.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: EU-Trace combines W3C Verifiable Credentials in the EUDI Wallet for authorization with a DGA-regulated Traceability Agent for delegated logging. The Agent stores and receives attestations; optional backends may use traditional databases or permissioned blockchain, with encrypted logs and off-chain handling of sensitive details.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: EU digital rulebook compliance for personal data traceability across privacy, platform governance, data sharing, and AI systems. The main use case is a multi-actor health/AI supply chain, including hospital data, consent, IoT telemetry, ad transparency, data intermediaries, and AI training/operational logs.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses cryptographic signatures, immutable logs, hashes, selective disclosure, encryption, and cryptographically verifiable credentials. Addresses tampering, weak accountability, privacy leakage, surveillance risk, unauthorized data use, and auditability gaps; blockchain privacy paradoxes are noted.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Strong emphasis on standardized, machine-readable, cross-border interoperability via the EUDI Wallet, eIDAS 2.0, W3C Verifiable Credentials, and DGA data intermediaries. The paper also calls for standardized vocabularies and profiles from W3C and ETSI.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Grounded in GDPR, DMA, DSA, DGA, Data Act, and AI Act, with traceability framed as evidence of accountability and compliance. Governance is assigned to DGA-regulated Data Intermediaries and supervisory authorities, with a proposed risk-based mandate and judicial-warrant limits for secondary access.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include inconsistent enforcement, gold-plating, SME burden, scalability limits, technical expertise gaps, privacy concerns, and fragmented national rules. Deployment context is the EU, with EU-Trace still conceptual and dependent on wider EUDI Wallet adoption and viable Traceability Agent business models.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation criteria are legal fit, scalability, interoperability, privacy, accountability, enforcement harmonization, and ability to handle high-volume logging. The paper identifies open gaps in governance models, wallet adoption, Traceability Agent sustainability, and extension to AI lifecycle governance.

Source: Hybrid AI-IoT-Blockchain frameworks for energy-efficient smart homes: a multidimensional review of technologies, policies, and socioeconomic implications
Abstract: The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and Blockchain technologies is reshaping residential energy management through predictive optimization, decentralized governance, and secure peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions. This review synthesizes many studies using an enhanced Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-guided methodology that incorporates structured quality appraisal, deployment classification, and evidence synthesis. Unlike prior technology-focused surveys, the study integrates technical performance, regulatory preparedness, and socioeconomic feasibility within a unified socio-technical framework. Evidence from validated experiments and pilot deployments indicates that AI-enabled demand response and predictive control can reduce household energy consumption under context-specific conditions. At the same time, blockchain-based settlement improves transparency but introduces measurable computational overhead. To evaluate sustainability trade-offs, the review benchmarks consensus mechanisms and compares permissioned and public ledgers with respect to energy footprint, latency, and residential suitability. It further examines real-world deployments, technology readiness levels, explainable and privacy-preserving AI approaches, and emerging business models such as Energy-as-a-Service and community microgrids. These insights support progress toward SDG 7, SDG 11, and SDG 13 by enabling efficient, transparent, and low-carbon residential energy systems, while highlighting the need for lightweight architectures, federated intelligence, and adaptive regulatory frameworks for scalable implementation.
Methods: PRISMA-guided systematic literature review with structured quality appraisal, bias assessment, TRL categorization, and quantitative evidence synthesis. Searches covered Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect for 2018â€“Sep 2025; 112 studies were retained.
Results: AI-enabled demand response and predictive control reduced household energy consumption in validated experiments and pilot deployments, while blockchain settlement improved transparency but added computational overhead. Permissioned ledgers generally outperformed public ledgers on energy footprint and latency.
Conclusions: Hybrid AI-IoT-Blockchain smart homes have strong potential, but scalable deployment depends on lightweight architectures, interoperable standards, privacy compliance, and adaptive regulation. The review frames them as socio-technical systems rather than purely technical innovations.
Study Classification and Maturity: Multidimensional systematic review of AI-IoT-Blockchain smart-home energy systems. Maturity spans conceptual models (TRL 2â€“3), simulation (TRL 4â€“5), pilots (TRL 6â€“7), and limited operational deployments (TRL 8â€“9), with most studies remaining at TRL 3â€“6.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is based on literature synthesis plus stratification by simulation, laboratory, pilot, and field deployments. Evidence includes quantitative metrics such as energy savings, latency, throughput, costs, and TRL, alongside policy/economic analyses.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain is used as a decentralized trust layer for P2P energy trading, smart metering, and settlement. Public Ethereum-type networks and private/permissioned Hyperledger Fabric-type systems are compared, with consensus mechanisms including PoS, DPoS, PBFT, and PoA.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Layered smart-home stack: IoT sensing/actuation at perception, AI at edge/cloud for prediction and control, and blockchain for secure transaction logging and smart contracts. Communication uses Zigbee, Z-Wave, MQTT, Wi-Fi, and BLE; federated learning keeps raw data local.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Residential smart-home energy management, including HVAC optimization, appliance scheduling, demand response, renewable integration, smart metering, and P2P energy trading in community microgrids. The focus is on household- and small-scale residential systems.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Security relies on immutable ledgers, decentralized trust, smart contracts, regulated access in permissioned systems, and privacy-preserving AI. Threats addressed include tampering, unauthorized access, privacy leakage, and fraud mitigation; key concerns also include cybersecurity and surveillance.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Interoperability is a major issue because device ecosystems lack coherent standards. The paper cites oneM2M, OpenHAB, and Matter, and calls for interoperable communication frameworks, shared data ontologies, and standardized benchmarking datasets.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Governance covers data ownership, consent, retention, liability, regulatory compliance, and blockchain immutability versus privacy law. The paper proposes off-chain PII storage, revocable encryption keys, permissioned ledgers, decentralized identifiers, and regulatory sandboxes.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include scalability, latency, interoperability, high installation cost, privacy concerns, regulatory ambiguity, and low digital literacy. Deployment is mostly at simulation, pilot, or testbed level in residential and community microgrid settings, with limited commercial rollout.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Key criteria are energy footprint, latency, throughput, transaction cost, scalability, privacy, and TRL. Major gaps are inconsistent validation protocols, scarce long-term field evidence, limited economic modeling, and insufficient standardized metrics for cross-study comparison.

Source: Blockchain technology and privacy regulation: Reviewing frictions and synthesizing opportunities
Abstract: As the application of Blockchain Technology (BCT) grows across several industries, its inherent decentralized and immutable nature raises some conflicting issues concerning privacy regulation. The enforcement of privacy regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) exemplifies these challenges, as certain stringent privacy requirements within GDPR may conflict with BCT's features. However, little attention is given to such critical issues. This study draws on the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) theoretical lens as a mechanism to unfold the issue. The current research focuses on exploring the tensions and the opportunities for synergy through the lens of TOE to prevent privacy regulatory compliance failure. We analyzed 71 multidisciplinary research studies that highlight the areas of friction and present a unifying structure for research synthesis. In response to the identified areas of friction and potential opportunities for coexistence, we formulate nine research propositions centered around six prominent and contentious data privacy and protection requirements within the GDPR. This research contributes to the broader discourse on privacy regulatory-compliant blockchain-based solutions by providing a theoretical foundation for future investigation into this critical area. The study suggests that reconciling BCT and privacy regulation requirements will unlock BCT's full potential, creating a secure, privacy-conscious technology infrastructure and offering practical implications and insights for policymakers.
Methods: Systematic review and synthesis of multidisciplinary literature using PRISMA and the TOE framework. The authors searched 10 databases and screened 3,061 records, yielding 71 studies published from May 2016 to April 2023.
Results: The review identifies major frictions around pseudonymization, data protection, interoperability, data control, consent, right to erasure, data portability, auditability, and transparency. It also highlights opportunities from smart contracts, zero-knowledge proofs, decentralized identity, off-chain storage, and permissioned blockchains.
Conclusions: BCT and GDPR are not inherently incompatible; the main issue is how blockchain is implemented relative to privacy requirements. The paper concludes that reconciling them can support a secure, privacy-conscious digital infrastructure and provides a theoretical foundation for future research.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual/systematic review and synthesis article, not an empirical implementation study. Maturity is at the conceptual proposal stage, with nine research propositions and no deployed system.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is through literature review and thematic synthesis rather than experiments or case studies. Evidence is qualitative and conceptual, based on 71 multidisciplinary studies and TOE-based classification.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Platform is generic blockchain technology, discussed across permissioned and permissionless designs rather than a specific implementation. Architecture is decentralized, immutable, cryptography-based, and consensus-driven, with public blockchains and private/permissioned variants considered.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: No implemented technical stack is described. The paper discusses off-chain databases, smart contracts, zero-knowledge proofs, decentralized identity, and cryptographic references to support GDPR-compliant blockchain designs.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: General blockchain use cases under privacy regulation, not a land/real-estate domain. The focus is on personal data processing, consent management, data access, erasure, portability, and breach notification under GDPR.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Mechanisms include cryptography, hashing, encryption, access control, smart contracts, zero-knowledge proofs, pseudonymization, and decentralized identity. Threats discussed include unauthorized access, privacy leakage, tampering, identity theft, data breaches, and non-compliance with erasure and consent requirements.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Interoperability is discussed as a compliance challenge, but no formal standards integration is described. The paper refers to blockchain platforms interacting with existing systems and mentions GDPR Recital 68, not LADM, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, or GIS.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Focuses on GDPR, including data controllers/processors, privacy by design, consent, erasure, portability, breach notification, and accountability. It proposes governance measures such as privacy impact assessments, regulatory sandboxes, data protection officers, and cross-border regulatory coordination.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include immutability, transparency, interoperability limits, data minimization conflicts, consent management difficulty, legal uncertainty, and operational friction. The context is GDPR-regulated blockchain adoption across general industries; the paper is review-based rather than pilot- or field-deployed.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation criteria discussed include privacy, security, interoperability, auditability, scalability, efficiency, and compliance, but no measured performance metrics are reported. Research gaps include lack of primary empirical studies, limited platform-specific analysis, and need for testing off-chain storage, dynamic consent, and breach-notification designs.

Source: MyDigitalHealth: Rethinking the health data management
Abstract: Background: The rapid expansion of digital health technologies â€“ including electronic health records (EHRs), wearable devices, and mobile applications â€“ has generated vast amounts of heterogeneous clinical data. However, current health information systems remain fragmented, poorly interoperable, and vulnerable to security breaches. These limitations hinder effective clinical decision-making, data integration, and patient autonomy. Objective: This study introduces the MyDigitalHealth (MDH) model, a patient-centric framework designed to enable secure, interoperable, and intelligent health data management. MDH aims to unify distributed clinical data sources through decentralized technologies, enforce granular consent mechanisms, and support AI-driven analytics for real-time and predictive healthcare applications. Methods: MDH employs blockchain technology and end-to-end encryption to ensure data privacy and security. The system supports granular consent management, real-time analytics, and decentralized data storage. Semantic interoperability is achieved through a domain ontology that is aligned with the HL7 FHIR and OpenEHR standards. Blockchain simulations were conducted to evaluate security and scalability. For predictive analytics, we developed and tested multimodal survival models that incorporate both structured and unstructured data. Results: MDH demonstrated effective semantic interoperability, enabling temporal clinical queries across decentralized environments. Blockchain simulations confirmed a trade-off between block size and propagation delay, supporting the secure and scalable storage of encrypted health records. In predictive modeling, our multimodal survival model, Multimodal DynamicDeepHit, achieved a concordance index (C-index) of 0.742, substantially outperforming the unimodal DynamicDeepHit baseline (C-index: 0.584). Conclusion: The MDH model offers a viable solution for secure, interoperable, and intelligent clinical data management. Its integration of blockchain, semantic standards, and multimodal AI supports real-time analytics and enhances predictive performance. These results highlight MDHâ€™s potential for real-world deployment in distributed, AI-driven healthcare systems.
Methods: Design-and-evaluation paper proposing the MDH architecture. It combines semantic ontology construction, blockchain simulation with SimBlock, and multimodal survival modeling tested on 1,815 retrospective COVID-19 records.
Results: The multimodal DynamicDeepHit achieved C-index 0.742 versus 0.584 for DynamicDeepHit; another setting showed 0.695 Â± 0.01 versus 0.666 Â± 0.02. Blockchain simulation showed propagation delay increased with block size, while larger blocks improved storage capacity.

Source: Distributed Ledger Technology-based land transaction system with trusted nodes consensus mechanism
Abstract: Blockchain technology is an emerging solution to various financial applications that require a secure and tamper-proof transactions system. One such application is the land registry. Management of transactions for land registration is a tedious task. It is highly insecure and subject to forgery land records, Issues in verification, mediators, etc. This article presents a scalable and novel property/land registration framework based on blockchain technology. The transparent and immutable nature of blockchain technology makes it reliable for intrusive and fraudulent land registration activities. The framework uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), a Peer-to-Peer (P2P) swarm network. It allows the sharing and storing of data in an efficient, decentralized, and transparent manner. This article also proposes a Trusted Node Consensus Algorithm (TNCA) based on the miners' trust value that minimizes the computational overhead of broadcasting the new block. The proposed approach - trusted node consensus algorithm requires lesser time to add the block into the blockchain, and message exchange per consensus is 58.94% lesser than the traditional Proof-of-Work (PoW) approach and 26.44% lesser time than the existing load-balanced method.
Methods: Proposed blockchain-based land/property transaction framework built on IPFS and a trust value-based consensus algorithm (TNCA). Performance evaluation used simulations comparing TNCA with PoW, PoS, DPoS, and a load-based trust approach.
Results: TNCA reduced message exchange per consensus by 58.94% versus PoW and reduced execution time by 67.59% versus PoW, 61.65% versus PoS, 47.99% versus DPoS, and 26.44% versus the load-based method. Communication overhead for the complete process was reduced by about 60%.
Conclusions: The authors conclude the framework is scalable, secure, and suitable for real-time land/property registration. They note limitations including lack of a generic uniform blockchain architecture and growing storage/search burden as transactions increase.

Abstract: With the increasing popularity of the Internet of things (IoT) and giving the end users the opportunity of collecting and analyzing the data by these IoT devices give rise to ultimate privacy concern and is attracting significant attention nowadays. These IoT devices may contain highly sensitive data and data sharing processes which may lead to security and privacy concerns. To surmount these issues, the interaction of IoT with blockchain for a secure transaction is accepted as a candidate solution. However, the innate behavior of blockchain containing complex mathematical proofs and consensus protocol requires high computational power making it less favorable for IoT devices to be connected with. Motivated by a private by-design framework and emphasizing greater control and setting of privacy preferences by the data owner, this paper complements our previous work on privacy preservation in IoT networks. In this paper, we design and propound a complete blockchain-based privacy-preserving framework by deploying service-oriented layers concepts and low computation cryptography, and a less complex consensus protocol to address the privacy concern. Moreover, this paper will unravel the complete end-to-end architecture of IoT-based blockchain purposely build for secure transactions in IoT networks. Security analysis is conducted using AVISPA tool to show that the proposed algorithms attain the desired security goals. This is followed by extensive simulation experiments and ultimate output results cultivating it much favorably for the deployment of IoT applications in real life.
Methods: Design and implementation of a consortium-blockchain IoT privacy framework on Quorum, organized into registration, authentication, privacy-enforcement, and transaction layers. Evaluated with AVISPA/SPAN security analysis and Chainhammer simulations on a Quorum testbed.
Results: RAFT outperformed IBFT and PoA in throughput and latency; the best reported throughput was 134.1 TPS for 5,000 transactions in sequential mode and 127.5 TPS for 2,000 transactions in multi-threaded mode. Lowest latency was 32.20 s for 10,000 transactions (sequential) and 24.50 s for 7,000 transactions (multi-threaded) with RAFT.
Conclusions: A private-by-design framework using Quorum, low-complexity consensus, and low-computation cryptography can support IoT privacy-preserving transactions. The authors propose future work on MUD-based restrictions and grouping streams with similar privacy preferences to improve performance.

Source: A lightweight UAV authentication scheme in blockchain-assisted fog networks
Abstract: With the widespread application of drone technology in intelligent transportation, post-disaster rescue and other fields, users have higher and higher requirements for the real-time and security of drone networks, so fog node-assisted Internet has emerged. Traditional UAV authentication schemes mostly use ground control stations to assist in authentication. However, fog nodes have more security issues than ground control stations, and existing identity authentication schemes are no longer applicable to fog node networks. In order to solve the above problems, we propose a lightweight identity mutual authentication scheme and introduce blockchain technology to solve the security problems of fog nodes. Our scheme is divided into two parts: (1) drones and fog nodes realize identity mutual authentication and establish secure session to ensure that drones safely use fog nodes for auxiliary functions such as task offloading; (2) mobile users realize identity authentication with the assistance of fog nodes and access the required drone sensor data. In addition, we conduct formal and informal security analysis of our method and use the Validation Tool for Internet Security Protocols and Applications (AVISPA) to prove the resilience of our scheme to various attacks. Comparative experiments with mainstream authentication schemes show that our scheme has greater advantages in terms of computational consumption, communication overhead and security features.

Results: AVISPA OFMC and CL-ATSE both returned SAFE, indicating no feasible attacks under the modeled conditions. Experiments report 23.511 ms computational overhead, 1632-bit communication cost, and 50-node latency reductions of 50.97%, 36.67%, 59.86%, and 41.01% versus four baselines.

Abstract: Blockchain-based platforms, particularly those based on permissioned blockchain, are increasingly popular in a broad range of settings. Source: Securing Land Registration using Blockchain
Abstract: The current land registration process involves a lot of vulnerabilities and people uses it to cheat the common people and the government. This paper discusses about a secure land registry implemented using blockchain which works on the basis of majority consensus. By implementing the land registry in blockchain, the security issue is resolved to a great extent. The hash value calculated for each block will be unique as it is linked to the hash of the previous block. The algorithm that is used for hashing is SHA256. Along with SHA256, Proof Of Work(PoW) algorithm is also used which makes the information related to each transaction more secure. Message digest that is generated for each block is of fixed size and each hash represents a complete set of transaction within a given block. The proposed land registry blockchain network consists of 12 nodes which calculates the proof of work. Nodes are responsible for verifying a transaction, mining a new block and adding the new block to the blockchain. A total of 200 land transactions are recorded using the blockchain methodology which offers a tamper proof and updated version of land registry. Elliptic curve cryptographic algorithm is used for signature generation which is used for verifying whether the transaction is signed by the owner or not. Merkle tree is used for linking the transactions using hash and in turn reduces the disk usage. The proposed implementation of land registry using blockchain thus offers a 99% reduction in manual effort spent in record keeping.
Methods: Prototype blockchain land registry with 12 nodes and 200 land transactions, using majority consensus, SHA-256 hashing, PoW, ECC signatures, and Merkle trees.
Results: The system is described as tamper-proof and updated, with a 99% reduction in manual effort for record keeping.
Conclusions: Blockchain is presented as a way to greatly improve land-registration security and reduce manual record-keeping effort.

Merging these two techniques have the potential to create a Fit-For-Purpose land administration framework that would meet land administration requirements while improving transparency. Source: Land Administration Standardization for the integration of cultural heritage in land use policies
Abstract: The understanding of the cultural space is vital for the implementation of successful integrated land use policies. While most countries have their own strategy for the protection of their cultural heritage, implied by the state or international organizations - UNESCO and the European Union - yet, there is a long way until they adopt a standardized modeling approach for the management of their cultural heritage. Nowadays, there is a great deal of interest in the digital documentation and visualization of the cultural objects, together with the quest for new technologies for efficient management. As a result, the utilization of international standards and models for land administration is in the forefront. In this paper, the utilization of standardized modeling and more specifically the Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) is examined, as a basic tool for the development of spatial infrastructure for the archeological space, in other words the immovable cultural heritage of Greece. The LADM (approved as an official International Standard on 1st December 2012) defines terminology for land administration and can include the identification and quantification of the various rights, restrictions and responsibilities (RRRs) that appear in the public or private properties with cultural interest, the detailed description of the spatial information of these properties, the extended representation of their spatial information on three dimensions and finally the adoption of good practices offered by the process of standardization. The interoperability of the systems in the land administration domain through the standardization process is another challenge that this paper aims to reach.
Methods: Conceptual paper using the LADM to model immovable cultural heritage in Greece and to compare it with the Hellenic Cadastre and Hellenic Archaeological Cadastre. The analysis is organized around cultural-space characteristics, international land administration standards, and a proposed interoperability schema.
Results: The paper proposes a LADM-based legal and spatial profile for Greek archaeological parcels, including RRRs, ownership status, and 2D/3D representation. It argues this can improve interoperability between cadastre and cultural-heritage registries and support integrated land-use policies.
Conclusions: Cultural heritage should be integrated into land management, but few countries have done so in national LASs. The proposed standardization approach for Greece could improve interoperability and sustainable land-use policy, but remains a conceptual attempt aligned with the ongoing cadastre project.

Source: Supporting land data integration and standardization through the LADM standard: Case of Morocco's country profile MA-LADM
Abstract: The land sector in Morocco exhibits significant diversity of land status, stakeholders, administration functions, and methods. A number of public and private parties involved in land administration use a combination of administrative, technical, and legislative management instruments as well as both paper-based and digitized land information systems. These indicate the important social and economic value of Moroccan land and real estate for owners, users, and public agencies. This paper presents the modeling of the Moroccan land administration domain according to a specific ontological model of land governance, and the derivation of a country profile model MA-LADM from the base standard Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) ISO 19152: 2012. The profile aims to provide a common terminology for Moroccan land administration, to allow a shared description of different formal or informal practices and procedures, to integrate the various systems into force, and to allow land administration information to be combined from different sources. The profile's components originate totally or partially from the original elements of LADM or a specialized version that matches existing elements in Moroccan land models to facilitate comprehensive integration. This model investigates the three LADM packages: Party, Administrative and Spatial Unit, as well as the Surveying and Representation Subpackage. The 2d and 3d representations of spatial units are studied to support the Moroccan cadastral practices using LADM.
Methods: Conceptual modeling study deriving the MA-LADM country profile from ISO 19152:2012. It combines analysis of Moroccan land administration practices with LADM package-based modeling and 2D/3D spatial representation review.
Results: MA-LADM defines a Moroccan country profile with specialized classes for formal/informal rights, restrictions, responsibilities, parties, and 2D/3D spatial units. The model supports integrating fragmented land data sources and reports a 3D parcel example where area increases from 75Ha18A62Ca to 79Ha95A59Ca (+6%).
Conclusions: LADM can unify Moroccan land administration concepts and improve 2D/3D spatial accuracy and archival robustness. Further work is needed for practical implementation in land administration systems and databases.

Source: A roadmap to adopt the Land Administration Domain Model in cadastral information systems
Abstract: With the introduction of the Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) as an International Standard (ISO 19152), land administration organisations worldwide are considering the adoption of this standard into their current processes and cadastral information systems. Although LADM is a data standard, its adoption can have significant impacts on the process of managing cadastral information. These impacts include the influence on existing institutions and their operations, the description of cadastral information, the organisation of data in cadastral databases and the knowledge and capacity of human resources utilising and managing cadastral information. Therefore, the adoption of the LADM requires a holistic approach that considers the LADM not only as a data model for cadastral information, but also as a cornerstone in systems of land administration. This paper aims to introduce a LADM implementation roadmap including important factors that can be used by land administration organisations when adopting the LADM. The paper methodology presents this roadmap using two case studies, the first in Victoria, Australia and the second in Belize, Central America. Using these case studies, this paper analyses the potential impact of the LADM adoption in a jurisdiction with an established cadastral information system (CIS) and in a jurisdiction that is in the process of establishing a CIS. These factors include consideration of organisational motivation, institutional arrangements, information interpretation, information organisation, involvement in the LADM governance and capacity building.
Methods: Conceptual roadmap paper using two case studies: Victoria, Australia and Belize. The authors apply a six-stage, top-down adoption framework to analyse technical and non-technical factors for LADM implementation.
Results: The roadmap identifies organizational motivation, institutional arrangements, information interpretation, data organization, governance, and capacity building as key adoption factors. Belize had proven data mappings and an operational landfolio-based system; Victoria faced greater complexity from many stakeholders and established services.
Conclusions: LADM adoption requires a holistic, non-technical and technical roadmap rather than a data-model-only approach. Adoption is easier in newer CIS settings like Belize, while mature systems like Victoria need stronger justification, stakeholder engagement, and capacity building.

Maturity ranges from established operational CIS in Victoria to a newly established, partially deployed landfolio-based system in Belize.

Belize uses the landfolio suite with separate Registry and ESRI geodatabase Cadastre databases linked by common keys such as parcel number.
