Source: An adaptive IOTA-based smart-contract framework for secure and scalable information extraction in WSN-based IoT
Abstract: Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are a core component of the Internet of Things (IoT), but they still face challenges in processing heterogeneous data, coordinating distributed nodes, and maintaining timely and verifiable operation. This paper proposes an adaptive IOTA-based smart-contract framework for secure and scalable information extraction in WSNâ€“IoT systems. The framework uses a three-layer architecture with event-driven and time-driven execution modes, a deterministic state-aware controller for mode switching, DAG-based primary and secondary cluster-head selection, and mobile-agent collection from selected cluster heads. The framework is evaluated through WSN-side simulations of the adaptive-control, clustering, and mobile-agent components, while the ledger-facing workflow is demonstrated through an IOTA EVM proof of concept using encrypted local content storage and on-chain content-reference anchoring. At 150 nodes, event-driven execution achieves a 74.11% completion ratio, whereas the time-driven and adaptive modes maintain 100% completion. The adaptive mode completes 4424.70 operations per workload minute, 34.94% more than event-driven execution, and achieves a mean paired per-run latency reduction of 6.73% relative to fixed time-driven execution, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.80â€“10.65%. The reported performance results exclude cryptographic processing, JSON-RPC communication, EVM execution, transaction inclusion, ledger confirmation, and native IOTA Streams publication.
Methods: Three-layer WSNâ€“IoT architecture with event-driven/time-driven execution, a deterministic state-aware controller, DAG-based primary/secondary cluster-head selection, and mobile-agent collection. Evaluated by WSN-side simulations plus an IOTA EVM proof of concept with encrypted local JSONL storage and on-chain content-reference anchoring.
Results: At 150 nodes, event-driven execution completed 74.11% of workloads, while time-driven and adaptive modes completed 100%. Adaptive mode achieved 4424.70 operations/minute, 34.94% more than event-driven execution, and reduced mean latency by 6.73% versus fixed time-driven execution.
Conclusions: The framework improves WSN-side extraction by switching between event-driven responsiveness and time-driven capacity, but results are limited to the evaluated workloads and simulation assumptions. Native IOTA Streams was not implemented, and future work targets Streams integration, physical/multi-host testbeds, and broader sensitivity analysis.

Evaluation Method and Evidence: WSN-side simulations evaluated adaptive control, clustering, mobility, and mobile-agent collection using paired runs and 95% Student-t confidence intervals. A separate IOTA EVM Testnet proof of concept validated encrypted local storage, contract interaction, and content-reference anchoring; evidence is mainly quantitative simulation with limited functional proof-of-concept validation.

WSN sensing, clustering, and mobile-agent collection are off-chain; the contract records controller state, mode transitions, publication references, and audit events.

Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses signatures, authenticated encryption, freshness validation, ledger anchoring, role-separated keys, revocation/epoch tracking, and bounded SQLite-based replay protection. Source: BlockHDFS: Blockchain-integrated Hadoop distributed file system for secure provenance traceability
Abstract: Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) is one of the widely used distributed file systems in big data analysis for frameworks such as Hadoop. HDFS allows one to manage large volumes of data using low-cost commodity hardware. However, vulnerabilities in HDFS can be exploited for nefarious activities. This reinforces the importance of ensuring robust security to facilitate file sharing in Hadoop as well as having a trusted mechanism to check the authenticity of shared files. This is the focus of this paper, where we aim to improve the security of HDFS using a blockchain-enabled approach (hereafter referred to as BlockHDFS). Specifically, the proposed BlockHDFS uses the enterprise-level Hyperledger Fabric platform to capitalize on files' metadata for building trusted data security and traceability in HDFS.
Methods: Prototype implementation of BlockHDFS using Hyperledger Fabric v1.1, Hadoop v3.1.2, and a NodeJS client bridging WebHDFS REST API to the blockchain. Evaluated on a single Ubuntu VM with a single NameNode/DataNode and 1 MBâ€“100 GB files.
Results: BlockHDFS added little execution-time overhead to Wordcount, with memory use rising from 5.46 GB to 6.16 GB. NodeJS/WebHDFS latency increased under load, especially for the 100 GB file, and a 1 s polling frequency performed worse than 3 s or 5 s.
Conclusions: BlockHDFS improves HDFS security and traceability by recording file metadata immutably on a blockchain. Limitations include only top-level directory listing, periodic rather than real-time updates, and minimal metadata in the current implementation.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical prototype and experimental evaluation of a blockchain-integrated HDFS security system. Implementation maturity is prototype/laboratory-tested, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Experimental benchmarking on a single-machine standalone Hadoop/Hyperledger setup, comparing baseline HDFS vs BlockHDFS. Evidence includes execution time, memory utilization, and load/frequency experiments with quantitative measurements.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Hyperledger Fabric permissioned blockchain with smart contracts, channels, ledger, and ordering service; no mining. Architecture uses an HDFS cluster plus a Fabric network, with metadata stored as assets on-chain.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: HDFS stores files; WebHDFS REST API exposes file metadata; a NodeJS client periodically pulls checksum, access time, and modification time; Hyperledger Fabric stores the metadata ledger. Docker and Docker-Compose host the Fabric components in the prototype.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Distributed file-system provenance and traceability for HDFS in big-data environments. On-chain data are file metadata (hash/checksum, access time, modification time, filename); file contents remain in HDFS.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses tamper-proof blockchain logs, authenticated permissioned access, ACL/Kerberos context, and checksum validation (CRC32/MD5-of-CRC32C). Addresses file tampering, unauthorized modification, spoofing, session replay, MITM, and compromised audit trails.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Integrates HDFS with WebHDFS REST API and Hadoop APIs; no LADM, INSPIRE, or cadastral standards are discussed. Data exchange is via REST calls and JSON between WebHDFS and the NodeJS client.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: No legal or regulatory framework is discussed. Governance is limited to permissioned access in Hyperledger Fabric and authenticated HDFS users managing the ledger.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Deployed as a laboratory prototype on Ubuntu VirtualBox with Hadoop, Docker, and Fabric; organization-oriented, private-network setting. Barriers include added latency, periodic polling, non-recursive directory listing, and the need for authenticated access.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluated using execution time, memory utilization, and NodeJS/WebHDFS latency under different file sizes and polling frequencies. Remaining gaps are real-time integration, recursive subfolder handling, and broader multi-node validation.

Source: Blockchain and NFT-based digital passports for UAV preoperational certification
Abstract: Digital passports for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are used to create a unified system for tracking and identifying UAVs, which ensures compliance and security. A digital passport holds details like the owner's information, drone model, and activity history, thereby enabling easy tracking and identification of UAVs. However, the absence of decentralized and secure digital passport management systems for UAVs makes it challenging to ensure tamper-proof records and transparent ownership verification across borders. This paper proposes a proof of concept for a decentralized blockchain and Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs)-based digital passport to improve the transparency, traceability, trust, and security of UAV preoperational certifications. The proposed solution secures UAVs' preoperational stages such as design, manufacturing, and distribution, integrating best practices from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) for standardized compliance. The proposed NFT-based digital passport consolidates certification records into a single verifiable document, providing access to compliance history. Four smart contracts are developed to enforce role-based access control, and off-chain decentralized storage using the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) is employed to manage large UAV records. Evaluation through implementation and testing demonstrates the solution's effectiveness in managing UAV certification workflows and enforcing regulatory compliance. Security analysis shows robustness against unauthorized modifications and common vulnerabilities, while cost analysis assesses deployment viability across multiple blockchain networks. A comparison of the proposed solution with existing UAV compliance and certification frameworks shows that it effectively fills the gap by addressing preoperational certification. The smart contract code is publicly available on GitHub.
Methods: Proof-of-concept blockchain and NFT-based UAV certification system with a modular smart-contract design. Implemented and tested on Ethereum Sepolia using Solidity, Remix, OpenZeppelin, IPFS, and Forge-based test scripts.
Results: The system successfully enforced role-based access control, workflow sequencing, and immutable certificate linking across four smart contracts. Benchmarking on Sepolia reported p50 latency of about 7â€“12 s and p95 of 20â€“40 s, with throughput peaking at 0.90 TPS in W1.
Conclusions: The prototype addresses the gap in preoperational UAV certification by improving transparency, traceability, security, and regulatory compliance. Future work includes generative AI for regulatory assessment, contract adaptation as standards evolve, and extension to other regulated domains.
Study Classification and Maturity: Proof-of-concept empirical evaluation of a blockchain/NFT certification prototype. Highest maturity demonstrated is prototype implementation and testnet validation, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Evaluated through implementation testing, functional contract tests, security analysis, cost analysis, and Sepolia benchmark workflows over 3,000+ UAVs. Evidence is quantitative and includes latency, throughput, gas cost, and static/dynamic security test results.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Ethereum-based architecture with four Solidity smart contracts, ERC-721 NFTs, on-chain/off-chain storage, and IPFS. The deployment was tested on Ethereum Sepolia; the paper also discusses public or private ledgers and Layer 2 options, but no custom consensus mechanism is proposed.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Stack includes Solidity, Remix IDE, OpenZeppelin, IPFS, MetaMask, Alchemy RPC, Sepolia testnet, and Forge tests. On-chain contracts store hashes, CIDs, status, and ownership; off-chain files and reports are stored in IPFS, with authenticated DApp interactions and encrypted handling of sensitive documents.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: UAV preoperational certification for design, manufacturing, distribution, registration, airworthiness, export/import approval, and ownership transfer. Data include UAV identity, serial numbers, inspection reports, compliance documents, and certification records; sensitive artifacts are kept off-chain in IPFS.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses role-based access control, digital signatures, encryption, hash commitments, ownership checks, checks-effects-interactions, and immutable on-chain references. Threats addressed include tampering, unauthorized modification, fraudulent issuance, reentrancy, front-running, key compromise, and common smart-contract vulnerabilities.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Integrates FAA and EASA certification practices through versioned jurisdictional profiles, equivalence declarations, and delta overlays. The paper does not implement LADM/ISO 19152 or other cadastral standards.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Regulatory authorities, manufacturers, notified bodies, and import/export authorities are the main actors, with FAA and EASA treated as issuing authorities. Legal requirements are encoded as machine-readable controls, with authority-gated issuance, jurisdiction profiles, and auditable evidence anchoring.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Targets cross-border UAV certification, where barriers include fragmented regulations, centralized paper records, verification bottlenecks, and scalability/cost concerns. Deployment was conceptual and testnet-based on Ethereum Sepolia, not operational.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Measured latency, throughput, gas cost, and scalability under concurrency levels 10â€“50 and batch sizes 200â€“1000. The main research gap is lack of unified preoperational UAV certification interoperable across jurisdictions; throughput is limited by public testnet congestion and RPC rate limits.

Source: Smart Contract Application for Managing Land Administration System Transactions
Abstract: Land administration systems are of great importance for a large number of stakeholders. One of the key problems related to land administration systems is the problem of the correctness of their state, meaning that data stored in land administration systems are not in concordance with the actual legal, spatial and topographic situation. The main causes of land administration systems' incorrect state are data collection and compilation, data processing, and data misuse. In this paper, we discuss the problems of data tampering, the long time needed for registering land administration system's transactions, and the possibility of double spending, which all can add incorrectness in a land administration system. Our research is based on the hypothesis that these problems may be addressed by means of distributed ledger technology, or to be more precise, by means of blockchain technology. The solution is presented in a form of a smart contract written in Solidity programing language that can cover even those more specific use cases in land administration systems such as sharing of ownership, transferring part of ownership, splitting or merging of real estate, and limiting the possibility of trading a real estate. The proposed smart contract represents an implementation of a programming interface that was created based on both ERC-20 and ERC-721 token standards, to satisfy the specific needs of land administration systems.

Results: The proposed smart contract is presented as covering ownership sharing, partial ownership transfer, splitting or merging real estate, and limiting property trading to address tampering, long registration times, and double spending.
Conclusions: Blockchain smart contracts may improve correctness and reduce transaction problems in land administration systems; no empirical evaluation or performance results are reported in the abstract.

Source: A survey of empirical performance evaluation of permissioned blockchain platforms: Challenges and opportunities
Abstract: Blockchain-based platforms, particularly those based on permissioned blockchain, are increasingly popular in a broad range of settings. In addition to security and privacy concerns, organizations seeking to implement such platforms also need to consider performance, especially in latency- or delay-sensitive applications. Performance is generally less studied in comparison to security and privacy, and therefore in this paper we survey existing empirical performance evaluations of different permissioned blockchain platforms published between 2015 and 2019, using a comparative framework. The framework comprises ten criteria. We then conclude the paper with a number of potential future research directions.
Methods: Systematic survey of empirical performance evaluations of permissioned blockchain platforms published from 2015â€“2019, using Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. A comparative framework with ten criteria was applied to the selected studies.
Results: Across the reviewed studies, Hyperledger Fabric generally outperformed Ethereum on throughput, latency, and execution time, while Parity often had the lowest latency and was more fault-tolerant. Raft-based Quorum and Hyperledger Fabric 1.4.1 outperformed IBFT-based Quorum and Libra on selected metrics, but scalability problems persisted across platforms.
Conclusions: Performance remains understudied, and the surveyed platforms are still far from suitable for large-scale data processing systems. The paper calls for more empirical studies on newer permissioned platforms, scalability, block size, and node-configuration effects.

Evidence is quantitative, drawing on throughput, latency, execution time, scalability, and fault-tolerance results from prior experiments.

Source: A systematic review of blockchain scalability: Issues, solutions, analysis and future research
Abstract: Blockchain is an inspiring emerging technology that takes much attention from various researchers and companies. The technology offers various benefits such as data security, autonomy, immutability, transparency, and auditability. Hence, blockchain is getting large adoptions for various applications besides cryptocurrencies. Despite these benefits, scalability is a big challenge to blockchain impeding its mainstream adoption. This paper gives a systematic review of blockchain scalability. We follow a systematic process to investigate the research trend on blockchain scalability and review its state of the art. We review the various proposed solutions and methods for blockchain scalability. We also review the performance analysis of blockchain systems. We assess the proposed scalability solutions, deduce future research directions on the blockchain scalability, and finally discuss the blockchain adoption. We hope this paper will serve as a guide for learning and research on blockchain scalability.
Methods: Systematic review of blockchain scalability using automated database searches and supplementary reference/citation screening. The review screened 351 papers from 2012â€“2020 across major academic databases and gray literature.
Results: Studies were classified into scalability solutions (71%), performance analysis (16%), and reviews/surveys (13%). Among performance analyses, 41% were evaluations, 35% benchmarking studies, and 24% modeling studies.
Conclusions: Scalability remains constrained by the tradeoff with security, decentralization, and trust, especially in throughput, latency, storage, and read performance. The paper calls for hybrid solutions, better read/storage methods, stronger benchmarking tools, and improved sharding designs.
Study Classification and Maturity: Systematic review and classification paper on blockchain scalability. It includes proposed conceptual models and summarizes maturity from conceptual/prototype ideas through PoCs, pilots, and production-ready adoption.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Evidence comes from systematic review synthesis plus performance analyses, benchmarking, and modeling studies. Validation across the reviewed literature includes simulations, implementations, cloud tests, and comparative experiments with quantitative metrics.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: The paper proposes a five-layer blockchain ecosystem model: application, data, consensus, network, and platform. It covers public, private, and consortium blockchains; PoW, PoS, PBFT, Raft, Tendermint, DPoS, and hybrid consensus; and architectures such as sharding, DAG, sidechains, cross-chains, and Hyperledger Fabric execute-order-validate.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: The stack includes blockchain platform layers, smart contracts/chaincodes, RPC and gossip networking, databases, off-chain storage (IPFS/DHT), and benchmarking tools. Integration is described through execute-order-validate in Fabric, two-way pegs in sidechains, and API-based benchmarking in tools like BlockBench and Caliper.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Targets blockchain transaction data, block headers, hashes, signatures, and ledger storage, with use cases in cryptocurrencies, smart contracts, supply chain, healthcare, identity management, registry, IoT, banking, and finance. It also covers read/write/storage scalability for these blockchain data types.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Mechanisms include hashing, Merkle trees, digital signatures, PKI-like authorization, zero-knowledge proofs, multi-signature/collective signing, and consensus-based validation. Threats discussed include tampering, double spending, forks, DoS, malleability, centralization, privacy leakage, and smart-contract vulnerabilities.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Interoperability is addressed mainly through cross-chain and sidechain designs such as Cosmos IBC, Polkadot relay chains, and two-way peg mechanisms. No substantive use of LADM, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE is described.

The paper does not discuss legal validity, statutory recognition, or formal land-registry governance.

Gaps include insufficient read-performance research, few storage solutions, limited benchmarking tools, and a need for secure, low-storage DAGs and better shard assignment.

Source: Performance evaluation of permissioned blockchains for financial applications: The ConsenSys Quorum case study
Abstract: Given the availability of several blockchain technologies in permissioned contexts, blockchain application designers have to cope with the increasing complexity of choosing which technology and consensus algorithm best fit a specific use case. However, the lack of a standard framework allowing to assess the scalability of permissioned blockchain platforms and to compare performances and features of consensus algorithms makes the development of a sensible evaluation a costly and difficult time-consuming problem. Throughout this article, we propose a practical scalability and applicability evaluation of the Quorum blockchain and its consensus algorithms. Although we apply our evaluation workflow to a financial use case, we define a methodology that can be generalized to any permissioned blockchain technology. We leverage Hyperledger Caliper as a benchmarking tool, and Docker as a deployment tool, making our analysis easy to be repeated, cross-platform, and cost-effective.
Methods: Comparative performance case study of ConsenSys Quorum using Hyperledger Caliper and Docker. Benchmarks were run on 4-, 8-, and 16-node networks across Raft, Clique, and IBFT with public and private SmallBank workloads.
Results: Raft generally had the highest throughput, while IBFT often showed comparable performance and was recommended for financial applications. Private transactions reduced throughput and increased latency; larger networks and higher input rates worsened both metrics.
Conclusions: The workflow is flexible, open-source, and replicable for benchmarking permissioned blockchains. The authors call for future work on security trade-offs, multithreaded Caliper workers, memory/CPU monitoring, and dynamic node joining.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical benchmarking case study / performance evaluation of a permissioned blockchain platform. Prototype/testbed maturity: implemented and experimentally evaluated on Docker-based networks, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Experimental benchmarking with controlled workloads, repeated three times per case, reporting mean TPS and latency plus standard deviation. Evidence is quantitative, based on Docker- and EC2-based tests with Caliper on Quorum.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: ConsenSys Quorum, an Ethereum-based permissioned blockchain with transaction privacy. It supports Raft, Clique PoA, and IBFT consensus, with private transactions handled through Tessera and separate public/private state tries.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Quorum Client (extended geth) handles p2p and consensus; Tessera handles encryption, decryption, peer discovery, and off-chain encrypted payload storage; Crypto Enclave isolates key management. Caliper and Docker/Docker Compose were used for benchmarking and deployment.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Financial applications using a SmallBank OLTP workload. The paper evaluates public and private transactions, including open, query, and transfer operations, with use cases such as stablecoins and CBDCs.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses encryption/decryption via Tessera, isolated Crypto Enclave key management, and network permissions management. Addresses privacy leakage and attack containment; consensus mechanisms also aim to resist Byzantine behavior and malicious nodes.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: No land-record standards are discussed. The paper uses Hyperledger Caliper for benchmarking and Docker for deployment, with an adapter developed because Quorum was not supported in Caliper v0.4.1.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Permissioned-network governance is based on selected authorities, node identity management, and voting to remove faulty nodes. No legal validity, regulatory compliance, or land-registry governance framework is discussed.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Main barriers are lack of standard evaluation frameworks, complexity of choosing platform/consensus, scalability limits, and benchmarking reproducibility. The testbed used an EC2/Docker setup with 4, 8, and 16 nodes and random network delays.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Primary criteria were throughput (goodput) and latency under varying node counts, transaction rates, workloads, and consensus protocols. Remaining gaps include security trade-offs, byzantine-node effects, more accurate multithreaded benchmarking, and tests of memory/CPU consumption.

Source: GuRuMarket: A guarantee & reputation-assisted framework for secure and efficient on-chain real-world service trading
Abstract: Recent initiatives have explored leveraging on-chain trust management to enhance blockchain maintenance and scalability. However, few solutions have effectively addressed both off-chain trust among real-world participants and on-chain trust intrinsic to blockchain nodes simultaneously. This paper presents GuRuMarket, a blockchain-powered real-world marketplace. It combines on-chain and off-chain trust management to build a system adapted to real-world commodity requirements. Beyond the recording of online transactions, the platform takes a step further by facilitating the provision of off-chain services. A key aspect of GuRuMarket involves the development of a mathematical model for assessing the reliability of each participant, reinforced by an incentive mechanism based on reputation and guarantee. In addition to helping buyers select services from sellers, the trust model we propose enables trustworthy participants to set up nodes and join the systemâ€™s network, thus playing an active role in managing the entire marketplace. Lastly, the security of our blockchain is ensured via the proposed consensus protocol, called Guarantee&Reputation Byzantine Fault Tolerance (GuRuBFT). GuRuBFT selects nodes based on a scoring formula that uses reputation and guarantee to achieve fairness. A thorough security analysis and a comprehensive performance evaluation validate the fairness, efficacy, and scalability of GuRuMarket.
Methods: Design science paper proposing GuRuMarket and GuRuBFT, with a mathematical reputation model and security analysis. Evaluated via Hyperledger Besu/Caliper benchmarks, Solidity gas tests, and comparative simulations against Clique, PBFT, QBFT, PoGR, and IPoT.
Results: GuRuBFT reached about 305 tx/s at 400 tx/s load and 396 tx/s in a 6-node setting, with stable latency and minimal degradation under Byzantine behavior. In heterogeneous tests it achieved 95%, 88%, and 40% block proposal success for core, edge, and mobile nodes, and outperformed PBFT, QBFT, PoGR, and IPoT.
Conclusions: GuRuMarket is presented as a secure, fair, and efficient dual-layer trust marketplace for real-world service trading. The authors conclude it is suitable for consortium environments, while noting future work is needed for stronger oracle security, governance decentralization, and large-scale scalability.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical blockchain systems paper proposing a conceptual-to-prototype framework with simulated and benchmarked implementation. Highest demonstrated maturity is lab-tested prototype on Hyperledger Besu with off-chain scripts, smart contracts, and local Docker-based experiments.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validated through security proofs, gas benchmarking, throughput/latency/scalability experiments, heterogeneous-network simulation, and Byzantine/rational-behavior tests. Evidence is quantitative, using 100-run averages, 10%/20% Byzantine fractions, and workload sizes of 3000â€“5000 transactions.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Built on an open-permissioned blockchain with consortium governance, partial synchrony, and an alive-but-corrupt fault model. GuRuBFT is a lightweight BFT protocol using reputation-and-guarantee scoring for leader and committee selection, with on-chain voting for admin decisions.

Off-chain scripts compute scores and verification, while on-chain contracts store state and enforce access control, trading, reputation, and guarantees.

Data includes service announcements, orders, delivery proofs, and reputation/guarantee state; off-chain service execution is central.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses guarantee deposits, reputation scoring, access control, RBAC, whitelisting, threshold-signature oracles, VRF-based committee selection, and on-chain voting. Addresses Sybil, double-spending, whitewashing, bad-collusion, malicious updates, and some DoS/bribery risks; oracle-collusion and physical-digital gaps remain open.

Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: A consortium of admins manages registration, permissioning, exits, and protocol updates through on-chain majority voting. Off-chain identity and legitimacy proofs are stored privately for regulatory compliance, but legal evidentiary recognition is not discussed.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Main barriers are oracle dependence, physical-digital mismatch, governance centralization, scalability overhead, and complexity of integrating off-chain service verification. Deployment context is a permissioned/consortium Ethereum environment, tested locally on two HPE servers with Docker-based nodes.

Gaps remain for hundreds/thousands of nodes, dynamic churn, stronger oracle/dispute security, and attacks beyond the standard <1/3 Byzantine bound.

Source: Blockchain-based auditing of legal decisions supported by explainable AI and generative AI tools
Abstract: Generative AI tools powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated advanced capabilities in understanding and articulating legal facts closer to the level of legal practitioners. However, scholars hold contrasting views on the reliability of the reasoning behind a decision derived from LLMs due to its black-box nature. Law firms are vigilant in recognizing the potential risks of violating confidentiality and inappropriate exposure of sensitive legal data through the prompt sent to Generative AI. This research attempts to find an equilibrium between responsible usage and control of human legal professionals over content produced by Generative AI through regular audits. It investigates the potential of Generative AI in drafting correspondence for pre-litigation decisions derived from an eXplainable AI (XAI) algorithm. This research presents an end-to-end process of designing the architecture and methodology for a blockchain-based auditing system. It detects unauthorized alterations of data repositories containing the decisions by an XAI model and automated textual explanation by Generative AI. The automated auditing by blockchain facilitates responsible usage of AI technologies and reduces discrepancies in tracing the accountability of adversarial decisions. It conceptualizes the two algorithms. First, strategic on-chain (within blockchain) and off-chain (outside blockchain) data storage in compliance with the data protection laws and critical requirements of stakeholders in a legal firm. Second, auditing by comparison of the unique signature as Merkle roots of files stored off-chain with their immutable blockchain counterpart. A case study on liability cases under tort law demonstrates the system implementation results.
Methods: Design and implementation study of a blockchain-based auditing framework with two algorithms: on-chain/off-chain storage and Merkle-root-based integrity auditing. Includes a case study on employer liability cases and experimental comparison on Ethereum 2.0 and Hyperledger Fabric 2.0.
Results: Pilot testing showed GPT-4 produced the highest-quality legal drafts, with 58.5% content utilization and 6 min average drafting time; Bard took 8 min. Hyperledger Fabric outperformed Ethereum in throughput and latency, and the proposed audit method improved throughput by 23.65% vs Method 1 and 21.67% vs Method 2.
Conclusions: The framework can audit XAI and Generative AI outputs while preserving integrity, confidentiality, and accountability under data protection constraints. Authors conclude it is robust against tampering and potentially adaptable to other legal and organizational settings.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical design-and-evaluation study with a prototype/pilot implementation. The maturity level is prototype tested in a case study, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validated through case study implementation, experimental user study with 50 law students, and blockchain benchmarking. Evidence includes quantitative drafting scores, utilization scores, throughput, latency, CPU/memory use, and tamper-detection tests.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Evaluated on Ethereum 2.0 and Hyperledger Fabric 2.0; Ethereum is public/permissionless and Hyperledger Fabric is private consortium-based. Architecture uses two blockchain nodes (hash storage and audit) plus smart-contract authentication, but consensus details are not specified.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Front-end dashboard, back-end API server, blockchain layer, IPFS, Azure Blob Cloud, and Azure Key Vault. The API integrates authentication, access control, legal facts/statutes modules, and encrypted/anonymized data exchange across cloud, IPFS, and blockchain.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Legal decision support and auditing for employer liability/tort cases. Data include XAI decision files, anonymized prompts, Generative AI outputs, legal facts, case IDs, hashes, and Merkle roots, with off-chain storage in Cloud/IPFS and on-chain hash pointers.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses anonymization, encryption, hashing, SHA-256, Merkle trees, PRE, digital signatures, and access control. Addresses tampering, unauthorized access, data leakage, hash-collision risk, and adversarial modification of on-chain and off-chain records.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: No cadastral or formal interoperability standards such as LADM, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE are discussed. Integration is via APIs, schema-like JSON files, IPFS, cloud storage, and blockchain hash pointers.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Designed for law-firm use with compliance to data protection laws, confidentiality requirements, and regular audits. Human lawyers retain control over prompts and access, while accountability is framed around lawyers, developers, and malicious actors.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Main barriers are confidentiality risk, key management, blockchain immutability vs data protection, scalability, latency, and need for technical expertise and managed node infrastructure. Context is a law-firm pilot in liability cases, using self-deployed nodes and third-party cloud/IPFS services.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluated on throughput, latency, memory/CPU use, audit time, and tamper detection; Hyperledger used 7x less memory than Ethereum and had higher throughput/lower latency. Gaps include limited scalability beyond 20 nodes, lack of full legal automation, and need for better node management and Lawyer-in-the-Loop support.

Source: RBT: A distributed reputation system for blockchain-based peer-to-peer energy trading with fairness consideration
Abstract: It has been proved by recent works that reputation can help to improve the efficiency of blockchain and enhance the fairness of energy trading markets. However, the application of distributed reputation in the energy field has not been fully studied yet. In this paper, we design a distributed reputation system to simulate real-world trust in blockchain-based peer-to-peer energy trading. It is a comprehensive reputation system in the sense that reputation scores are decided by the behavior of participants as consensus nodes, energy buyer, and energy sellers. Its implementation relies on blockchain, especially the smart contract technology, to achieve distributed and automatic reputation management. The distributed reputation system in turn helps to implement a delegated consensus algorithm for blockchain and a reputation-based k-double auction matchmaking scheme for peer-to-peer energy trading. In addition, we define a fairness indicator to capture the reputation-based average benefits and costs when considering reputation as the contribution to the peer-to-peer energy trading market. By simulating the comprehensive system, the numerical results demonstrate the effects of distributed reputation in improving the efficiency of blockchain and balancing fairness indicators between sellers and buyers during peer-to-peer energy trading. As far as we know, this paper is one of the few works to provide a formal method of evaluating the fairness of the peer-to-peer energy trading market.
Methods: Design and simulation study of a blockchain-based distributed reputation system for P2P energy trading. The authors implement the system in Go and compare reputation-based delegated PBFT with original PBFT using repeated simulations and a case study.
Results: Simulation showed reputation improved blockchain efficiency and balanced fairness between sellers and buyers. Reputations-based blockchain outperformed PBFT in server scalability, client scalability, and fault tolerance; the fairness factor increased to 3.7615 versus 1.1442 without reputation.
Conclusions: RBT shows that blockchain can decentralize reputation and energy trading, while reputation can improve blockchain efficiency and P2P trading fairness. The paper concludes that the proposed fairness indicator makes reputation a useful incentive for participants.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical design-and-evaluation paper proposing a blockchain-based reputation mechanism for energy trading. Maturity is simulation-tested prototype level, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation uses simulation plus a case study. Evidence is quantitative, including repeated runs, scalability tests, fault-tolerance tests, and fairness metrics compared against PBFT and a non-reputation double auction.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain-based distributed system using smart contracts and delegated PBFT. Committee members with higher reputation handle consensus, while non-committee nodes perform offline verification.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Stack includes blockchain distributed ledger, smart contracts for reputation and trading rules, Go implementation, and smart-meter peer nodes. Reputation scores and transaction records are stored on-chain; order submission, matchmaking, execution, and audit are integrated through smart contracts and consensus.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Blockchain-based peer-to-peer energy trading in a regional energy Internet, using day-ahead electricity orders. Data include supply/demand orders, transaction records, reputation scores, and smart-meter peer-node identities.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses hashing, smart contracts, distributed ledger transparency, and blockchain immutability to resist tampering and manipulation. Threats addressed include double spending, conspiracy/forgery, malicious reputation changes, and unfair or dishonest trading behavior.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to LADM, ISO 19152, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, GIS, or legacy cadastral database integration.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Governance is handled by distributed consensus among participants; no formal legal or regulatory framework is described. Smart-contract changes and reputation updates require participant approval, but statutory recognition or institutional roles are not specified.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Key barriers are scalability, message overhead, maintenance complexity, and compatibility issues. The context is a regional energy Internet P2P trading system; the system is simulated and case-studied, not field-deployed.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Criteria include client-side latency, server-side throughput, server/client scalability, fault tolerance, and fairness factor. RBT reduced latency growth, improved throughput, and remained nonzero up to 80% Byzantine fault rate; the paper notes a lack of scientific fairness metrics and distributed energy-trading supervision rules.

Source: Blockchain and NFT-based digital passports for UAV preoperational certification
Abstract: Digital passports for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are used to create a unified system for tracking and identifying UAVs, which ensures compliance and security. A digital passport holds details like the owner's information, drone model, and activity history, thereby enabling easy tracking and identification of UAVs. However, the absence of decentralized and secure digital passport management systems for UAVs makes it challenging to ensure tamper-proof records and transparent ownership verification across borders. This paper proposes a proof of concept for a decentralized blockchain and Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs)-based digital passport to improve the transparency, traceability, trust, and security of UAV preoperational certifications. The proposed solution secures UAVs' preoperational stages such as design, manufacturing, and distribution, integrating best practices from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) for standardized compliance. The proposed NFT-based digital passport consolidates certification records into a single verifiable document, providing access to compliance history. Four smart contracts are developed to enforce role-based access control, and off-chain decentralized storage using the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) is employed to manage large UAV records. Evaluation through implementation and testing demonstrates the solution's effectiveness in managing UAV certification workflows and enforcing regulatory compliance. Security analysis shows robustness against unauthorized modifications and common vulnerabilities, while cost analysis assesses deployment viability across multiple blockchain networks. A comparison of the proposed solution with existing UAV compliance and certification frameworks shows that it effectively fills the gap by addressing preoperational certification. The smart contract code is publicly available on GitHub.
Methods: Proof-of-concept blockchain/NFT digital passport for UAV preoperational certification, implemented with four smart contracts and IPFS-backed off-chain storage. Evaluated through functional testing, security analysis, and gas/latency benchmarking on Ethereum Sepolia.
Results: Testing showed the contracts enforced workflow sequencing, access control, and immutable certificate linking, with zero violations in 2000 fuzzing trials and invariant checks. Benchmarking reported p50 latency of about 7â€“12 s and p95 of about 20â€“40 s; W1 peaked at 0.90 TPS at C=10.
Conclusions: The paper concludes the system is a feasible proof-of-concept that improves transparency, traceability, security, and regulatory compliance for UAV preoperational certification. Future work includes generative AI for regulatory assessment, evolving contracts with standards, and broader sector deployment.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical proof-of-concept system study with prototype implementation and testnet validation. Maturity is prototype-level, with a deployed and tested modular blockchain system but no operational production deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation combines functional contract testing, security analysis, static analysis with Slither, dynamic fuzzing/invariant testing, and performance benchmarking on Ethereum Sepolia. Evidence is quantitative and implementation-based, including latency, throughput, gas cost, and zero-violation security tests.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Ethereum-based design with smart contracts and ERC-721 NFTs; evaluated on the Sepolia Ethereum testnet, with discussion of Ethereum mainnet and L2s such as Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, and zkSync. The architecture is hybrid on-chain/off-chain, and the paper notes public or private ledger deployment options but does not specify a new consensus mechanism.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Stack includes Solidity, Remix IDE, OpenZeppelin, MetaMask, Forge, Alchemy RPC, ERC-721 NFTs, and IPFS. On-chain contracts manage certification logic and references; off-chain documents are stored in IPFS and linked by CIDs/hashes.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: UAV preoperational certification data: design dossiers, inspection reports, compliance records, type certificates, airworthiness approvals, export/import certificates, and ownership history. Use case is a digital passport for UAV registration, certification, and cross-border compliance verification.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses hashing/CIDs, digital signatures, encryption, role-based access control, ownership checks, and checks-effects-interactions, with IPFS content addressing and on-chain commitments. Threats covered include unauthorized modification, tampering, reentrancy, misbinding, front-running, and unauthorized issuance; Slither found no high-severity issues.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Integrates FAA and EASA certification practices through versioned jurisdictional profiles, equivalence declarations, and delta overlays. No LADM/ISO 19152 or INTERLIS is mentioned; interoperability is implemented via profile-checked linking and content-addressed evidence.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Regulatory authorities, manufacturers, notified bodies, and import/export authorities are the main institutional actors. Legal requirements are encoded as machine-readable controls tied to recognized authority attestations, but the paper presents this as a proposed/implemented compliance framework rather than a statutory legal ruling.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include fragmented cross-jurisdiction rules, centralized paper-based recordkeeping, tampering risk, manual verification burden, and scalability/cost concerns. Deployment context is UAV certification across FAA/EASA settings, tested on Ethereum Sepolia and discussed for mainnet, L2, and private-chain options.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluated latency, throughput, gas cost, and scalability; p50 latency was about 7â€“12 s and p95 about 20â€“40 s, with W1 peaking at 0.90 TPS at C=10. The main gap identified is lack of unified preoperational UAV certification integrated with FAA/EASA frameworks.

Source: A comprehensive IoT and blockchain-integrated framework for autonomous water management in sustainable urban ecosystems
Abstract: Different approaches to urbanization, decaying infrastructure, and climate change may blend into multiple pressures on the urban water management system. It would turn the limelight towards the intrinsic weaknesses of the systems in terms of traditional, centralized-inherently reactive, opaque, and unreliable-public systems. This proposed research brings a new decentralized paradigm synergistically utilizing IoT, blockchain technology, and machine learning in mutual respect and strength for resilient urban ecosystems. The architecture consists of IoT sensors for real-time monitoring and data collection, with water quality sensors and flow meters sending data through edge devices to a blockchain network, thereby ensuring integrity, security, and resistance to tampering. Respectively, machine learning algorithms embedded in the system will use historical and real-time data to perform predictive analytics to forecast future water demand and detect water-quality anomalies. This multi-layer architecture allows for real-time monitoring, transparency, automated decision-making, and intelligent resource reallocation. The results show significant improvements: predictive analytics for water demand forecasting achieved an F1-score of 91 %; the blockchain achieved 95 % fault tolerance; and energy efficiency improved by as much as 75 % at low-load conditions. Furthermore, the system provided low-latency communication and high transactions throughput, proving its scalability and applicability in different urban settings.
Methods: Conceptual framework with a simulated urban water-management setup. Uses IoT sensor data, blockchain logging, and LSTM-based predictive analytics with preprocessing, hold-out validation, and comparative benchmarking.
Results: pH sensing reached 95% accuracy and turbidity 90%, with 20â€“30 ms sensor latency and 55 mW average power. ML achieved F1 91% for water-quality prediction, 88% precision/85% recall for anomaly detection, and 90% F1 for demand forecasting; blockchain latency averaged 120 ms and fault tolerance reached 95%.
Conclusions: The framework improves visibility, predictive accuracy, energy performance, and equitable water allocation compared with current methods. Future work should improve peak-load blockchain efficiency, sensor accuracy (especially temperature), and test larger field deployments.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual architecture paper with simulation-based evaluation and comparative benchmarking. Highest maturity demonstrated is a simulated prototype/proof-of-concept, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation uses simulated IoT-water management data, blockchain performance testing, and LSTM model benchmarking against RNN, CNN, SVM, and Random Forest. Evidence is quantitative, reporting accuracy, F1, AUC-ROC, latency, throughput, energy use, and fault tolerance.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Private Ethereum blockchain using Proof of Authority (PoA). The design is permissioned, with Solidity smart contracts for automated water allocation, metering, and quality verification.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: IoT sensors and edge devices send water-quality and flow data to a private Ethereum blockchain; smart contracts automate decisions and dashboards visualize outputs. Machine learning/LSTM modules preprocess data and generate forecasts and anomaly alerts from historical and real-time sensor inputs.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Urban water-management data: pH, turbidity, temperature, conductivity, and flow-rate readings, plus blockchain transaction and resource-allocation data. Use case is autonomous monitoring, water-demand forecasting, anomaly detection, and equitable water distribution in smart cities.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses blockchain hashing, previous-block links, PoA consensus, and smart contracts to provide tamper resistance, integrity, traceability, transparency, and secure storage. Addressed threats include tampering, fraud, and centralized manipulation; privacy encryption is mentioned but not detailed.

Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Technical knowledge and infrastructure investment are major barriers; energy use and dependence on reliable IoT/communication networks are concerns, especially in low-income settings. The target context is urban smart-city water management, evaluated in simulation rather than field deployment.

Reported gaps include blockchain energy cost, sensor calibration/accuracy issues, and limited integration of monitoring, predictive analytics, and resource allocation in prior work.

Source: IBS-ECDHE: A blockchain-enhanced lightweight protocol for secure cloud-IoT in biomedical HCPS
Abstract: The rapid adoption of cloud-Internet-of-Things (CIoT) systems in biomedical human-cyber-physical systems (HCPS) has raised significant concerns regarding data security, privacy, and scalability. To address these challenges specifically within healthcare environments, we propose a novel IBS-ECDHE framework that integrates Identity-Based Signatures (IBS) and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (ECDHE) key exchange to provide robust and lightweight security for biomedical HCPS. Our framework leverages blockchain technology to decentralize identity management and access control, ensuring secure authentication and maintaining the integrity of sensitive biomedical data exchanged between IoT-enabled medical devices. By incorporating smart contracts, we automate key management and enforce stringent privacy and data integrity guarantees critical to biomedical applications. The proposed system was implemented on a Windows 10 PC and evaluated using various performance metrics, including authentication time, message size, transaction latency, and computational overhead. Experimental results demonstrate that IBS-ECDHE reduces authentication time by up to 76 % compared to traditional PKI systems, decreases message size by 40 %, and achieves lower blockchain transaction latency. The system also ensures scalability and energy efficiency, with parallel processing reducing latency by 37 %. The innovation of this approach lies in the combination of IBS with ECDHE for mutual authentication and the use of blockchain for decentralized identity management and secure real-time biomedical data exchange. This solution offers substantial improvements in security, privacy, and performance, making it highly suitable for next-generation biomedical HCPS.
Methods: Proposed blockchain-based IBS-ECDHE framework for biomedical CIoT, implemented on Windows 10 and evaluated with Hyperledger Fabric 2.4. Analysis combines experimental benchmarking, ProVerif formal verification, and gas/latency/energy measurements.
Results: Authentication time dropped up to 76% versus PKI, message size fell 40%, and latency was reduced 37% with parallel processing. Experimental evaluation also reported 142 ms transaction latency, 1,240 TPS, and 34.6% lower energy per transaction than BCmECC.
Conclusions: The IBS-ECDHE blockchain framework is presented as a scalable, lightweight solution for secure biomedical HCPS/CIoT. Future work should improve large-scale scalability, energy efficiency, and post-quantum security.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical prototype and protocol evaluation study with formal verification. Highest maturity is a simulated/implemented laboratory prototype, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation used implementation on a PC and a Hyperledger Fabric simulation, plus ProVerif proofs. Evidence is quantitative, reporting latency, throughput, gas, energy, and authentication-time metrics.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Hyperledger Fabric 2.4 permissioned blockchain with one orderer and three peer nodes, private channels, and Go chaincode. Consensus is described as peer validation/orderer sequencing and also referenced as modified PBFT/2-phase commit in scalability discussion.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Three-layer IoTâ€“cloudâ€“blockchain architecture linking medical sensors, gateways, cloud storage, and smart contracts. Stack includes Python, Go chaincode, OpenSSL, custom IBS scripts, and blockchain-based access control and logging.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Biomedical healthcare CIoT/HCPS for secure exchange of sensitive health data from IoT medical devices, including DICOM images and FHIR-based records. Use cases include authentication, access control, secure storage, and real-time monitoring.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses IBS, ECDHE, hashing, digital signatures, encryption, smart contracts, and blockchain immutability for authentication, confidentiality, and integrity. Threats addressed include impersonation, replay, MITM, tampering, key compromise, metadata leakage, and unauthorized access.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: FHIR APIs and DICOM are integrated for standardized healthcare data exchange. The paper states semantic consistency and interoperability via FHIR/DICOM, but gives no detailed schema mapping or versioning.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Mentions HIPAA and GDPR compliance, smart-contract-based consent and erasure, and auditable access logs. Governance remains partly proposed, with KMA/SAU, validator, and gateway roles defined but no formal legal deployment framework.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Deployment context is biomedical HCPS/CIoT in healthcare, tested in a simulated lab environment rather than operational hospitals. Main barriers are scalability, computational overhead, energy use, key escrow, and future post-quantum risk.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluated using authentication time, message size, transaction latency, throughput, gas cost, computational overhead, and energy consumption. Reported gaps include scalability limits, smart-contract overhead, key escrow, and need for real-world biomedical deployment and post-quantum upgrades.

Source: Performance Evaluation of Blockchain of Things Cyber-Physical System Using Geth Metrics
Abstract: Blockchain of Things (BCoT) has recently found many applications in vital industrial and service fields, as it can provide feasible solutions to security, data integrity, and system availability issues inherent to IoT networks. Blockchain limitations, such as scalability and latency, and IoT security concerns, need to be investigated to realize the full potential of BCoT ecosystems. Several performance parameters of BCoT, such as latency, throughput, disk I/O, CPU utilization, and memory usage, must be measured and quantified while the system operates. A system comprising a private Ethereum PoA network utilized edge-computing techniques to mitigate resource constraints, while Geth Metrics tested the operational architecture. Improvements in latency reached (45%), throughput (65%), disk I/O (46%), and CPU utilization decreased by 33%, and memory usage never exceeded 200 MB compared to similar BCoT systems. During the mining stage, the architecture could execute up to 5000 transactions under realistic conditions. A low-latency, scalable, secure, real-time BCoT architecture suitable for IoT applications could be realized with improved metrics, efficiency, and decision-making capabilities, thus significantly impacting practical situations and overcoming limitations in resource-constrained IoT network infrastructure.
Methods: Performance evaluation of a BCoT system using a private Ethereum PoA network and Geth Metrics. Edge-computing techniques were used to mitigate resource constraints.
Results: Latency improved by 45%, throughput by 65%, disk I/O by 46%, and CPU utilization decreased by 33%; memory usage stayed under 200 MB. The architecture executed up to 5000 transactions during mining.
Conclusions: A low-latency, scalable, secure, real-time BCoT architecture for IoT applications is feasible. The authors claim improved efficiency and decision-making in resource-constrained IoT infrastructure.

Evaluation Method and Evidence: Experimental benchmarking with Geth Metrics on a private Ethereum PoA network. Quantitative performance evidence is reported for latency, throughput, disk I/O, CPU, memory, and transaction capacity.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Private Ethereum network using Proof of Authority (PoA). The system is a BCoT architecture evaluated under operational conditions.

Source: Design and evaluation of a blockchain-integrated BIS for decentralized energy management
Abstract: Motivation: Local energy communities represent a compelling use case for Blockchain-based Information Systems (BISs), where mutually distrusting participants must share and verify energy data without relying on centralized authorities. However, integrating real-time IoT monitoring, photovoltaic (PV) generation modeling, and blockchain infrastructures raises challenges of scalability, governance, transparency, and data management. Objective: This study investigates the design of a BIS that integrates IoT-based energy monitoring, PV system simulation, and blockchain transaction management to provide a transparent, efficient, and fair framework for decentralized energy communities. Methods: This study presents a framework design and validation methodology that combines empirical monitoring with simulation-based assessment. Real household electricity consumption was monitored over six days using smart meters interfaced through MQTT to a Raspberry Pi. Photovoltaic generation was simulated using PVsyst with site-specific meteorological data 1642 kWh/m<sup>2</sup>. Energy surplus scenarios were modeled by combining measured consumption with simulated PV output and submitted to a Hyperledger Fabric network to measure transaction performance. Multiple blockchain platforms were evaluated against latency, throughput, energy overhead, and cost metrics. Results: Measured blockchain performance on operational hardware shows permissioned networks with PBFT consensus achieve 2.35Â±0.11 second latency and 0.99Â±0.07% energy overhead for 10-household communities. Simulated PV optimization demonstrates that 35Â° panel tilt increases annual yield by 15.9% over a horizontal baseline (3877 kWh/year baseline; 4495 kWh/year optimized) with 75.1% performance ratio. Infrastructure costs are measured at 240 EUR/household for the validated 10-household baseline and projected to scale to 40 EUR/household at 60-household deployments through fixed cost distribution, with intermediate validation through Hyperledger Caliper simulations confirming sub-linear latency scaling to 20 households (2.68 Â± 0.18 s). The 10-household configuration represents a pilot-scale baseline for controlled validation, with demonstrated architectural scalability through simulation. The framework validation demonstrates technical feasibility and quantifies design trade-offs in consensus selection, data management, and system optimization. Conclusion: This work contributes a reproducible validation framework for blockchain-based energy management systems, validated through controlled component testing prior to field deployment. The methodology addresses scalability, governance, and transparency challenges while offering practical design guidelines for implementing fair and efficient local energy communities.
Methods: Framework design and validation combining 6-day household electricity monitoring, PVsyst simulation, and blockchain performance testing on Hyperledger Fabric. Performance was evaluated with latency, throughput, energy overhead, and cost metrics, plus Caliper-based scaling simulations.
Results: Permissioned PBFT networks achieved 2.35Â±0.11 s latency and 0.99Â±0.07% energy overhead for 10 households. PV tilt optimization increased annual yield by 15.9% (3877 to 4495 kWh/year), and cost fell from 240 EUR/household to about 40 EUR/household at 60 households.
Conclusions: A reproducible validation framework was demonstrated for blockchain-based local energy communities, showing technical feasibility and quantified trade-offs in transparency, scalability, and cost. The authors note the work remains pilot-scale and needs real-world field deployment and broader governance validation.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical design-and-evaluation study of a blockchain-integrated BIS for decentralized energy management. Maturity is pilot-scale validation with real household monitoring, operational testbed blockchain experiments, and simulation-based scaling; no full field deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation combined real hardware monitoring, PV simulation, and blockchain testing on an operational Hyperledger Fabric test network. Evidence included quantitative metrics, paired t-tests, regression, variance analysis, and Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Permissioned Hyperledger Fabric network using PBFT consensus, with four validator nodes and on-chain commitment of aggregated energy records. A hybrid on-chain/off-chain architecture stores raw household data locally and writes only hashes and five-minute surplus values to the ledger.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Shelly EM smart meter â†’ MQTT â†’ Raspberry Pi 4B/Mosquitto/Python subscriber â†’ CSV off-chain storage â†’ SHA-256 hash anchoring on blockchain. PVsyst simulation and Hyperledger Fabric/Caliper are integrated through post-hoc surplus detection and transaction testing.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Residential electricity consumption data from a household in Cagliari, Italy, combined with simulated PV generation for local energy community trading. The use case is decentralized peer-to-peer energy sharing, settlement, and surplus verification.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: SHA-256 hashing, blockchain immutability, permissioned access, PBFT finality, and MQTT authentication are used. The design addresses tampering, privacy leakage, unauthorized access, and traceability; smart-contract and adversarial stress testing were not conducted.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: MQTT is used for IoT data exchange, CSV for storage, and PVGIS/Meteonorm are used to cross-check PV meteorological inputs. No LADM, ISO 19152, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE integration is described.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Governance is framed around decentralized decision-making, smart-contract enforcement, on-chain auditability, and dispute resolution. Compliance is discussed in relation to EU RED II, Italian Decreto Legislativo 199/2021, ARERA rules, and GDPR tensions with blockchain immutability.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include scalability, privacy, transaction cost, governance overhead, regulatory constraints, and potential centralization of the four-node testbed. Deployment context is a pilot-scale 10-household Italian setting, with simulation-based projections to 20-100 households rather than field operation.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Criteria were latency, throughput, energy overhead, cost, PV yield, and scalability. Reported results include 2â€“3 s latency, up to 3500 TPS capacity, 0.99Â±0.07% energy overhead, and 15.9% PV yield gain; remaining gaps are field validation, adversarial testing, and real governance outcomes.

Source: Tokenising judicial system unavailability: A blockchain-based mechanism for verifiable certificates and tamper-evident auditability
Abstract: The availability of judicial information systems is a precondition for procedural continuity and reliable access to digital justice, yet the security and integrity of unavailability records remain underaddressed. In practice, unavailability events are handled through institution-centric administrative procedures that rely on trust and provide limited support for independent verification and retrospective auditability. This paper examines whether the Unavailability of Judicial Information Systems (UJIS) process is a suitable candidate for blockchain-based tokenisation and reports the design, implementation, and evaluation of an operational solution. Using the Process Tokenisation Model for the Public Sector, the UJIS process was assessed through stakeholder interviews and regulatory/document analysis, confirming suitability in terms of process requirements, blockchain capabilities, sustainable incentives, and expected outcomes. Based on this assessment, we designed and implemented a permissioned blockchain solution using Hyperledger Fabric, Node.js smart contracts, and PHP/Laravel interfaces to record and verify unavailability events and to generate digitally signed certificates linked to immutable on-chain records. Verification relies on cryptographic hashes and QR-code deep links, enabling third parties to validate integrity and provenance against a tamper-evident record under permissioned governance, without contacting the issuing department. A Hyperledger Caliper benchmark indicates throughput well above historical demand with sub-second write latency, and integrity verification tests confirm reliable tamper detection through cryptographic hash comparison. Overall, the results show that assessment-driven tokenisation yields a technically feasible mechanism that strengthens transparency, auditability, and cryptographic assurance for managing judicial system unavailability, contributing to the information security of judicial digital infrastructures within the trust assumptions of a permissioned network.

Conclusions: Blockchain-enabled tokenisation can provide a verifiable, auditable mechanism for judicial system unavailability within a permissioned institutional setting. The authors limit claims to technical feasibility and performance; user acceptance, legal admissibility, and cross-court scaling remain future work.

Source: Permissioned Distributed Ledgers for Land Transactions; A Case Study
Abstract: Considering the inefficiency and ineffectiveness of the current manual land registration systems being practiced in Sri Lanka and the emergence of the concept of blockchain based land registries as a successful replacement for badly kept, mismanaged and/or corrupt land registries from around the world, this research proposes and evaluates the applicability of a permissioned distributed land ledger solution for Sri Lanka. The final solution presents optimal content for the ledger (extracted from the current folio), preserves current land transactions, has reassigned duties to state validators and has got away with the folio system while ensuring derivation of the pedigree/folio tree for a land at a given time. A regional distributed land ledger representing the present regional ledger system and an island wide unified land ledger which addresses unequal regional land transaction density conditions across the island were proposed as solution models. The proposed models of the solution were implemented using Hyperledger Fabric v1.2. They were evaluated for performance on an AWS t2.large instance with 2 vCPUs, 8GiB memory, under different land transaction density conditions and node failure conditions. A community consisting of twenty-one peers belonging to nine organizations, was subject to evaluation. The island wide solution records higher throughput, lower latency and tolerance for fail-stop conditions than the regional distributed land ledger. Further, the island wide solution does not show a significant drop in throughput upÂ to two crash failures out of seven Kafka brokers in production scale deployment.

Conclusions: A permissioned distributed land ledger is applicable for Sri Lanka and the island-wide model performed better than the regional model. The design replaces the folio system while preserving land transaction history and pedigree/folio-tree derivation.

Source: Blockchain-enhanced optimization for a secure and transparent global energy supply chain with reduced environmental impact and cost
Abstract: The rapid evolution of energy systems necessitates innovative solutions to ensure efficient, transparent, and secure energy distribution. This paper introduces a novel blockchain-based model for decentralized energy trading, aiming to optimize the global energy supply chain. The proposed model leverages smart contracts for automated peer-to-peer transactions, allowing for a significant reduction in intermediary costs and enhancing the robustness of the energy market. The equilibrium model ensures market clearance, while the pricing algorithm dynamically responds to real-time supply and demand fluctuations. Moreover, the study formulates an optimization objective focused on maximizing social welfare, encompassing consumer and producer surplus, and minimizing environmental impacts. The model is flexible, capable of integrating future advancements in renewable energy and storage technologies. Our findings indicate that blockchain technology not only has the potential to revolutionize the way we trade energy but also to significantly contribute to a more sustainable and environmentally friendly energy landscape.

Source: Security and privacy-preserving mechanisms in collaborative machine learning: A systematic review with novel taxonomy
Abstract: Collaborative Machine Learning (CML) architectures, such as Federated Learning (FL), Split Learning (SL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD), mitigate direct data leakage but remain highly vulnerable to sophisticated adversarial attacks and privacy breaches. Current literature often fragments these vulnerabilities by architecture, lacking a generalized framework to assess underlying threat vectors. This paper introduces a novel, mechanism-driven taxonomy that unifies CML approaches based on their shared communication medium-categorized into Weight/Gradient Sharing, Model/Smashed-Data Sharing, and Knowledge Sharing-to systematically evaluate state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving mechanisms. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted in strict adherence to the PRISMA workflow. Following a highly transparent search and multi-stage screening process across leading academic databases, 160 primary studies were selected based on robust mathematical and methodological quality assessments. The empirical synthesis quantifies critical trade-offs between privacy guarantees and model utility (e.g., accuracy degradation vs. Differential Privacy budgets) and evaluates the computational overheads of cryptographic protocols, including Homomorphic Encryption and Secure Aggregation. The proposed taxonomy successfully maps specific adversarial threats directly to topological nodes, revealing critical vulnerabilities in current cut-layer and gradient-sharing mitigations under specific network constraints. By bridging theoretical cryptographic frameworks with practical implementation realities, this review provides a strategic roadmap for deploying secure, regulatory-compliant CML defenses in resource-constrained edge networks.
Methods: Systematic literature review of 160 primary studies on collaborative machine learning security and privacy (2019â€“2026), following Kitchenham and Charters and PRISMA. Search used six databases plus backward/forward snowballing, with quality assessment and structured data extraction.
Results: A mechanism-based taxonomy grouped threats and defenses into WS, MS, and KS, showing the shared medium determines attack surface and defense choice. WS dominated the corpus (115 studies, 71.9%) and was most vulnerable to poisoning and gradient inversion, while KS was most exposed to model extraction.
Conclusions: The shared knowledge medium is the main determinant of CML security and privacy trade-offs, and no single defense is universally effective. The review also finds the evidence base is weak for deployment because 73.1% of studies assume IID data and many MS defenses are only tested against passive adversaries.

Source: Blockchain-enabled precision agriculture: A scoping review of data infrastructures and decision-support systems
Abstract: Precision Agriculture (PA) is a rapidly growing domain that integrates distributed sensing technology and data-driven decision making mechanisms aiming to optimize the production process. Given the increasing complexity of this ecosystem, which involves multiple stakeholders, from farmers to suppliers and consumers, challenges related to data integrity, trust, and coordination arise. Existing studies highlight the potential of blockchain technology to resolve these challenges through decentralized data governance and secure data storage and acquisition. However, research on blockchain in the context of precision agriculture remains fragmented and insufficiently synthesized making the use of this technology challenging for the community. This study offers a scoping review of blockchain-enabled PA systems in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR methodology. We examined one hundred peer-reviewed papers that were published between 2019 and 2025 in order to determine the factors that influence the adoption of blockchain technology, as well as architectural integration patterns, evaluation techniques, and obstacles that have been documented. The results present blockchain as a data governance and trust architecture that primarily supports environmental monitoring and precision agriculture decision-support systems rather than as a stand-alone technology. With few real-world implementations, the majority of systems continue to be simulation-based. The findings offer a methodical cross-layer view of how blockchain infrastructures can support dependable data management and decision making in precision agriculture, while also highlighting research gaps in integration modeling, thorough validation, and sustainability-focused evaluation of blockchain-enabled agricultural systems.
Methods: Scoping review of 100 peer-reviewed papers (2019â€“2025) using PRISMA-ScR, with structured search in Scopus and Google Scholar, screening, data extraction, thematic analysis, and descriptive quantitative mapping.
Results: Blockchain was mainly used as a trust and coordination layer for precision agriculture, with 74% of studies using simulations, 18% real-world deployments, and 8% hybrid evaluations. Ethereum was the most reported platform, and smart contracts were strongly associated with atmospheric sensors (0.50) and soil sensors (0.45).
Conclusions: Blockchain-enabled PA is promising for secure data exchange, access control, and automation, but large-scale deployment is constrained by scalability, energy, connectivity, complexity, and adoption barriers. The review calls for more real-world validation and environmentally sustainable evaluation.
