This study, therefore, considers blockchain technology as a medium for delivering information transparency and explores the application of a blockchain-based tool for reducing clients' influence in property valuation. Specifically, this study is pioneering in proposing, developing, and testing a blockchain-based solution for reducing client influence in property valuation, suggesting a promising avenue for increasing transparency in the process. This study involves several stages. Firstly, propchain, a blockchain-based mobile application, was developed and deployed on the Hyperledger Fabric Network, a permissioned blockchain network. The efficacy of the proposed solution was qualitatively tested by a single-round focus group held with valuers, bankers, and a loan customer who used the application to simulate a property valuation exercise for a mortgage. The findings suggest that blockchain technology could be a viable tool for reducing client influence in property valuations. However, specific challenges in the Nigerian context, such as data access, information verification, and stakeholder trust, present significant obstacles. These issues highlight the need for robust institutional support systems to enhance the efficacy of blockchain solutions in this domain. This study supports Levy and Schuck's (2005) assertion that increased information transparency can reduce client influence. Nevertheless, our research indicates that the successful implementation of blockchain in property valuation will require overcoming systemic barriers unique to the Nigerian environment. The implication of key findings is also discussed.
Methods: Design science and qualitative methods were used to develop Propchain and validate it through a single-round focus group. The application was deployed on Hyperledger Fabric and tested in a simulated mortgage valuation workflow with five participants.
Results: Five themes emerged: blockchain as useful for reducing client influence, ease of use, process modification, limiting challenges, and adoption mechanisms. Participants viewed Propchain positively, but noted that data access, verification, trust, and regulatory integration limited effectiveness.
Conclusions: Propchain on Hyperledger Fabric showed promise for improving transparency and reducing client influence in valuation, but could not fully eliminate it in Nigeria. The authors conclude that databases, legal-regulatory support, stakeholder trust, and monitoring systems must improve for effective adoption.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical design science study with qualitative validation of a prototype; proof-of-concept prototype tested in a simulated mortgage valuation workflow. Maturity is prototype/developmental, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation used a single-round Zoom focus group after a simulated valuation exercise, analyzed with thematic analysis in NVivo 12. Evidence is qualitative only; no quantitative performance metrics or benchmarking were reported.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Propchain was developed on Hyperledger Fabric, a permissioned blockchain network. The system used one CA, one orderer, two organizations, and two peer nodes; consensus specifics were not stated.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: An Android mobile app interfaced with Hyperledger Fabric via the client SDK, with Java chaincode on the backend. The deployment used AWS EC2 and AWS S3 for hosting and document storage; submitted documents were shared through the app without off-chain communication.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: The use case is property valuation for mortgage lending in Nigeria. Data include valuation requests, property documents, reports, and uploaded files used to support valuation transparency and reduce client influence.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Permissioned enrollment with username/password and role-based access, plus hashed transaction records, tamper resistance, and immutable timestamps were used. The paper addresses tampering, unauthorized access, and report revision; hacking and fraud are discussed as concerns.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: No formal standards integration such as LADM, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE is described. The system instead integrates blockchain with a mobile app and AWS storage through SDK-based implementation and file uploads.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The paper emphasizes regulatory oversight, professional association involvement, and compliance with valuation standards, especially ESVARBON in Nigeria. Legal support and institutional trust are presented as unresolved barriers rather than established arrangements.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Nigeria is the deployment context, and the system remains prototype-level. Main barriers are weak databases, data verification problems, stakeholder trust, regulatory compliance, access to property, safety concerns, and limited institutional capacity.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation focused on transparency, ease of use, and perceived ability to reduce client influence; no scalability, throughput, latency, or cost metrics were measured. The authors identify missing databases, no technical performance evaluation, and the need for real-life testing as key research gaps.

Source: Widening and deepening: territorial strategies and state building in Africa
Abstract: This article challenges the view of African states as weak regulators vis-Ã -vis foreign large-scale land acquisitions. Instead, building on theories of state building and territorialization, we argue that state power is contested but reasserted through two strategies: widening, that states actively leverage investment, infrastructure, and conservation to extend territorial authority; and deepening, that states further intensify its capacity to govern territory over time through increasingly sophisticated legal frameworks, policy instruments, and socio-technical innovations. We illustrate these two strategies through 24 empirical cases across 14 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, drawing on the authorsâ€™ primary fieldwork since 2018 in Uganda, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, and Kenya, together with an extensive review of secondary literature covering additional cases across the region. By tracing these processes, we recast the debate on land and power in Africa by showing that far from being eclipsed by the forces of global and local capital, African states actively instrumentalize it to entrench authority, reconfigure territorial relations with communities, and reshape spatial dimensions of governance, thus contributing to wider scholarship on state infrastructural power and the politics of territorialization.
Methods: Conceptual/theoretical article using a structured comparative analysis of 24 empirical cases across 14 sub-Saharan African countries. Evidence comes from primary fieldwork (2018â€“2024) in Uganda, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, and Kenya plus a review of secondary literature and policy/legal documents.
Results: The paper identifies two recurring state strategies: widening territorial authority through investment, infrastructure, and conservation, and deepening it through legal, bureaucratic, and socio-technical tools. Cases from Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania, Kenya, Mozambique, Uganda, and others show states reclassifying land, recentralizing control, and using digital systems to consolidate governance.
Conclusions: African states are not simply weak regulators; they actively instrumentalize external actors and land interventions to build territorial power. The authors also note limits from capacity constraints, fragmentation, donor agendas, and local resistance, so territorialization is contingent rather than fully coherent.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual/theoretical comparative study with empirical illustrations; not a technical implementation paper. Highest maturity is analytical framing and documented real-world policy/administrative practice, not a prototype or operational system.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is by mechanism-focused comparison of 24 cases, supported by fieldwork interviews, participant observation, and secondary literature review. Evidence is qualitative and illustrative, not quantitative benchmarking or experimentation.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain is mentioned only as an emerging tool for digitizing land registries, with a Ghana pilot involving Bitland Global and IBM and a planned DRC project with Duna RWA. No consensus mechanism or blockchain architecture is described.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: The paper discusses digital cadaster, GIS, e-governance platforms, land administration information systems, drones, and blockchain-based land recordation, but gives no detailed implementation stack. Integration is described only broadly as digitalization of registries and land administration.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: The domain is land governance, territorial control, and state building in African countries. Data and use cases include cadastral and land-registry data, titling, land allocation, customary tenure, conservation areas, and land-use mapping for investment, planning, and regulation.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: The paper does not describe explicit security mechanisms such as hashing, signatures, encryption, or access control. It mainly addresses threats of land dispossession, unauthorized access to land, and contested ownership through administrative and legal reclassification.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to LADM, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, or other interoperability standards, nor any detailed schema-mapping or API integration approach.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The paper emphasizes legal frameworks, policy instruments, land acts, zoning rules, conservation laws, and land boards as tools of territorial control. Governance is centered on state agencies working with donors, NGOs, investors, parastatals, and customary authorities, with frequent recentralization and administrative reclassification.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Key barriers include local resistance, capacity constraints, intra-state fragmentation, donor dependence, and contested customary tenure. The context is conceptual and comparative across sub-Saharan Africa, with many cases at policy, pilot, or administrative reform stages rather than fully operational deployment.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: No technical performance metrics are reported; the paperâ€™s criteria are territorial reach, administrative legibility, centralization, and normalization of authority. The main research gap identified is the need for fine-grained single-case and subnational studies of when widening and deepening succeed, stall, or are renegotiated.

Source: Blockchain technologies for interoperation of business processes in smart supply chains
Abstract: The Smart Manufacturing paradigm requires support by smart supply chains with capabilities of self-organizing and self-optimizing capabilities to accommodate uncertainties. Conventional supply chains face challenges in optimizing logistic processes and reducing overall costs of products and services. The emerging Internet of Things, Cyber-Physical Systems, and blockchain have laid the foundation to support interoperation in satisfying scalability, security, flexibility, and responsiveness of supply chains. Blockchain has shown potential in improving scalability and security. We are highly motivated to scrutinize technical obstacles of integrating blockchain into smart supply chains in the industrial Internet of Things environment. Our attempt is to integrate blockchain into Service-oriented Architecture for seamless interoperations. The system architecture and framework are presented and prototyped to enable Blockchain for the cooperation of business processes. The simulation has shown the effectiveness in improving the scalability, robustness, and adaptability of business processes in a smart supply chain.
Methods: Conceptual framework paper with a prototyped smart-supply-chain architecture and a land-ownership-transfer case example. Includes an implementation and simulation in AWS/RoR/PostgreSQL with PBFT and 10,000 transactions.
Results: Simulation showed linear time growth with transactions and logarithmic decrease with more nodes. With 10, 20, 50, and 100 nodes, maximum transactions per one-minute interval were 2200, 2000, 1500, and 1200; 1000 nodes could not be processed.
Conclusions: Blockchain integrated with SoA and PKI can improve interoperation, trust, scalability, robustness, and adaptability in smart supply chains. The authors note existing work is still highly fragmented and plan a prototype for land-ownership transfer and broader operations.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical design paper with conceptual framework and prototype/simulation validation. Maturity is prototype-level, with an implemented test system and case-study illustration rather than operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation combines a land-transfer case study, prototype implementation, and simulation/performance testing. Evidence is quantitative, reporting transaction throughput and timing under varying node counts.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Uses a permissioned blockchain system with PBFT consensus, 100 validator nodes, and 2/3 voting for block inclusion. Architecture combines public cryptocurrencies, permissioned government blockchains, sidechains, multisig/notary schemes, and smart contracts.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Implemented on AWS EC2 with Ruby on Rails 5.1.5, Puma, and PostgreSQL used as the blockchain ledger. Components include blockchain brokers, web APIs, smart contracts, SoA encapsulation, PKI/QoS blockchains, and callback functions.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Smart supply chains and business-process interoperation, illustrated by land ownership transfer with identity, tax, cryptocurrency payment, and land registry records. Data include ownership, identity, tax, and payment transactions.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses SHA-1 hashing, ECDSA digital signatures, multisig authorization, PKI endorsement, access control, and smart contracts. Addressed threats include tampering, trust problems, double spending, finality uncertainty, and malicious entities.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Integrates blockchain with Service-oriented Architecture using standardized APIs, message relays, smart contracts, sidechains, and blockchain brokers. Mentions standardization efforts including IEEE Project 2418, ISO/TC 307, and DIF.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Land transfer requires identity verification, legal rights checking, tax handling, and registry involvement. Governance relies on government agencies, permissioned consortium nodes, and certificate authorities; formal regulations for the blockchain interoperation are described as lacking.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include heterogeneous APIs, trust deficits, lack of standards/regulation, finality uncertainty, scalability limits, and permissioned/private-chain access constraints. Deployment context is a smart supply-chain/IoT setting, with prototype implementation and simulation.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluated scalability and processing time for 50-10,000 transactions across 10-100 nodes; throughput ranged from 2200 to 1200 transactions per minute as nodes increased. Research gaps include semantic interoperability, generic cross-chain interoperability, and scalable support beyond cryptocurrency use cases.

Source: Blockchain governance in the public sector: A conceptual framework for public management
Abstract: A key challenge behind the adoption of blockchain in the public sector is understanding the dynamics of blockchain governance. Based on a systematic literature review, this article analyzes different approaches to blockchain governance across disciplines and develops a comprehensive conceptual framework for the study of blockchain governance decisions in the public sector. The framework clusters nine types of governance decisions (infrastructure architecture, application architecture, interoperability, decision-making mechanism, incentive mechanism, consensus mechanism, organization of governance, accountability of governance, and control of governance) into three levels of analysis (micro, meso, and macro-levels). Drawing on public management theories and concepts, the article elucidates the implications of various governance choices in each level of governance and provides a primer for researchers and policy practitioners on the design of blockchain-based systems in the public sector.
Methods: Systematic literature review of 67 publications from ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Web of Science, followed by grounded theory and thematic analysis with open, axial, and selective coding.
Results: The review identified nine blockchain governance decisions clustered into micro, meso, and macro levels. It also derived 23 trade-off conditions among seven DLT properties and mapped governance choices such as consensus, incentives, accountability, and control.
Conclusions: Blockchain governance in the public sector requires aligning architecture and governance choices with policy objectives, public values, and institutional context. The authors call for more empirical, interdisciplinary research and note that the framework may apply beyond the public sector.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual framework paper based on systematic literature review and theory synthesis. It is at the conceptual proposal stage, not an implemented or operational system.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is through systematic review and conceptual/theoretical synthesis, using grounded theory and thematic coding of prior literature. No experimental, simulation, or prototype evidence is reported.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Discusses public, private, permissioned, and permissionless blockchains rather than proposing a single platform. Mentions Bitcoin, Ethereum, Hyperledger Fabric, R3 Corda, Quorum, PoW, PoS/DPoS, and PoA, plus a two-layer Swedish land-registry design storing hashes from a private chain on Bitcoin.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Focuses on blockchain infrastructure architecture, modular smart contracts, decentralized applications, and interoperability with existing IT infrastructure. Integration is discussed conceptually through cross-chain messaging, hardware/TLS links, and anchoring data between private and public chains.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Public-sector use cases include land registration, identity management, notarization, supply chain traceability, healthcare, education, corporate registration, data management, auditing, energy markets, taxation, and voting. The paper is not a single-domain implementation study.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Addresses immutability, integrity, traceability, cryptographic consensus, smart contracts, and keyless signature infrastructure. Threats discussed include tampering, security/privacy risks, 51% attacks, denial-of-service, malicious software modifications, and compromised validators.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Interoperability is treated as a governance decision involving legal, technical, semantic, and organizational alignment. The paper cites EIF, ISO, ISDA, FPL, KSI, and EBSI, but does not report a specific implemented standards mapping.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Emphasizes policy objectives, public values, institutional frameworks, accountability, and constitutional/legal foundations. It discusses legislative, market, political-administrative, and socio-technological conditions, plus GDPR and sectoral regulations as determinants of governance choices.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include lack of regulation, security and privacy concerns, insufficient interoperable infrastructure, energy-intensive transactions, and absence of effective governance models. Context spans public-sector organizations globally, with examples from Estonia, Sweden, the EU/EBSI, and the Netherlands.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Key criteria are scalability, security, privacy, throughput, finality, energy use, and transaction costs. The paper reports qualitative trade-offs only and identifies gaps in empirical evidence, grey literature coverage, and interdisciplinary research.

Source: Further modelling of LADM's rights, restrictions and responsibilities (RRRs)
Abstract: This paper proposes a more detailed classification of the legal part of the Land Administration Domain Model (LADM), ISO 19152 (i.e. interests in land), than described in the current standard by further developing the LADM's 'right', 'restriction' and 'responsibility' (RRR) class and associated code lists. Besides the more obvious formal right descriptions, this paper also deals with informal rights' descriptions as introduced in the Social Tenure Domain Model (STDM) as a foundation for further LADM development. The authors base their research on the Legal Cadastral Domain Model, as developed by and described in the Ph.D. thesis of Paasch, which is used as a conceptual basis for adding an additional level to the LADM. Interests in land can be classified in this model as limiting or beneficial to real property ownership. The extended classification is further based on the paradigm that there are two major types of interest in land, privately agreed interests and regulations imposed by a public agency. The incorporation of a specialized classification of RRRs in the LADM is of value for more inclusion of social tenure in (inter-)national land administration registers. The LADM allows national profiles to be added to the standard, however, such profiles are relevant within a country. These profiles are needed in cases where detailed data of interests in land have to be exchanged internationally. International data exchange requires maintenance of code tables representing the different RRRs in use within countries. OICRF has announced an initiative in support to this.
Methods: Conceptual LADM extension paper using the Legal Cadastral Domain Model and STDM as the basis for refining RRR classes and code lists. It develops a hierarchical modeling proposal with UML and ontology-oriented discussion, illustrated by examples from customary and informal tenure.
Results: Proposes new or refined RRR subclasses for private and public law, plus code-list based refinement for common, property-to-property, party-to-property, latent, general, and specific interests. Argues that code lists, not more classes, are often the better way to represent detailed RRR types and supports this with examples.
Conclusions: LADM can be extended to represent formal, customary, and informal RRRs at a more detailed level, but international exchange requires maintained code tables. Further research is recommended on code-table governance and semantic technologies for defining RRR types.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual standards/modeling paper proposing an extended LADM legal classification; no implemented system or field deployment is reported. Highest maturity is a conceptual proposal with example class and code-list design.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is by conceptual analysis, comparison with existing standards/models, and illustrative modeling examples. No experiments, simulations, or quantitative evaluation metrics are reported.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to blockchain platforms, consensus mechanisms, or blockchain architecture.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Discusses LADM, UML, code lists, semantic technologies (RDF/SKOS), and linked data for representing land-administration concepts. No implemented software stack, database, API, or deployment architecture is described.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land administration and cadastral/legal land records, especially rights, restrictions, responsibilities, and tenure types. The use case is modeling and exchanging formal, customary, and informal interests in land in national and international registers.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to security mechanisms or specific threats.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Built around LADM ISO 19152:2012, with references to STDM, Legal Cadastral Domain Model, INSPIRE, ISO 19135, ISO 3166, RDF, SKOS, and EULIS. Integration is discussed through code-table harmonization, hierarchical identifiers, and linked-data/semantic approaches rather than implemented data exchange.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Focuses on legal recognition of formal, customary, and informal tenure, and on how RRRs relate to private and public law. Governance issues include who maintains code tables, possible roles for ISO/TC211, FIG, and OICRF, and the need for institutional arrangements for international exchange.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Key barriers are complexity of adding new classes, lack of internationally maintained code tables, and limitations of existing land information systems for informal and customary tenure. The context is an international land-administration standards setting rather than a deployed country system.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: No performance metrics are reported. The paper identifies gaps in standardized definitions, maintenance of code lists, and semantic modeling of RRR types for international interoperability.

Source: LADM-compliant field data collector for cadastral surveyors
Abstract: Completeness in land registration and efficiency in land-information services have emerged as global prerequisites to achieve sustainable development goals (SDG) and ease of doing business (EoDB). Land registration is a national priority for Indonesia, which aims to complete the process for all unregistered land parcels in the country and validate the quality of previously registered and certified land parcels before 2025. Efforts on this front uncovered the need for adopting mobile technology, including various data collection tools for surveyors and project contractors. Unfortunately, these tools present data standardization and data usability challenges, hindering efficient first titling and forensic titling, or title validation for imposing quality improvements. Data collection could be executed quickly and efficiently by aligning to Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) standards. This paper presents the design for and the test results of an LADM-compliant field data collector to help surveyors support first-titling and forensic-titling survey scenarios. The mobile application utilizes Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) GeoPackage to access and locally store spatial and textual data retrieved from national cadastral databases. The mobile app allows surveyors to connect with external sensors including the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) to accurately survey land. It employs a fingerprint reader for validating personal information via Bluetooth. Surveyors can map and edit data by applying drawing tools like snapping, splitting, and merging parcels. In addition to spatial data creation, this tool captures physical documents and records boundary validation digitally. This paper presents a field test for real field activities to validate old land titles.
Methods: Design-and-test study of an LADM-compliant mobile field data collector. Tested in two pilot villages in Bali, including GNSS surveying, field interviews, and title-validation workflows.
Results: The app was tested on 20 parcels for spatial accuracy and used over three months to plot and validate 5,970 titles. It reduced the land-registration workflow from 13 sub-activities to 5 and supported direct synchronization to the survey dashboard.
Conclusions: GeoPackage-based mobile data capture improved efficiency, usability, and collaboration for first titling and forensic titling. The authors conclude it can increase the completeness and reliability of land-administration information relative to traditional surveys.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical design-and-testing study of an implemented mobile application; proof-of-concept/pilot field evaluation with real-world use in Indonesian villages.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Field pilot testing, GNSS-based parcel measurement, field interviews, and comparison of mapped titles against survey documents. Quantitative evidence includes 20 parcels, 5,970 titles, and workflow reduction claims.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to blockchain platform, consensus, or blockchain architecture.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Android mobile app built with NGA GeoPackage mobile libraries and Google Maps SDK, plus civil registry web services, WMS requests, a survey dashboard website, and OAuth 2.0 single sign-on. Data are stored in a single GeoPackage file and synchronized with national cadastral and civil registry systems.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land administration and cadastral surveying for first titling and forensic title validation. Data include parcel boundaries, party/identity data, ownership documents, cadastral maps, and civil registry records.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Fingerprint authentication, OAuth 2.0 secure access, and digital capture of documents support validation and controlled access. The app addresses overlapping claims, title fraud/invalid titles, and data reliability issues.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: LADM/ISO 19152 is the main organizing standard, integrated with OGC GeoPackage, WMS, and civil registry web services. The app also references LADM classes and synchronizes with national cadastral databases.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Built around Indonesian land registration regulations and government-to-government access to civil registry data. Local land offices approve third-party users, and surveyors collect legal/administrative evidence for official titling workflows.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Deployment context is Indonesia, with pilots in Bali villages and support for seven provinces under AARP. Barriers include fragmented data, non-certified parcels, overlapping claims, poor interoperability, and the need for offline use and user training.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Criteria included spatial accuracy, attribute accuracy, boundary correctness, and less than 5% difference between old and new measurements. The paper notes no exact metric for title-validation performance beyond field-test outcomes and acknowledges accuracy trade-offs.

Source: Easement spatialization with two cases based on LADM and BIM
Abstract: An easement is an important usufructuary right, and its main purpose is that one party wants to use the property of others to improve the benefits and interests of his own real estate. Because of the increasing population and accelerating urbanization urban planners have focused on the development and utilization of three-dimensional urban space, namely, underground, near ground and aboveground space, to use the spatial resources fully. Therefore, jurisprudence-confined planar easement must be combined with spatial information from two dimensions (2D) to three dimensions (3D), as well as 2D property boundaries to be extended to 3D to adapt to urban development. This paper focuses on the easement of access, which is the right to cross the property to go to and from another, under the context of 3D cadastres. The model of easement spatialization based on BIM (Building Information Model) specified by IFC (Industry Foundation Class) standards is constructed and analysed. The servient owner and the dominant owner of the easement can be linked because they are both attached to the same physical space. This paper takes a multistory building having individually owned condominium units as an example to demonstrate how to access the semantic information associated with the geometric information of 3D property objects in the BIM/IFC. The research results show that BIM/IFC can optimize the complex presentation of 3D property attributes and is an effective carrier of easement spatialization. The combination of legal information and spatial information of 3D properties not only optimizes the operation and maintenance of buildings but also improves land management and accelerates the development of 3D cities.
Methods: Conceptual modeling paper with two case studies. It combines LADM for legal modeling and IFC/BIM for 3D spatial modeling, then illustrates the approach in a multistory building with underground space.
Results: The model links servient and dominant owners through shared 3D physical space and supports spatial analysis of easements. The cases show IFC/BIM can represent 3D legal property objects and visualize access paths across aboveground and underground spaces.
Conclusions: Easement spatialization in 3D is feasible using LADM and IFC, and it can improve understanding of ownership boundaries and reduce disputes. The authors conclude that easements can apply to arbitrary points in a 3D environment, not only ground-surface access.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual model with illustrative case-study validation; prototype-level 3D cadastral spatialization for easements. The highest maturity demonstrated is a modeled and visualized proof of concept, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is by two illustrative case studies implemented in BIM tools (Revit and Solibri) on a multistory building. Evidence is qualitative and visual, showing path and ownership-space representation rather than quantitative benchmarking.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to blockchain platforms, consensus mechanisms, or blockchain architecture.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: LADM models legal concepts and IFC/BIM models physical building space, with legal documents linked as external references in IFC. The implementation uses Revit for space partitioning and Solibri for 3D visualization and querying.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: 3D cadastre and land administration for easement of access in multistory buildings with underground, surface, and aboveground space. The use case is modeling property ownership, access paths, and legal space for condominium units.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: The paper addresses legal-spatial clarity rather than cryptographic security. It mentions avoiding ownership disputes and linking owners to shared space, but no hashing, signatures, encryption, or explicit threat model is presented.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: LADM (ISO 19152) is combined with IFC/BIM standards, and IFC is described as an exchange format for interoperability. The paper also references ISO and OGC-based spatial representations, but gives no detailed schema mapping or versioned implementation.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The paper grounds easements in civil-law concepts and cites Chinese, German, French, Swiss, and U.S. legal treatments. It does not propose a governance process, but notes China lacks comprehensive regulation for land-space rights registration and effectiveness.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Main barriers are unclear spatial rights, abstract legal descriptions, and lack of comprehensive regulation for land-space rights in China. The context is China and 3D cadastral management for multistory buildings; the system is conceptual with case-study demonstration.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: The main goal is better spatial representation of 3D legal property objects and clearer access-path visualization. A research gap is the limited attention to aboveground-surface-underground connectivity and the lack of comprehensive metrics or quantitative performance evaluation.

Source: Design and implementation of a LADM-based external archive data model for land registry and cadastre transactions in Turkey: A case study of municipality
Abstract: It is pointed out that even though Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) standards offers a conceptual scheme defining the legal and geometrical components of real estate, it is important to be compatible with other databases (e.g. with land cover data, archive data, land valuation data and taxation data) that may be related to the model. In the model, the archive data model, which is defined as one of the external data structures, provides a class structure in which the information and documents necessary for land registry and cadastral transactions are represented. According to this class structure, necessary information and documents are kept in archive. Thanks to this structure which enables follow-up of transactions, similar transactions are prevented from being repeated. The General Directorate of Land Registry and Cadastre (GDLRC) performs 25 different land registry and cadastral transactions. During these transactions, some documents (e.g. power of attorney, real estate value statement, building occupancy permit, authority certificate, etc.) are requested from various external institutions (e.g. Municipality, Notary, Governor's Office, Court, etc.). Considering the fact that 8 million transactions are made annually, approximately 20 million documents are manually controlled. The manual control of such an amount of documents can cause waste of time and paper and some forgery. There is a need for external data management in accordance with LADM that enables data sharing between institutions to check whether the documents requested from external institutions during the transactions have up-to-date and correct information content. This study focuses on the online management of the information and documents requested by the GDLRC from the Municipality during the land registry and cadastral transactions. In this context, an external data model for the management of relevant information and documents is proposed. A web-based application was developed to prove that the proposed model is feasible. The application made possible the online exchange and inquiry of information and documents in the digital environment. As a result, it has been observed that thanks to the application, the time for the transaction was shortened, no document in paper form was required as the documents were inquired in a digital environment and fraud was reduced.
Methods: Case study in Turkey using LADM/ISO 19152 as the framework. The authors performed transaction-document and document-institution analyses, designed UML-based external data models, built a SQL Server database, and tested a web service with four municipal document queries.
Results: The web-based application enabled online exchange and inquiry of municipal documents, shortened transaction time, removed paper-document handling, and reduced fraud. The model standardized external data sharing and supported integration with TAKBIS and MEGSIS via a Real Property ID.
Conclusions: A LADM-compatible municipality external data model can support digital archiving, online inquiry, and better document management for land registry and cadastre transactions. The authors note that legal regulation, institutional readiness, security, and broader institutional integration are still needed.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical case study / prototype development and feasibility test. The work proposes a conceptual-to-implemented external data model and demonstrates it in a web-based test application, but not as an operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Evaluation was through prototype implementation and functional testing using four web-service queries for municipal documents. Evidence is mainly qualitative with implementation demonstration and observed workflow improvements, not formal statistical benchmarking.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to blockchain, consensus mechanisms, or blockchain architecture.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: UML-based external data model, MS SQL Server 2012 database, MS Visual Studio 2013 / Visual C# interface, and a C# web service with XML-based query methods. The system exchanges document data through web services and uses a 19-digit Real Property ID for lookup and integration.

Abstract: We extend the Camenisch-Lysyanskaya anonymous credential system such that selective disclosure of attributes becomes highly efficient. Abstract: BBS signatures were implicitly proposed by Boneh, Boyen, and Shacham (CRYPTO â€™04) as part of their group signature scheme, and explicitly cast as stand-alone signatures by Camenisch and Lysyanskaya (CRYPTO â€™04). Finally, we show that BBS satisfies one-more unforgeability in the algebraic group model in a scenario, arising in the context of credentials, where the signer can be asked to sign arbitrary group elements, meant to be commitments, without seeing their openings.

Abstract: Public-key based certificates provide a standard way to prove one's identity, as attested by some certificate authority (CA). However, plain certificates provide a binary identification: either the whole identity of the subject is known, or nothing is known. Additionally, we demonstrate how trees from multiple sources can be combined together by modifying the tree structure. The results show that our approach can perform about 200 identity verifications per second, while the best competing approach can perform only about 2-5 verifications per second. Source: Revisiting cryptographic accumulators, additional properties and relations to other primitives
Abstract: Cryptographic accumulators allow to accumulate a finite set of values into a single succinct accumulator. For every accumulated value, one can efficiently compute a witness, which certifies its membership in the accumulator. However, it is computationally infeasible to find a witness for any non-accumulated value. Since their introduction, various accumulator schemes for numerous practical applications and with different features have been proposed. Unfortunately, to date there is no unifying model capturing all existing features. Such a model can turn out to be valuable as it allows to use accumulators in a black-box fashion. To this end, we propose a unified formal model for (randomized) cryptographic accumulators which covers static and dynamic accumulators, their universal features and includes the notions of undeniability and indistinguishability. Additionally, we provide an exhaustive classification of all existing schemes. In doing so, it turns out that most accumulators are distinguishable. Fortunately, a simple, light-weight generic transformation allows to make many existing dynamic accumulator schemes indistinguishable. As this transformation, however, comes at the cost of reduced collision freeness, we additionally propose the first indistinguishable scheme that does not suffer from this shortcoming. Finally, we employ our unified model for presenting a black-box construction of commitments from indistinguishable accumulators as well as a blackbox construction of indistinguishable, undeniable universal accumulators from zero-knowledge sets. Latter yields the first universal accumulator construction that provides indistinguishability.

Source: Succinct Zero-Knowledge Batch Proofs for Set Accumulators
Abstract: Cryptographic accumulators are a common solution to proving information about a large set S. They allow one to compute a short digest of S and short certificates of some of its basic properties, notably membership of an element. Accumulators also allow one to track set updates: a new accumulator is obtained by inserting/deleting a given element. In this work we consider the problem of generating membership and update proofs for em batches of elements so that we can succinctly prove additional properties of the elements (i.e., proofs are of constant size regardless of the batch size), and we can preserve privacy. Solving this problem would allow obtaining blockchain systems with improved privacy and scalability. The state-of-the-art approach to achieve this goal is to combine accumulators (typically Merkle trees) with zkSNARKs. This solution is however expensive for provers and does not scale for large batches of elements. In particular, there is no scalable solution for proving batch membership proofs when we require zero-knowledge (a standard definition of privacy-preserving protocols). We design and implement two main schemes: 1) harisa, which proves batch membership in zero-knowledge; 2) insarisa, which proves batch updates. For batch membership, the prover in harisa is orders of magnitude faster than existing approaches based on Merkle trees (depending on the hash function). For batch updates we get similar cost savings compared to approaches based on Merkle trees; we also improve over the recent solution of Ozdemir et al. [USENIX'20].

Source: Oblivious Accumulators
Abstract: A cryptographic accumulator is a succinct set commitment scheme with efficient (non-)membership proofs that typically supports updates (additions and deletions) on the accumulated set. When elements are added to or deleted from the set, an update message is issued. The collection of all the update messages essentially leaks the underlying accumulated set which in certain applications is not desirable. In this work, we define oblivious accumulators, a set commitment with concise membership proofs that hides the elements and the set size from every entity: an outsider, a verifier or other element holders. We formalize this notion of privacy via two properties: element hiding and add-delete indistinguishability. We also define almost-oblivious accumulators, that only achieve a weaker notion of privacy called add-delete unlinkability. Such accumulators hide the elements but not the set size. We consider the trapdoorless, decentralized setting where different users can add and delete elements from the accumulator and compute membership proofs. We then give a generic construction of an oblivious accumulator based on key-value commitments (KVC). We also show a generic way to construct KVCs from an accumulator and a vector commitment scheme. Finally, we give lower bounds on the communication (size of update messages) required for oblivious accumulators and almost-oblivious accumulators.
Methods: The paper defines oblivious and almost-oblivious accumulators in a trapdoorless, decentralized setting and gives generic constructions based on key-value commitments (KVC). It also derives lower bounds on update-message communication and a generic KVC construction from an accumulator and a vector commitment scheme.

Conclusions: Cryptographic accumulators can be strengthened to hide element membership and, in the stronger variant, set size as well. The work concludes with communication lower bounds showing the cost of such privacy.

Source: EPA: An efficient and privacy-aware revocation mechanism for vehicular ad hoc networks
Abstract: Security is vital for the reliable operation of vehicular ad hoc networks (VANETs). One of the critical security issues is the revocation of misbehaving vehicles. While essential, revocation checking can leak private information. In particular, repositories receiving the certificate status queries could infer the identity of the vehicles posing the query and the target of the query. An important loss of privacy results from this ability to tie the checking vehicle with the query's target, due to their likely willingness to communicate. In this paper, we propose an Efficient and Privacy-Aware revocation Mechanism (EPA) based on the use of Merkle Hash Trees (MHT) and a Crowds-based anonymous protocol, which replaces the time-consuming certificate revocation lists checking process. EPA provides explicit, concise, authenticated and unforgeable information about the revocation status of each certificate while preserving the users' privacy. Moreover, EPA reduces the security overhead for certificate status checking, and enhances the availability and usability of the revocation data. By conducting a detailed performance evaluation, EPA is demonstrated to be reliable, efficient, and scalable.

Abstract: Cryptographic accumulators allowto succinctly represent a set by an accumulation value with respect to which short (non-)membership proofs about the set can be efficiently constructed and verified. Traditionally, their security captures soundness but offers no privacy: Convincing proofs reliably encode set membership, but they may well leak information about the accumulated set. In this paper we put forward a strong privacy-preserving enhancement by introducing and devising zero-knowledge accumulators that additionally provide hiding guarantees: Accumulation values and proofs leak nothing about a dynamic set that evolves via element insertions/ deletions. We formalize the new property using the standard realideal paradigm, namely demanding that an adaptive adversary with access to query/update oracles, cannot tell whether he interacts with honest protocol executions or a simulator fully ignorant of the set (even of the type of updates on it). We rigorously compare the new primitive to existing ones for privacy-preserving verification of set membership (or other relations) and derive interesting implications among related security definitions, showing that zero-knowledge accumulators offer stronger privacy than recent related works by Naor et al. [TCC 2015] and Derler et al. [CT-RSA 2015]. We construct the first dynamic universal zeroknowledge accumulator that we show to be perfect zero-knowledge and secure under the q-Strong Bilinear Diffie-Hellman assumption. Finally, we extend our new privacy notion and our new construction to provide privacy-preserving proofs also for an authenticated dynamic set collectionâ€”a primitive for efficiently verifying more elaborate set operations, beyond set-membership. We introduce a primitive that supports a zero-knowledge verifiable set algebra: Succinct proofs for union, intersection and set difference queries over a dynamically evolving collection of sets can be efficiently constructed and optimally verified, whileâ€”for the first timeâ€”they leak nothing about the collection beyond the query result.

Source: ALLOSAUR: Accumulator with Low-Latency Oblivious Sublinear Anonymous credential Updates with Revocations
Abstract: A cryptographic accumulator is a compressed data structure with associated algorithms used for secure membership testing. In the growing space of digital credentials, accumulators are used to manage sets of valid credentials, giving efficient and anonymous methods for credential holders to prove their validity. Unlike traditional credentials like digital signatures, one can easily revoke credentials with an accumulator; however, each revocation forces existing credential holders to engage in an expensive update process. Previous works make this faster and easier by sacrificing anonymity. To improve performance without compromising privacy, we present ALLOSAUR, a multi-party accumulator based on pairings. In ALLOSAUR, we eliminate the cost of accumulating new credentials, let â€œcredential managersâ€ manage the accumulator values with secure multiparty computation, and allow anonymous credential updates with a square-root reduction in communication costs as compared to existing work. A deployed digital credential system is a vast and complicated system, and existing formalisms do not fully address the scope or power of a real-world adversary. We develop a thorough â€œUC-styleâ€ formalism that allows arbitrary malicious behaviour from an adversary controlling a minority of credential managers and arbitrary numbers of users, credentials, and verifiers. In our new formalism we present a novel definition of privacy that captures as much anonymity as possible while accounting for inevitable losses from interaction with the system. The detail in our formalism reveals real-world issues in existing accumulator constructions, all of which ALLOSAUR avoids. The typical bottleneck in accumulator-based digital credential systems is handling revocations of credentials. Our proof-of-concept implementation of ALLOSAUR can update over 1000 revocations with less than half a second of total computation and 16 kB communication, which is at least a 5x improvement over the previous state-of-the-art in both metrics.

Source: An accumulator based on bilinear maps and efficient revocation for anonymous credentials
Abstract: The success of electronic authentication systems, be it e- ID card systems or Internet authentication systems such as CardSpace, highly depends on the provided level of user-privacy. Thereby, an important requirement is an efficient means for revocation of the authentication credentials. In this paper we consider the problem of revocation for certificate-based privacy-protecting authentication systems. To date, the most efficient solutions for revocation for such systems are based on cryptographic accumulators. Here, an accumulate of all currently valid certificates is published regularly and each user holds a witness enabling her to prove the validity of her (anonymous) credential while retaining anonymity. Unfortunately, the users' witnesses must be updated at least each time a credential is revoked. For the know solutions, these updates are computationally very expensive for users and/or certificate issuers which is very problematic as revocation is a frequent event as practice shows. In this paper, we propose a new dynamic accumulator scheme based on bilinear maps and show how to apply it to the problem of revocation of anonymous credentials. In the resulting scheme, proving a credential's validity and updating witnesses both come at (virtually) no cost for credential owners and verifiers. In particular, updating a witness requires the issuer to do only one multiplication per addition or revocation of a credential and can also be delegated to untrusted entities from which a user could just retrieve the updated witness. We believe that thereby we provide the first authentication system offering privacy protection suitable for implementation with electronic tokens such as eID cards or drivers' licenses. Source: A novel game theory based reliable proof-of-stake consensus mechanism for blockchain
Abstract: The prominent achievement of blockchain technology stimulates exceptional innovation. The major component of blockchain is the consensus mechanism. The standard consensus mechanisms specifically Proof-of-Work (PoW) rely on mining procedures and stake-based mechanisms such as Proof-of-Stake (PoS) rely on massive stake investment as the sole criteria for selection of leader nodes. However, PoW impose huge computational power requirements and latter may incorporate malicious nodes as leader nodes in anonymous blockchain. These issues might fuel the way for distrust among the participants in blockchain. Henceforth, a novel game theory based reliable PoS mechanism for blockchain has been proposed. Federated learning has been used to compute trust_score for each node. The nodes are trained on locally generated dataset. Further, a game theoretic approach has been proposed that uses a reward and punishment scheme to ensure threshold level of trust_score maintenance by each node. Finally, a crop insurance use case has been developed with the consensus mechanism and blockchain coded in python. The insurance claims are made to operate through smart contract based mobile app system to impart more authenticity. The system is tested and results show an intrusion accomplishment rate reduced by approximate 40% when compared to the standard PoS mechanism and by approximately 33% for algorand, 29% for ouroboros and 20% for tendermint. The mean absolute error also decreases by 30% within specific time. Furthermore, the proposed federated learning-based system is compared with basic neural network-based machine learning model and the results reveal that a significant reduction in average training time amounting to 8.35 second is achieved. Test accuracy has also been analyzed for various learning mechanisms.

Source: A survey of blockchain consensus algorithms performance evaluation criteria
Abstract: How to reach an agreement in a blockchain network is a complex and important task that is defined as a consensus problem and has wide applications in reality including distributed computing, load balancing, and transaction validation in blockchains. Based on their inherent specifications, each algorithm has a different domain of applicability that yields to propose several performance criteria for the evaluation of these algorithms. To overview and provide a basis of comparison for further work in the field, a set of incommensurable and conflicting performance evaluation criteria is identified and weighted by the pairwise comparison method. These criteria are classified into four categories including algorithmsâ€™ throughput, the profitability of mining, degree of decentralization and consensus algorithms vulnerabilities and security issues. Based on the proposed framework, the pros and cons of consensus algorithms are systematically analyzed and compared in order to provide a deep understanding of the existing research challenges and clarify the future study directions.

Abstract: In this paper, the researcher suggests a secure deep learning-based DDoS detection system that implements a Modified AlexNet with Dual Attention Mechanism, Paillier Homomorphic Encryption (PHE), and blockchain technology to ensure data integrity and confidentiality in the IoT setting. Source: Challenges and opportunities of blockchain energy applications: Interrelatedness among technological, economic, social, environmental, and institutional dimensions
Abstract: The energy sector is undergoing a transition of decarbonization, decentralization, and digitalization. This paper explores the application of blockchain in this transition. Source: Proof of service power: A blockchain consensus for cloud manufacturing
Abstract: With the gradual promotion and in-depth application of cloud manufacturing platform, some deep-seated problems restricting enterprises to go to the cloud are gradually exposed. Lack of trust and security of cloud manufacturing platforms are the bottleneck problems. How to ensure the credit of both trading sides and reduce the transaction risk and transaction cost are still urgent problems to be solved. In recent years, with the continuous development and maturity of blockchain technology, it has attracted widespread attention in the manufacturing field. Its characteristics of trustlessness, anti-tampering, traceability, and high transparency provide new ideas for the development of cloud manufacturing platforms and solving the above problems. However, the traditional consensus protocol has problems such as token dependence and high energy consumption, which is not suitable for the special scenario of cloud manufacturing with a large number of big deals. This paper proposes a blockchain consensus protocol of â€œProof of Service Powerâ€ (PoSP) for application scenarios of cloud manufacturing. The consensus mechanism uses historical transaction information accumulated by member nodes in a cloud manufacturing system to calculate the service power of member nodes, which greatly reduces energy consumption in the Proof of Work (PoW) process. An introduction of the credit incentive mechanism makes PoSP consensus protocol get rid of token dependence while providing a quantitative basis for trust evaluation for each participant in the cloud manufacturing system. The experimental results show that the consensus mechanism for proof of service power has a good incentive effect, and it has lower energy consumption and higher transaction per second (TPS) than the proof of work and proof of stake (PoS). This study provides new ideas and a reference pattern for the application of blockchain technology in cloud manufacturing platform.

Conclusions: PoSP is presented as a cloud-manufacturing-oriented consensus that reduces token dependence and improves trust management. Future work should expand service-power features and improve decentralization while preserving node incentives.

Abstract: In this paper, the researcher suggests a secure deep learning-based DDoS detection system that implements a Modified AlexNet with Dual Attention Mechanism, Paillier Homomorphic Encryption (PHE), and blockchain technology to ensure data integrity and confidentiality in the IoT setting. Source: The Byzantine Generals Problem
Abstract: Reliable computer systems must handle malfunctioning components that give conflicting information to different parts of the system. This situation can be expressed abstractly in terms of a group of generals of the Byzantine army camped with their troops around an enemy city. Communicating only by messenger, the generals must agree upon a common battle plan. However, one or more of them may be traitors who will try to confuse the others. The problem is to find an algorithm to ensure that the loyal generals will reach agreement. It is shown that, using only oral messages, this problem is solvable if and only if more than two-thirds of the generals are loyal; so a single traitor can confound two loyal generals. With unforgeable written messages, the problem is solvable for any number of generals and possible traitors. Applications of the solutions to reliable computer systems are then discussed. Abstract: Clients' influence remains a significant issue in the property valuation industry, particularly in emerging countries like Nigeria, where existing solutions have proven ineffective. Source: A systematic review of the institutional success factors for blockchain-based land administration
Abstract: The land administration systems have witnessed many innovative technologies in the attempt to revolutionalize the task of recording land and property rights. One such revolution is the transition toward blockchain-based land administration. Like most technologies, blockchain-based land administration projects are not immune to failures, early adopters have encountered challenges, and several pilot cases have failed. Institutional factors have proven to be issues that can hinder the successful adoption of technological innovations such as blockchain-based land administration.
