A systematic literature review of 37 studies resulted in the extraction of 18 related institutional factors critical to adopting blockchain-based land administration projects. Using Scott's three-pillar framework, the factors were divided into three dimensions: regulatory, organisational and cultural environment. Despite the popular opinion that the regulatory environment is integral to adopting blockchain-based land administration, our review suggests that a mutual co-existence and interplay between all the factors is key to the success of blockchain-based land projects. This study concludes that the adoption of blockchain-based land projects can be enhanced by understanding the institutional factors necessary to adopt blockchain-based land administration.
Methods: Systematic literature review of blockchain-based land administration using Scopus, 2008â€“2022. Final synthesis covered 37 studies and used Scottâ€™s three-pillar framework to categorize institutional factors.
Results: The review extracted 18 institutional success factors. The most emphasized were government support, political stability, public-private partnership, public trust, stakeholder knowledge/experience, collaboration/communication, and regulatory clarity.
Conclusions: Blockchain-based land administration success depends on the interplay of regulatory, organizational, and cultural-cognitive support, not regulation alone. The review proposes a conceptual framework and notes future empirical testing is needed.
Study Classification and Maturity: Systematic review and conceptual framework paper on blockchain-based land administration. Maturity is conceptual/synthesis level, not an implemented or tested system.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is by systematic review and thematic/citation-frequency synthesis of 37 studies, plus conceptual framework development. No prototype, simulation, or field experiment is reported.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: No specific blockchain platform is evaluated; the paper discusses blockchain generically. It describes public, private, and hybrid architectures, and mentions consensus protocols and proof of work in general terms.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: No implementation stack is described. The paper only mentions blockchain, smart contracts, and interoperable land administration systems at a conceptual level, without backend, database, API, or deployment details.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land administration and land registration, focused on land rights, ownership records, spatial information, valuation, taxation, and land dispute resolution. The paper addresses legal, geospatial, and technical land data.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Discussed mechanisms include hashing, immutability, consensus, smart contracts, digital identity authentication, and multi-signature transactions. Threats include tampering, unauthorized alteration, corruption, identity fraud, privacy leakage, and cyberattacks.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Interoperability is discussed generally as sharing and verifying information across blockchain networks and coordinating land agencies. No LADM/ISO 19152, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, or specific schema integration is implemented.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The paper emphasizes regulatory clarity, legal compliance, governance mechanisms, and statutory compatibility for blockchain land administration. It notes the need to align smart contracts, identity management, privacy, and land-dispute handling with existing laws.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include political instability, regulatory ambiguity, cultural resistance, low digital literacy, limited internet connectivity, lack of expertise, incomplete digitization, scalability, security, and high electricity consumption. The context is blockchain-based land administration across countries such as Georgia, Ghana, Sweden, Ukraine, Honduras, and Dubai.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation criteria were citation frequency and institutional relevance, not system performance metrics. The paper identifies a gap in empirical testing and notes no rigorous quantitative assessment; future work should test factors with primary survey data.

Source: Blockchainâ€™s Grand Promise for the Real Estate Sector: A Systematic Review
Abstract: In recent years, blockchain technology has received increasing attention in the real estate literature. Moreover, recent evidence suggests that blockchains could provide some added benefits for the real estate sector even in the current hybrid settings, where blockchain is usually just an add-on to existing systems. This research provides an up-to-date and systematic understanding of blockchainâ€™s theoretical potential, pros, and cons for the real estate sector. The research aims to understand why and where to apply blockchain in real estate by conducting a systematic review that identified 296 relevant documents and performed a thematic content analysis. The identified blockchain adoption proposals were classified using standardized real estate vocabulary. Most of the literature focused on blockchain possibilities within land administration, followed by property transactions, real estate investment, leasing and renting, and real estate administration. However, real estate development and real estate maintenance did not appear as attractive real estate subsectors for blockchain. This paper provides a detailed analysis of blockchain technologyâ€™s possibilities for each real estate subsector, i.e., blockchain merits, and discusses the pros and cons. Last, this review provides suggestions for future research directions.
Methods: Systematic review of real estate blockchain literature identifying 296 relevant documents, with thematic content analysis and classification using standardized real estate vocabulary.
Results: Most literature focused on land administration, followed by property transactions, real estate investment, leasing/renting, and real estate administration. Real estate development and maintenance were not attractive subsectors for blockchain.
Conclusions: Blockchain has theoretical promise for real estate, especially as an add-on to existing hybrid systems, but its pros and cons vary by subsector and more research is needed.
Study Classification and Maturity: Systematic review of blockchain applications in real estate; conceptual synthesis rather than an implemented system, with evidence centered on proposed adoption use cases.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Evidence is a systematic review and thematic content analysis of 296 documents; no prototype, simulation, or empirical field evaluation is reported.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Information Not Found: The abstract does not contain any reference to a specific blockchain platform, consensus mechanism, or architecture.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Information Not Found: The abstract does not contain any reference to a technical implementation stack, system components, or integrations.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Real estate sector applications, especially land administration, property transactions, real estate investment, leasing/renting, and real estate administration.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Information Not Found: The abstract does not contain any reference to security mechanisms or specific threats addressed.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Standardized real estate vocabulary was used to classify adoption proposals; no specific interoperability standards or integration methods are named.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Information Not Found: The abstract does not contain any reference to legal validity, governance arrangements, or institutional roles.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: The paper emphasizes blockchainâ€™s pros and cons and notes current hybrid settings where blockchain is usually an add-on to existing systems; no specific barriers or deployment setting are detailed.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Future research directions are suggested, but no performance metrics, benchmarks, or optimization criteria are reported.

Source: Blockchain in real estate: Recent developments and empirical applications
Abstract: The real estate sector is often presented as an exemplary field that benefits from practical blockchain applications. The general hypothesis is that, in theory, blockchain could solve some significant challenges the real estate sector is facing, such as nontransparency, inefficiencies, fraud and corruption, high costs, and trust issues. However, the literature focuses on blockchain's theoretical benefits, challenges, or concepts. This research aims to understand the recent developments in the blockchain literature, specifically in the real estate sector, and to understand the current real-world applications by collecting empirical evidence from blockchain studies. The systematic literature review identified 262 relevant documents, after which a thematic content analysis was performed. Conceptual blockchain literature was identified to propose blockchain benefits for the real estate sector in four categories: land administration, real estate transactions, tokenization, and real estate management. The thematic content analysis also identified 26 empirical applications, of which all except one were related to land administration. Although the conceptual and theoretical blockchain literature presents blockchain as a disruptive and transformative technology for the real estate sector, the empirical applications suggest that blockchain adoption materializes more in hybrid, smaller-scale settings, where blockchain is merely an add-on layer to existing systems. Overall, most of the conceptual blockchain benefits remain empirically unconfirmed. On the other hand, the empirical applications suggest that blockchain could, for example, increase efficiency, reduce time, and provide verifiability, transparency, and automation, even in smaller-scale, hybrid settings. In addition, the applications indicate that blockchain could, in some cases, help reduce fraud and increase security and trust compared with centralized digital solutions. Finally, the empirical insights emphasize the role of political will, regulatory framework, availability of reliable digital data, publicâ€“private partnerships, and educational aspects in blockchain applications.
Methods: Systematic literature review of 262 English peer-reviewed documents (plus some reports, theses, and magazine articles) using PRISMA and thematic content analysis in ATLAS.ti.
Results: Blockchain proposals clustered into land administration, transactions, tokenization, and real estate management. Twenty-six empirical applications were identified, mostly hybrid land-administration systems; blockchain often improved efficiency, time, verifiability, transparency, and sometimes trust/security, but most theoretical benefits remained unconfirmed.
Conclusions: Blockchain in real estate is currently mainly a small-scale, hybrid add-on to existing systems rather than a disruptive replacement. Further work is needed on scaling, legal/regulatory change, reliable data, and country-specific institutional conditions.
Study Classification and Maturity: Systematic literature review with thematic content analysis and empirical application mapping. Maturity is largely conceptual review of proposals, with empirical evidence at pilot, test, and a few in-use or small-scale production deployments.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is through systematic review plus thematic analysis of 26 empirical applications, with comparative synthesis against theoretical claims. Evidence is mixed and mostly qualitative, with some quantitative counts such as 262 documents, 26 applications, and 12 empirically evaluated cases.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain is discussed generically as DLT/blockchain, with several permissioned or hybrid applications and no single platform standardized across cases. The dominant architecture is hybrid: blockchain as an add-on layer over existing registry systems rather than full replacement.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Architectures combine blockchain with existing databases and registry systems, often storing hashes on-chain while keeping original data off-chain. Cases also mention smart contracts, digital identity, electronic signatures, APIs/web interfaces, and conventional online public services integrated with blockchain.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Primary domain is land administration and land/title registration, with some coverage of real estate transactions and tokenization. Data include land records, titles, cadastral/registry data, and property registry information; on-chain use is often limited to hashes or references.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Security relies on cryptography, hashes, smart contracts, and in some cases digital identity and permissioned nodes; Estonia also reportedly used KSI Blockchain for critical data. Threats discussed include fraud, corruption, tampering, cyberattacks, trust issues, and data vulnerability in hybrid models.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to LADM, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, or specific interoperability standards integration in the reviewed applications.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Legal uncertainty, regulatory validity, and governance are central barriers; electronic signatures were not yet valid in Swedish real-estate transactions, and tokenization legality varied across countries. Public-private partnerships, governmental support, and institutional roles remained essential in most implementations.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Key barriers are legal uncertainty, scalability, complexity, lack of reliable digitized data, limited expertise, resistance to change, and coordination problems. Deployment is mostly in pilots or small-scale production, concentrated in transitioning/developing countries and often supported by public-private partnerships.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Reported gains include shorter processing time, efficiency, transparency, verifiability, automation, and some fraud reduction; costs were mixed and implementation-cost evidence was scarce. Major gaps are limited empirical data, weak large-scale evidence, and insufficient comparison across blockchain types and economic viability.

Source: Are emerging technologies helping win the fight against corruption? A review of the state of evidence
Abstract: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is often thought of as a uniformly positive tool making governments more transparent, accountable, and less corrupt. However, the evidence on it is mixed and often misunderstood. Hence, this article carries out a systematic stocktaking of ICT toolsâ€™ impact on corruption, offering a nuanced and context-dependent assessment. The tools reviewed are digital public services, crowdsourcing platforms, whistleblowing tools, transparency portals, distributed ledger technology, and artificial intelligence. We scrutinise the evidence both on ICTsâ€™ anticorruption effectiveness and misuse for corruption. Drawing on the commonalities across technologies, we find that ICT can support anti-corruption by impacting public scrutiny in numerous ways: enabling reporting on corruption, promoting transparency and accountability, facilitating citizen participation and government-citizen interactions. However, ICT can also provide new corruption opportunities through the dark web, cryptocurrencies, or the misuse of technologies such as centralised databases. The introduction of ICT tools does not automatically translate into anti-corruption outcomes; rather, impact hinges on the matching between ICT tools and the local context, including support for and skills in using technology.
Methods: Systematic review of academic and policy literature using Google Scholar and Web of Science, with five steps: search, screening, quality appraisal, data extraction, and synthesis.
Results: ICT can reduce petty corruption through transparency, monitoring, and process automation, with stronger evidence for e-government than for crowdsourcing, whistleblowing, transparency portals, blockchain, or AI. It can also enable misuse, and effects are highly context-dependent.
Conclusions: ICT is not a panacea: anti-corruption effects depend on local context, institutional capacity, and user skills, and are strongest for petty corruption. The review highlights weak evidence for DLT/blockchain and AI, and calls for more rigorous studies, especially field experiments.
Study Classification and Maturity: Systematic review and conceptual framework paper on ICT-enabled anti-corruption tools. It assesses mostly evidence at the review/case-study/regression level; most technologies discussed are mature in concept but uneven in implementation, with blockchain and AI largely under-tested.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Evidence base includes systematic literature review, country-level regressions, case studies, and qualitative investigations. Validation is mainly observational and comparative, with few field experiments and limited direct causal evidence.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain is described as a decentralized, synchronized peer-to-peer ledger with immutable records. No specific platform, consensus mechanism, or deployed architecture is evaluated; applications are proposed for registries, contracts, payments, and file storage.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: The paper discusses ICT systems at a high level, including web platforms, electronic data management systems, databases, mobile/telephone interfaces, and blockchain-ledger storage. No concrete implementation stack or integrated technical architecture is specified.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Anti-corruption ICT applications across public services, corruption reporting, transparency portals, whistleblowing, and blockchain-based registries. Data include complaints, budget/open data, public-service records, corruption reports, and land/company records.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Mentions anonymization, encrypted reporting, secure data transfer, and immutable blockchain records. Threats covered include tampering, hacking, identity exposure, false reports, misuse of databases, and anonymous cryptocurrency-enabled corruption.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to standards such as LADM, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, or formal interoperability integration with cadastral systems.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Legal protection for whistleblowers, regulatory frameworks, and accountability institutions are emphasized as prerequisites. Governance roles involve governments, civil society, NGOs, and anti-corruption agencies, but no specific statutory regime is analyzed.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Major barriers include weak capacity, digital divide, poor infrastructure, lack of skills, mistrust, privacy concerns, limited finance, and misfit with local context. The systems discussed range from conceptual to pilot and case-study evidence, with blockchain and AI especially under-deployed.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Key criteria are transparency, accountability, corruption reduction, participation, and detection risk, with some quantitative results such as 77% explained variation and 13% corruption reduction in e-government studies. Major gaps are scarce causal evidence, few field experiments, and limited study of DLT and AI.

Source: Improving implementation of the Blockchain technology in real estate registration
Abstract: Difficulties are caused by the introduction of the Blockchain in the field of registration of rights to real estate and real estate turnover since this requires the establishment of a balance between public and private interests. The article proposes a set of measures, the implementation of which would improve the implementation of the Blockchain technology to modernize the registration of rights to real estate and real estate turnover. The main hypothesis of the study is the assumption that the wider use of the Blockchain will increase the reliability of the register of real estate rights and make the circulation of real estate more secure. During the research were used the comparative legal research method, the method of legal modeling, the method of economic analysis of law. The article identified and characterized the vectors of modernization of real estate registration using the Blockchain have been identified and characterized. The regional aspect of introducing Blockchain technology for registering rights to real estate and improving legal regulation has been considered. The use of virtual reality and augmented reality technology for real estate accounting has been proposed, through the creation of a virtual real estate registry. The possibility of using online arbitration when challenging the right to real estate, which is registered using Blockchain technology, has been argued. The main directions of legal regulation of Smart factory and Digital Enterprise have been proposed.
Methods: Comparative legal research, legal modeling, and economic analysis of law were used. The paper also applies interdisciplinary and systematic approaches and mentions experimental assessment of proposed solutions.
Results: Four development directions are identified: blockchain-based document flow, blockchain register maintenance, real-estate tokenization, and a VR/AR-based virtual cadastre. Regional pilots in Russia and other countries are emphasized, and online arbitration is proposed for disputes.
Conclusions: Blockchain can simplify real-estate registration and improve indisputability only if the deposit principle is fully implemented. Implementation should be gradual through pilot regions and regulatory sandboxes, with cadastral reform via VR/AR and future empirical validation.
Study Classification and Maturity: Conceptual/legal analysis with comparative and modeling methods, grounded in regional pilot examples. Maturity is proposal and framework stage, with some pilot-region experimentation but no full operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is mainly doctrinal and comparative, using legal analysis of Germany, France, Russia, Belgium, and pilot experiences in several countries. No quantitative experimental metrics are reported; the authors call for further empirical research.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: A blockchain distributed ledger is proposed, but no specific platform, consensus mechanism, or smart-contract implementation is named. The architecture is described as a decentralized registry with mirrored/linked register copies and immutable blocks.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: The stack centers on a blockchain registry linked to online applications for submitting documents and a virtual real-estate registry using VR/AR, 3D scanning, and spherical panoramas. Integration with state registers is discussed conceptually as decentralized repositories, but no concrete software stack is implemented.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Real-estate rights registration, cadastral accounting, transactions, and dispute resolution are the main use cases. Data include title documents, registry entries, land-parcel and object characteristics, and virtual copies of real estate objects.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Tamper resistance, immutability, transparency, and cryptographic security are emphasized, along with reduced human-factor error. The paper targets distortion of registry entries, unreliable records, and unauthorized alteration, but does not test specific cryptographic controls.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: The paper discusses harmonization of international and national legal norms, not technical standards such as LADM or INSPIRE. Integration is framed as moving from centralized state registers to decentralized repositories and mirrored registers, without substantive standards implementation.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The paper focuses on balancing public and private interests, registrar roles, state control, and court/arbitration jurisdiction. It argues that blockchain registration still requires legal regulation, regional pilots, and possible changes to permit online arbitration.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Key barriers are legal uncertainty, regional fragmentation, need for public-private balance, and the centralized nature of current registries. Deployment is context-specific, starting in pilot Russian regions and regulatory sandboxes before broader rollout.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Criteria are reliability, security, reduced registration time, lower costs and risks, and stronger indisputability of rights. No measured performance values are reported; the main gap is the lack of post-implementation empirical validation and generalizability testing.

Source: Blockchain technology adaptation for land administration services: The importance of socio-cultural elements
Abstract: The adoption of efficient technologies in support of land administration services is still a challenge in Ghana. Data on land ownership, use, and value in Ghana remain fragmented, and technological systems enabling information services automation, and accessibility to reliable land information remain inefficient. This continues to cause societal problems like; double sales of land, unauthorized changes to land documents, corruption, and bribery. In this study, we argue that the absence of a context-focused guide for technology adaptation is a major factor for failures in previous technology adoption attempts in Ghana's land sector. We evaluate how a past technology (GELIS) adoption at Accra Lands Commission in Ghana was executed and why it led to unrealized expectations. We relied on elicited expert views followed by content analysis, and validated against a meta-synthesis qualitative review methodology of secondary data. We then extrapolated these results to possible outcomes and trajectories for the adaptation of a new technology like blockchain. Based on blockchain's interdependent feature, Ghana's contextual land issues, and the GELIS adoption experience, we develop suggestions covering an extended TOE framework to include socio-cultural elements as a guide for blockchain technology adaptation in Ghana, and other developing land administration systems with similar land issues as Ghana. Policy implications underlining these suggestions are highlighted.
Methods: Qualitative case study of the GELIS adoption at Accra Lands Commission, combining seven unstructured staff interviews with literature review and meta-synthesis/content analysis of 522 retrieved documents.
Results: GELIS achieved only about 60% of intended functionality; missing scanners, weak internet/servers, limited staff training, low staff involvement, funding shortfalls, and bureaucratic delays constrained full automation. The project produced operational difficulties and backlogs, prompting introduction of ELIS.
Conclusions: A blockchain adaptation guide should extend TOE with socio-cultural elements to fit Ghanaâ€™s customary land tenure context. The authors conclude the suggestions need empirical validation and note limitations from the still-burgeoning blockchain land literature.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical qualitative case study with literature-based meta-synthesis and framework development. The paper is at the conceptual/proposal stage for blockchain adaptation; GELIS was a case study of partial implementation, not an evaluated blockchain system.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation used expert views, qualitative content analysis, and secondary-literature meta-synthesis, then the proposed framework was discussed with land-sector experts for validation. Evidence is qualitative, with no quantitative performance testing of blockchain.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: No blockchain system was implemented or tested in the study; blockchain is discussed as a proposed public, decentralized, consensus-based ledger. Examples cited include Ethereum in Kenya and a public blockchain in Rwanda, but no platform is proposed for the paperâ€™s own framework.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: GELIS used a computer-based land information system with sub-systems for valuation, document management, spatial objects, parties, user management, cases, and addresses, linking graphical spatial data to textual attribute data. The proposed blockchain adaptation remains conceptual, with off-chain verification and integration across land-sector institutions mentioned but no implemented stack.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land administration in Ghana, focused on land ownership, use, value, titles, documents, spatial data, and transaction records. The use case is technology adaptation for land services automation, land registration, and secure transfer processes.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Blockchain is discussed as providing immutability, traceability, transparency, PKI, digital signatures, time-stamping, and tamper-proof records; Rwandaâ€™s app also uses biodata and fingerprints. Threats addressed include fraud, corruption, double sales, document tampering, repudiation, identity fraud, and unauthorized data changes.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Interoperability is discussed generally through integration with existing institutional systems and data-format migration. No LADM/ISO 19152, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE implementation is mentioned.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The paper cites Ghanaâ€™s constitutional customary-land arrangements and Land Act 2020 (Act 1036), including electronic conveyance, customary land secretariats, and monthly submission of records to the Commission. It also highlights governance issues such as top-down decision-making, government approval, and regulatory compatibility.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Key barriers were technological incompatibility, weak infrastructure, limited funding, low staff capacity, top-down governance, political/bureaucratic delays, public mistrust, and weak stakeholder involvement. Deployment context is Ghanaâ€™s Accra Lands Commission, with the proposed guidance aimed at similar developing-country land systems.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: No formal performance metrics such as throughput, latency, or cost were reported. The main evaluation criteria were TOE readiness, organizational acceptance, external support, and socio-cultural fit; the paper identifies the need for empirical testing of the proposed blockchain-adaptation suggestions.

Source: Decentralized document version control using ethereum blockchain and IPFS
Abstract: In this paper, we propose a blockchain-based solution and framework for document sharing and version control to facilitate multi-user collaboration and track changes in a trusted, secure, and decentralized manner, with no involvement of a centralized trusted entity or third party. This solution is based on utilizing Ethereum smart contracts to govern and regulate the document version control functions among the creators and developers of the document and its validators. Moreover, our solution leverages the benefits of IPFS (InterPlanetary File System) to store documents on a decentralized file system. The proposed solution automates necessary interactions among multiple actors comprising developers and approvers. Smart contracts have been developed using Solidity language, and their functionalities were tested using the Remix IDE (Integrated Development Environment). The paper demonstrates that our smart contract code is free of commonly known security vulnerabilities and attacks. The code has been made publically available at Github.
Methods: Design-and-implementation study proposing an Ethereum smart-contract framework with IPFS-based off-chain document storage. Functional testing was done in Remix IDE using three Ethereum addresses, plus security analysis with ChainSecurity, Securify, and Oyente.
Results: The implemented contract approved or rejected document versions based on registered-actor checks and IPFS-hash matching; approvals triggered events such as NewVersionSigned and ApprovalGranted. Security tools reported no known vulnerabilities, with Oyente producing all False reports.
Conclusions: The framework is presented as a secure, decentralized alternative for document version control that removes the need for a trusted third party. The authors state it is generic enough to extend to other shared digital assets and contents.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical prototype/implementation paper with proof-of-concept testing on Ethereum and IPFS. Maturity is laboratory-tested code, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validated through prototype implementation, scenario-based functional testing in Remix IDE, and static/security analysis with ChainSecurity, Securify, and Oyente. Evidence is both quantitative and qualitative, but no performance benchmark metrics are reported.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Ethereum smart contracts on a permissioned document-sharing workflow, with IPFS for off-chain file storage. The system uses Ethereum consensus/miner validation and one smart contract per document, with approvals requiring all approvers or two-thirds of approvers.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Stack includes Ethereum, Solidity smart contracts, EVM execution, IPFS storage, and Remix IDE testing. Documents are stored off-chain on IPFS, while hashes, approvals, registrations, and version references are recorded on-chain in the contract.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Document sharing and version control for multi-user collaboration. The paper cites applicability to healthcare, finance, and land registry documents, but the implemented use case is generic document management.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses cryptographic signing, Ethereum addresses/public-private keys, smart-contract access modifiers, and immutable ledger records; IPFS hashes bind versions to content. Threats addressed include tampering, unauthorized access, identity misuse, and common smart-contract vulnerabilities.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to interoperability standards such as LADM, ISO 19152, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, GIS, or legacy cadastral database integration.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: No formal legal framework is established; the system replaces third-party notarization with consensus among approvers. Governance is handled by smart contract rules for registration and approval, with all approvers or two-thirds required depending on the action.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Targets document-management and version-control settings, with discussion of centralized-system fragility, tampering risk, and expensive large-file storage on-chain. Deployment is a conceptual/prototype system tested in Remix, not field-deployed.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation criteria were functional correctness, access control, version approval logic, and security/vulnerability resistance; no throughput, latency, gas cost, or scalability measurements are reported. The paper notes a future need for multi-operation workflows and domain-specific extensions.

Source: The real estate time-stamping and registration system based on Ethereum blockchain
Abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing interest in real estate investments that utilize blockchain technology. Traditional real estate investments usually involve third-party intermediaries for verifying and recording informal real estate transactions. This paper proposes a blockchain-based real estate investment model and presents a detailed description of the real estate register authentication aspect of the model. The model uses blockchain technology to create tamper-evident records of real estate transactions and provide secure authentication and verification for informal real estate transactions. Meanwhile, each real estate transaction is recorded in a block, and all transaction records are kept on the blockchain. This means that inventors can access these transaction records and verify their authenticity and validity. The system can also use smart contracts to automate the process of real estate transactions, which further improves transaction efficiency and reduces costs. Furthermore, the model's timestamp and authentication mechanism can eliminate third-party intermediaries and ensure the authenticity and validity of real estate transactions through distributed ledgers and verification mechanisms. Overall, blockchain-based real estate systems offer advantages of security, transparency, efficiency, and cost reduction. With ongoing blockchain advancements, these systems are expected to play a crucial role in future real estate investment transactions.
Methods: Proposed blockchain-based real estate time-stamping and registration system for Australia, with framework design and implementation on Ethereum. Evaluation used Sepolia test network simulations plus cost comparisons against traditional registration and transaction fees.
Results: The platform reduced real estate certification/registration time from days to minutes and lowered costs versus the traditional model. Simulations showed more stable, predictable transaction costs and removal of intermediaries.
Conclusions: The Ethereum-based system is presented as a secure, transparent, immutable alternative to cumbersome and costly traditional registration, but key limitations remain: immature technology, key management risk, legal uncertainty, cybersecurity exposure, interoperability issues, and dependence on network participants.
Study Classification and Maturity: Applied design-and-implementation paper with a prototype system and simulated evaluation on a test network. Highest maturity demonstrated is testnet-deployed proof of concept, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation used Sepolia Ethereum testnet simulation, five runs per price range, and comparison with traditional fee structures. Evidence is quantitative cost/time comparison plus qualitative system demonstration.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Ethereum blockchain with Solidity smart contracts on a PoS-based consensus network; Sepolia testnet used for simulation. Architecture is public decentralized Web3-style, with blockchain storing registration and transaction records and smart contracts handling logic.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Browser frontend connects through web3.js and ethers.js to MetaMask, provider/signer, smart contracts, and Ethereum. IPFS plus INFURA store and retrieve encrypted file hashes; Remix was used to deploy contracts.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Australian real estate registration, authentication, and transaction management for land/property records. Data include owner identity, property number, location, area, usage, legal documents, prices, pictures, and hashed files.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses hashing, timestamps, RSA public/private key encryption, digital signatures, 2FA, KYC, access whitelisting, OpenZeppelin SafeMath/ReentrancyGuard/Ownable/Pausable, and IPFS encryption. Addresses tampering, fraud, unauthorized access, key compromise, reentrancy, and privacy leakage.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Integrates with government land databases and compares uploaded data against official records; IPFS/INFURA are used for document storage and retrieval. No formal land-administration standard such as LADM or INSPIRE is mentioned.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Government approval and land management department authorization are required for registration; a blockchain land/real estate registration department and financial institutions are part of the workflow. The paper notes unclear legal status of blockchain in many countries and says digital signatures are legally recognized.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Target context is Australia, with smart-city deployment envisioned. Barriers include high traditional costs, intermediaries, scalability/interoperability concerns, immature technology, key-loss risk, legal uncertainty, cybersecurity, and dependence on distributed network participants.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation focused on registration/transaction cost and time; blockchain fees were compared across $600,000-$1,600,000 property prices and simulated five times each. The paper identifies research gaps in FT integration, rental investment/management, and extension to other asset types.

Source: Transparency of land administration and the role of blockchain technology, a four-dimensional framework analysis from the ghanaian land perspective
Abstract: Existing studies on blockchain within land administration have focused mainly on replacing or complementing the technology for land registration and titling. This study explores the potential of using blockchain technology to enhance the transparency of all land administration processes using an integrative review methodology coupled with a framework analysis. This study draws on the Ghanaian land administration perspective to make this insightful. It appears possible to apply a permissionless public blockchain across all land administration processes. This integrates all departments, processes, and stakeholders of land administration to enhance openness, improve availability and accessibility to information, and foster participation for transparency simultaneously. This can change the transparency variation in land administration to be more equal and homogenous regardless of land type. This, however, depends on the standardization of processes across the divisions, as well as negotiation and consensus amongst all stakeholders, especially with chiefs. Limitations include: limited storage and scalability, as well as huge electricity consumption for operation. This studyâ€™s policy implications are a review of all paper-based land transactions, a comprehensive digitization of land administration processes, publicâ€“private partnership on blockchain-based land administration, and professionals and stakeholder education on the technology.
Methods: Integrative review methodology coupled with framework analysis, using the Ghanaian land administration perspective.
Results: Blockchain could be applied across all land administration processes with a permissionless public blockchain to improve openness, information accessibility, and participation. It could make transparency more equal and homogenous across land types.

Source: User-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance in blockchain adoption for land administration systems: A systematic literature review
Abstract: Blockchain technology has emerged as a disruptive force with the potential to support the securitisation of tenure in land administration systems (LAS). Like in every new and emerging technologies, â€˜trust and acceptanceâ€™ play significant roles in stakeholdersâ€™ intention to either embrace or reject the adoption of blockchain technology in LAS. While previous research on the topic has placed considerable attention on the potential of adopting blockchain for improving LAS, limited attention has been placed on understanding the user-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance. To address this gap, this study conducted a systematic literature review on the user-centric dimensions of trust and acceptance influencing blockchain technology adoption for LAS. The analysis employs two complementary theoretical frameworks: the Multilevel Trust (MLT) framework to categorize trust factors, and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) to guide the analysis of acceptance factors. The results categorize the key factors influencing stakeholders' trust into three dimensions: trust in technology (data privacy and control, security), trust in administrative processes (traceability and transparency), and trust in institutions (regulation and legal compliance), while performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions emerge as the key factors that influence stakeholdersâ€™ acceptance. Drawing upon these findings, a conceptual framework was developed to illustrate the interrelationship between the trust and acceptance factors influencing stakeholdersâ€™ intention to either embrace or reject the adoption of blockchain for LAS. This research contributes to the literature on emerging technology adoption for LAS, which may help land administration stakeholders take suitable measures to address stakeholder concerns and thereby promote blockchain technology adoption.
Methods: Systematic literature review using PRISMA and two frameworks: Multilevel Trust (MLT) and UTAUT. The search covered Scopus, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and ProQuest, yielding 68 included peer-reviewed articles from 2014â€“2024.
Results: Trust factors clustered into data privacy and control, security, traceability and transparency, and regulation/legal compliance, with additional factors including immutability, provenance, decentralization, education, collaboration, and past experience. Acceptance was driven by performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions.
Conclusions: Trust is presented as the basis for acceptance of blockchain in land administration systems, and a conceptual framework was proposed to show their reciprocal relationship. The review remains exploratory and calls for future empirical validation with survey data.
Study Classification and Maturity: Systematic literature review and conceptual framework paper on blockchain adoption for land administration. Maturity is conceptual/exploratory, with no implemented system or field deployment evaluated.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Evidence comes from synthesis of 68 peer-reviewed studies using PRISMA-based screening, not from experiments or a prototype. Validation is qualitative and review-based, with a proposed conceptual framework and no quantitative performance testing.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: No single platform is implemented; the paper reviews blockchain generally and cites public, private, permissioned, permissionless, and consortium models. It discusses a hybrid/private blockchain approach, with no consensus protocol beyond cryptographic hashing and consensus algorithms.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: A conceptual socio-technical framework integrates MLT and UTAUT with blockchain-based LAS. No detailed backend, database, API, or deployment stack is described beyond mention of secure digital identity services, smart contracts, and hybrid blockchain models.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land administration systems for land registration, ownership records, land transactions, and land rights. Data discussed include ownership histories, property data, transaction records, geographic information, and cadastral/land records.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Mechanisms include cryptographic hashing, encryption, access control, digital identities, zero-knowledge proofs, homomorphic encryption, role-based access control, and hybrid blockchain designs. Threats covered include tampering, fraud, unauthorized access, identity theft, privacy leakage, 51% attacks, smart-contract flaws, double-spending, and cyberattacks.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: No LADM, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, or other formal standard is implemented. The paper only mentions compatibility with existing LAS and standardization of processes across divisions.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Legal validity, GDPR compliance, data protection, and regulatory support are central, with clear frameworks needed for recognition of blockchain land records and authorized modifications. Governance is framed around land institutions, policymakers, regulators, and formal supervisory structures.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Barriers include privacy concerns, regulatory uncertainty, weak infrastructure, fragmented laws, lack of technical expertise, cost, and compatibility issues. The context is exploratory, with pilots in Georgia, Cyprus, the UAE, Sweden, and Rwanda, but no operational deployment studied end-to-end.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Key evaluation criteria are trust, acceptance, transparency, security, privacy, efficiency, and usability, but no measured throughput, latency, gas cost, or energy metrics are reported. Source: Enhancing land management policy in Bangladesh: A blockchain-based framework for transparent and efficient land management
Abstract: This paper introduces a blockchain-based framework designed to enhance the land management system in Bangladesh by addressing issues such as data fragmentation, corruption, and inefficiencies in land registration and titling. The proposed system integrates blockchain technology with smart contracts, IoT capabilities, and AI across five distinct layers: blockchain layer, stakeholder access layer, AI layer, IoT layer, and integration layer. These layers automate processes such as land sales, ownership verification, and real-time monitoring, reducing manual intervention and minimizing opportunities for fraudulent activities. The study combines a detailed review of existing challenges and technological solutions with an assessment of the system's performance based on metrics like transaction speed, resource consumption, and cost efficiency. Findings indicate that the framework enhances transparency, reduces corruption, and improves efficiency in land management, aligning with international best practices. Additionally, the discussion highlights the importance of integrating off-chain solutions to manage transaction costs and emphasizes the need for legal and regulatory adaptation for the successful implementation of blockchain technology. A phased implementation strategy begins with local community engagement and scales to broader oversight, aiming for a sustainable and effective approach to land governance.
Methods: Mixed-methods study combining a qualitative literature review with quantitative performance analysis of a proposed blockchain-based land management framework for Bangladesh.
Results: The framework is reported to improve transparency, reduce corruption and manual intervention, and support secure land transactions. Performance results include RegisterLand gas use of 314146 units and costs of about $5.08-$27.35 depending on transaction type and input size.
Conclusions: The authors conclude the blockchain framework, with off-chain support, smart contracts, AI, and IoT, could modernize Bangladesh land management and make transactions more secure, transparent, and cost-effective. They note legal/regulatory adaptation, digital literacy, and further research are still needed.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical framework proposal with literature review and prototype implementation on a local Ethereum test environment. Highest maturity demonstrated is proof-of-concept / laboratory-tested, not operational deployment.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validated through literature synthesis plus a prototype deployment using Ganache and a local Ethereum network, with simulation-based benchmarking. Evidence is quantitative, using gas consumption, execution time, and cost metrics.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Ethereum-based blockchain with smart contracts, tested locally on Ganache; consensus mechanism is not explicitly specified. The design is a permissioned-style, multi-layer architecture with blockchain, stakeholder access, AI, IoT, and integration layers.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Node.js backend, Solidity smart contracts, Truffle and Ganache for development/testing, React frontend, and MetaMask for blockchain access. IoT, AI, and an integration layer exchange real-time data, analytics, and policy enforcement across stakeholders.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land management and land registration in Bangladesh, focused on titles, deeds, ownership verification, mutation, land transfers, and real-time land-use monitoring. Data include land records, transaction histories, sensor data, and ownership documents.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses immutability, smart contracts, role-based access control, KYC, and cryptographic protections to secure records. Threats addressed include corruption, forgery, tampering, unauthorized access, fraud, and illegal land grabbing.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: No formal interoperability standard such as LADM, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE is implemented. Integration is described conceptually through an integration layer and secure data sharing between agencies, with off-chain components used to reduce transaction costs.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The system includes government oversight, regulatory compliance, KYC, and legal authorities validating transactions. The paper argues that Bangladesh needs legal and regulatory adaptation for blockchain records to be recognized and enforceable.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Bangladesh faces data fragmentation, corruption, outdated records, weak synchronization, scalability limits, interoperability issues, and low digital literacy. The system is conceptual/prototype-level, with phased implementation proposed and no field deployment reported.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation criteria are gas consumption, execution time, and cost efficiency; RegisterLand used 314146 gas and about $27.35, while simpler actions cost about $5.08. Key research gaps are empirical field testing, socio-economic impacts, scalable IoT deployment, real-time dispute resolution, and regulatory frameworks.

Source: A Proof of Concept of the integration of blockchain with an ISO 19152:2012 based Land Administration System
Abstract: In recent years, we witnessed extensive study of the integration of blockchain technology in Land Administration System. It is believed that it would enhance transparency and trust. Besides, since 2012 and the publication of the ISO 19152 Land Administration Domain Model we have evidence of it increasing adoption as the de facto domain model to use when creating new Land Administration System or refactoring existing one. To allow a broader implementation of blockchain technology in Land Administration System, we propose to blend those two trends to create a system that would integrate major technological advancement (blockchain) with international standards on effective land administration. Merging these two techniques have the potential to create a Fit-For-Purpose land administration framework that would meet land administration requirements while improving transparency. The main contribution of this paper is the proposition of a Proof of Concept of integrating blockchain technology in a land administration system based on the ISO 19152 Land Administration Domain Model.
Methods: Conceptual proof of concept proposing integration of blockchain with an ISO 19152/LADM-based land administration system; no empirical study, sample, or formal evaluation method is described.
Results: The paper proposes that combining blockchain and ISO 19152/LADM could improve transparency, trust, and fit-for-purpose land administration.
Conclusions: The authors conclude that integrating blockchain with ISO 19152/LADM may create a fit-for-purpose land administration framework that improves transparency and meets land administration requirements.

Source: How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations are Affecting Real Estate
Abstract: Blockchain technology is innovating the real estate industry, providing greater accessibility, and streamlining the process for investors, buyers, and sellers. Three approaches that utilize blockchain technology for real estate are: virtual real estate, real estate tokenization, and fractional investment. Virtual real estate enables users to purchase digital properties in virtual worlds and monetize their investment. Real estate tokenization creates digital tokens that represent ownership of real estate assets, while fractional investment enables users to share ownership of properties by purchasing tokens that represent a percentage of the asset. Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) and Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) can offer a new way for clients to access exclusive real estate properties and services. In this research we suggest a Real Estate membership by buying properties or NFTs. In a hypothetical use case, clients can enjoy special advantages such as priority access to off-market properties, individualized counseling, and revenue-sharing options. However, there are still challenges to overcome, such as regulation, mass adoption, and lower gas fees that can be analyzed deeper on future research.
Methods: Conceptual discussion in an abstract-only paper proposing a real-estate membership model using blockchain, DAOs, and NFTs. No formal method, dataset, or analytical procedure is described.
Results: Three blockchain approaches for real estate are identified: virtual real estate, tokenization, and fractional investment. The proposed membership concept offers priority access to off-market properties, individualized counseling, and revenue-sharing options in a hypothetical use case.
Conclusions: DAOs and NFTs may create a new access model for real estate services and properties. Regulation, mass adoption, and lower gas fees remain unresolved challenges for future research.

Abstract: The blockchain land records management system solves the inefficiencies, fraud, and untransparency inherent in traditional land record systems using blockchain technology, decentralized storage (IPFS), and smart contracts. Source: Blockchain real estate: The messy landing of digital property
Abstract: This paper analyzes the bridging of digital-based crypto capital with one of the most long-standing and material parts of the economy, real property. Specifically, it uses two cases focused on US-based efforts to use blockchain to fractionalize the ownership and administration of land and housing. We frame this paper around the disconnect between rhetorics of frictionless capital and their dependence on the materiality of real property. Thus, rather than being exclusively a technology for transparency and investment (as proponents stress) blockchain engagements with the materiality of real estate embroiled within centuries long processes of dispossession, predation and exploitation. The two case studies are CityDAO, an online business/community focused on building the â€œcrypto city of the futureâ€ holding two rural parcels of land in Wyoming and Colorado, and RealT, a fractional, tokenized real estate platform that invests in rental housing, using Section 8 vouchers as a means of â€˜bridgingâ€™ global crypto-capital into the materiality of Detroit's housing market.
Methods: Critical qualitative case study using two US examples: CityDAO and RealT. The paper combines theoretical framing with close textual and contextual analysis of project materials, platform practices, and reported market/institutional data.
Results: CityDAO tokenized a 40-acre Wyoming parcel into 950 NFTs and raised about $2.5 million; RealT managed over 450 properties, 1,700 units, moved over $100 million in property tokens, and distributed $13 million in rent checks. RealT held 384 Detroit properties, 96.6% in majority-African American tracts.
Conclusions: BRE is context-dependent and political, not a neutral technological fix, and is likely to reinforce financialization, elite control, and exploitation. The authors conclude that calculation, law, and local social conditions constrain disruption and that failed projects can still normalize blockchain imaginaries.

Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Smart contracts, token voting, and KYC/SEC compliance are the main mechanisms mentioned; no hashing, encryption, or PKI details are provided. Source: Widening and deepening: territorial strategies and state building in Africa
Abstract: This article challenges the view of African states as weak regulators vis-Ã -vis foreign large-scale land acquisitions. Instead, building on theories of state building and territorialization, we argue that state power is contested but reasserted through two strategies: widening, that states actively leverage investment, infrastructure, and conservation to extend territorial authority; and deepening, that states further intensify its capacity to govern territory over time through increasingly sophisticated legal frameworks, policy instruments, and socio-technical innovations. We illustrate these two strategies through 24 empirical cases across 14 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, drawing on the authorsâ€™ primary fieldwork since 2018 in Uganda, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, and Kenya, together with an extensive review of secondary literature covering additional cases across the region. By tracing these processes, we recast the debate on land and power in Africa by showing that far from being eclipsed by the forces of global and local capital, African states actively instrumentalize it to entrench authority, reconfigure territorial relations with communities, and reshape spatial dimensions of governance, thus contributing to wider scholarship on state infrastructural power and the politics of territorialization.
Methods: Comparative qualitative study using 24 empirical cases across 14 sub-Saharan African countries, combining primary fieldwork (2018â€“2024) in Uganda, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, and Kenya with a review of secondary literature, government policy, and legal documents.
Results: The cases show African states widening territorial control through investment, infrastructure, and conservation, and deepening it through legal, bureaucratic, scientific-technical, and digital land governance. Examples include Ethiopiaâ€™s 3.3 million ha leasing target, Rwandaâ€™s 11 million parcels registered, and Tanzaniaâ€™s relocation of about 30,000 people in Loliondo.
Conclusions: African states are not merely weak regulators; they actively instrumentalize land interventions to consolidate territorial authority, though outcomes are limited by capacity constraints, fragmentation, donor agendas, and resistance. Widening and deepening are mutually reinforcing but often fragile and contingent on external alliances.

Source: A survey of breakthrough in blockchain technology: Adoptions, applications, challenges and future research
Abstract: Blockchain technology gets more attention and adoptions in various countries and companies all over the world. Blockchain is currently bringing a revolution in many enterprises like finance, healthcare, supply chain, insurance, registry, and the internet of things. Many enterprises integrate blockchain with their systems for the benefits of the blockchain. Despite its strength, blockchain has some challenges in security, privacy, scalability, and other few. This paper surveys the breakthrough in blockchain technology, its applications, and challenges. As many blockchain papers focus on cryptocurrencies, IoT, and security, this paper focuses on the overall state of the art of blockchain technology, its recent developments, and adoptions, especially in areas besides cryptocurrencies. We give a comprehensive review of the cryptography behind the blockchain for a better understanding of the technology. We also review quantitative surveys and analysis on both the public and the enterprise blockchains. Finally, we review the future research opportunities and directions on the blockchain technology.
Methods: Narrative survey of blockchain breakthroughs, applications, challenges, and future research, with a separate review of cryptography and quantitative survey studies. The paper synthesizes prior literature and reported survey statistics rather than presenting a new empirical experiment.
Results: Blockchain adoption is widespread across finance, healthcare, supply chain, insurance, registry, IoT, and other sectors; many enterprise projects were already in production. Surveyed enterprise networks showed Ethereum most used generally, Hyperledger Fabric most used in enterprise, and PBFT the most common enterprise consensus.
Conclusions: Blockchain is presented as a promising technology with benefits in security, cost savings, transparency, and removal of intermediaries, and the authors expect further mainstream adoption. They conclude that scalability, regulation, privacy, and understanding remain key obstacles and future research needs.

Source: Transformations, transitions, or tall tales? A global review of the uptake and impact of NoSQL, blockchain, and big data analytics on the land administration sector
Abstract: Unstructured data, non-relational databases, distributed databases, and big data analytics potentially change the landscape for digital land data creation, use, management, and dissemination. The way land data is governed and the resultant impact on land tenure security delivery is open to substantial re-thinking. Drawing from international cases, this paper provides a state-of-the-art examination of prototypes and demonstrators from the global land sector. The aim is to deliver an insight into the opportunities, challenges, impacts, and future scenarios regarding the application of the emerging technologies. The paper finds that whilst uptake of non-relational and distributed databases is occurring, it remains largely at the level of proof-of-concept, demonstrator or pilot. Scaled uptake is occurring slower than anticipated, and to a lesser degree than in other sectors. However, the broader and longer-term impacts on the land sector remain difficult to judge. Meanwhile, emerging distributed analytical databases appear to be under-exploited or at least underexplored within the land sector. Overall, the examined technologies are seen to enable new operational approaches for conventional land sector transactions, and also entirely new land related services, digital products, and actors: the ways and means of holding, transferring, and securing land may become more nuanced, fractionalized, and/or automated. Whether these observed embryonic developments lead to sector transformation or orderly transition, is seen to be heavily reliant on the prevailing political, socio-cultural and institutional settings within a jurisdiction.
Methods: Systematic research synthesis of global land-sector literature, conference proceedings, grey literature, and two unpublished case studies (Land Layby and Brickx) using thematic analysis and contextual frameworks.
Results: Uptake of NoSQL, distributed databases, and blockchain in land administration remained mostly proof-of-concept, demonstrator, or pilot. Relational systems still dominated, while distributed analytics and NewSQL were scarcely used; DLT cases showed emerging private/public hybrid registry experiments.
Conclusions: The technologies are enabling new operational approaches and new land-related services, but broad impacts are still premature to judge. The authors recommend deeper study of legal, ethical, and institutional barriers and a likely near-term shift toward hybrid 1st-, 2nd-, and 3rd-generation LIS.

Source: Safe storage and access control method of real estate registration information based on blockchain technology
Abstract: The security of real estate registration information is very important, but the traditional centralized system has some problems, such as data tampering, privacy leakage and cross-departmental coordination difficulties. Abstract: The origins of digital money and blockchain technology goes back to the 1980s, but in the last decade, the blockchain technology gained large popularity in the financial sector with the appearance of cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin. Drawing on this analysis, we derive an endogenous demand for auditing to overcome what we label the â€œfirst mile problemâ€ (FMP) with blockchains: ensuring that the data stored on the blockchain distributed ledger is isomorphic with the real life data that it purports to represent. The first mile problem arises only when the blockchain is used to store data about physical items, especially ones involving a service component, rather than being native digital, as is the case with the genesis blockchain application, bitcoin. We show that unless it is feasible to store a â€œdigital twinâ€ of the item (Roberts, 2017), there is a role for auditors, with the training in professional skepticism, to help alleviate the first mile problem. There is no guarantee, however, that this new demand for auditing will be met by the traditional financial statement auditors.

Results: The paper finds blockchain cannot ensure that on-chain data matches physical reality, creating the â€œfirst mile problem.â€ Digital twins help for purely physical goods, but human-action cases need third-party assurance and auditing.

Source: A Blockchain-based Land Title Management System for Bangladesh
Abstract: Bangladesh is a small country with a large population. Its increasingly developing economy further makes land a lucrative source of fixed capital. On the other hand, land titling is a cumbersome and lengthy process, where different government bodies process different sets of documents, and bureaucratic loopholes encourage fraudulent activities by organized people. As a result, the current model suffers from good governance. In this paper, we propose a Blockchain-based solution that offers data synchronization and transparency, ease of access, immutable records management, a faster and cheaper solution. Considering the technological knowledge and capacity of the people and the government, we introduced a phase by phase Blockchain adoption model that starts with a public Blockchain ledger and later gradually incorporates two levels of Hybrid Blockchain. We provide detailed smart contracts design of the public Blockchain and implement a prototype system using Ethereum. Our experimental setup uses local and live Ethereum test networks to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed system. Our analysis shows that the proposed model reduces the number of required travels, the overall cost of information processing as well as provide easy access to vital information. As a result, Blockchain adoption can improve the land title digitization effort of Bangladesh.
Methods: Conceptual three-stage blockchain adoption model for Bangladesh land titling, with a public blockchain prototype implemented on Ethereum. Evaluation used local Ganache and Ropsten test networks with smart contract testing.
Results: The prototype reduced required travel, processing time, and operating cost while improving accessibility, transparency, and synchronization. Reported average cost was about 0.00004 USD per 100 gas, and local testing used 1.5 GB storage.
Conclusions: A phased blockchain approach could improve land title digitization in Bangladesh, but real deployment requires new policies, laws, PKI governance, training, and government-led adoption. Future work includes hybrid blockchain, land-related currency, attack simulation, and smart contract security analysis.
