Source: Paperless Everything: A Systematic Literature Review for the Design of Blockchain-based Document Management Systems
Abstract: Digitalization pushes organizations to increasingly rely on digital documents over physical documents. They offer unprecedented scalability and provide the foundation for fully digital processes. Despite their advantages, digital documents also have drawbacks compared to physical documents. Two key drawbacks are ownership transfer and document integrity. Blockchain technology can address these drawbacks. First, blockchain immutability characteristics enable tamper-proofing of digital documents. Second, consensus algorithms solve the â€œdouble-spending problemâ€ for the ownership transfer of digital assets. The technical feasibility of such blockchain-based document management systems has been prototyped in different domains. However, these studies focus on their respective domain only and do not communicate their insights back to the blockchain community. As a result, insights into the design and architecture of blockchain-based document management systems are scattered across domains. Best practices remain inaccessible to the blockchain community at large, impeding the gradual accumulation of knowledge and lasting impact. This study reports on a systematic literature review of the architectural building blocks and patterns of blockchain-based document management systems. It is based on 1,737 initially identified papers, of which 113 papers were analyzed in detail. The findings show that the commonly used architectures are proxy-based (48%) and dApp-based (38%), along with a favor for off-chain storage (68%). It is also shown that only 22% of papers mentioned best practices when it comes to testing and that the majority do not report implementation details. Based on the findings, this study recommends more rigorous justification and documentation of the architectural building blocks. Addressing concerns related to smart contract descriptions, storage, testing, and legal regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation is encouraged, and future research opportunities for the design of blockchain-based document management systems are outlined to achieve impact in practice.

Conclusions: The study recommends more rigorous justification and documentation of architectural building blocks, including smart contract descriptions, storage, testing, and GDPR-related legal considerations.

Abstract: The Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) is one of the first ISO spatial domain standards, and has been proven one of the best candidates for unambiguously representing 3D Rights, Restrictions and Responsibilities. Consequently, multiple LADM-based country profile implementations have been developed since the approval of LADM as an ISO standard; however, there is still a gap for technical implementations. This paper summarizes LADM implementation approaches distilled from relevant publications available to date. Models based on land administration standards do focus on the legal aspects of urban structures; however, the juridical boundaries in 3D are sometimes (partly) bound by the corresponding physical objects, leading to ambiguous situations. To that end, more integrated approaches are being developed at a conceptual level, and it is evident that the evaluation and validation of 3D legal and physical models-both separately and together in the form of an integrated model-is vital. This paper briefly presents the different approaches to legal and physical integration that have been developed in the last decade, while the need for more explicit relationships between legal and physical notions is highlighted. In this regard, recent experience gained from implementing INTERLIS, the Swiss standard that enables land information system communications, in LADM-based country profiles, suggests the possibility of an integrated LADM/INTERLIS approach. Considering semantic interoperability within integrated models, the need for more formal semantics is underlined by introducing formalization of code lists and explicit definition of constraints. Last but not least, the first results of case studies based on the generic LADM/INTERLIS approach are presented.

Source: A proposal for modeling and implementing an integrated system for Brazilian cadastres according to iso 19152: 2012 land administration domain model
Abstract: This article proposes the modelling and implementation of an integrated system for Brazilian cadastres, based on the standardized model of land administration described in the ISO 19152:2012 LADM. The model was developed from the identification of the essential elements of the urban, the National Rural Cadastre System and the cadastres of public assets of the Secretariat of the Patrimony of the Union. At all stages of this work, free and/or open source software was used to validate this proposal. The results confirm the viability of the application of the concepts proposed by LADM to the Brazilian system of cadastres, allowing the integration between the systems of different institutions. The model is flexible and allows for the inclusion of additional classes according to changing needs of land administration data users. The current form of the model can be regarded as the basic module to be used as a starting point in the structuring of the National System of Management of Territorial Information, which is aimed at the integration of all existing cadastres and land registries in Brazil.
Methods: Conceptual modeling and implementation proposal for Brazilian cadastres based on ISO 19152:2012 LADM, derived from essential elements of urban, rural, and federal public-asset cadastres. Free and open-source software was used to validate the proposal.
Results: The proposed model supports integration among cadastre systems from different institutions and is flexible enough to include additional classes as needs change. It is presented as a basic module for the National System of Management of Territorial Information.
Conclusions: LADM concepts are viable for Brazilian cadastre integration, and the model can serve as a starting point for a national territorial information system integrating cadastres and land registries.

Source: Domain-Driven Design applied to land administration system development: Lessons from the Netherlands
Abstract: The introduction or renewal of information systems conventionally begins with data modelling. In the domain of land administration, like others, the process is challenging: complex laws and regulations, lengthy process descriptions, shared organisational responsibilities, differing information encodings and formats, and seeking compliance with the LADM ISO 19152 standard, must be considered. Between 2016 and 2018, The Netherlandsâ€™ Cadastre, Land Registry and Mapping Agency â€“ in short, Kadaster â€“ successfully undertook the renewal of the information system supporting its deeds registration. The previous system dated back to the 1980s. In-house data modelling specialists led the program, the most extensive undertaken in decades. Inspired by action-research principles, the process and resultant lessons are documented using a case study approach. It is shown that beyond Model Driven Architectures, other model-driven methodologies, such as Domain-Driven Design, are entirely useful in the land administration domain. A domain is usually more extensive than a few objects, and to make it more manageable, DDD divides a domain into subdomains. The DDD term â€˜problem domainâ€™ is used to define a functional area within a context such as an organisation or department. The terms domain in DDD and LADM have common characteristics as considering contexts such as a land registry and a cadastre. Evans (2003) and Vernon (2013) articulate how DDD is a set of design practices, techniques and fundamental principles, terms, and implications to facilitate the development of software projects within complex domains, used to guide software developers and domain experts to share and represent models of knowledge from the domain. In DDD, the ubiquitous language is also essential in intersecting the jargons between domain experts and IT experts. The LADM provides a formal language for describing similarities and differences for describing the many aspects of the land administration domain. The approach demands greater participation from domain experts: they lead modelling of the current state and its evolution: the events. The Annex N of ISO 19152 describes that LADM covers both event-based and state-based modelling via LA_Source and VersionedObject. The application of Event-Based Modelling and Event Sourcing is still relatively novel to the LA domain. Event Sourcing ensures that all current state changes are stored as a sequence of events, enabling querying and state reconstruction. The new information system is considered futureproof, delivering improvements for deed registration times, monitoring, traceability/auditing, history management and interoperability. Further research suggestions include undertaken Domain-Driven Design in other contexts, particularly those implementing LADM.
Methods: Case study with action-research principles on Kadasterâ€™s 2016â€“2018 deeds-registration renewal in the Netherlands. Data came from observations, interviews, questionnaires, and participation in the development team, alongside analysis of the DDD/CQRS/event-sourcing design.
Results: DDD with CQRS and Event Sourcing supported a new deeds-registration system with audit trail, history management, traceability, and interoperability. The parallel system ran for a year, then went live in a weekend â€œbig bangâ€ migration.
Conclusions: DDD can improve land-administration system design by focusing on subdomains, events, and interoperability, especially for deeds registration. Challenges remain in DDD-to-UML/model-to-code translation, tool support, and standardizing exchange formats.

Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validated through a real-world implementation case, including parallel operation, migration to live use, and practitioner feedback from developers and business experts. Evidence is mainly qualitative, with operational observations rather than formal quantitative benchmarking.

Source: Blockchain-based governance models supporting corruption-transparency: A systematic literature review
Abstract: Corruption and lack of transparency remain critical challenges in governance systems around the world. These issues are often perpetuated by centralized systems and their manipulation by system administrators. Furthermore, the lack of data ownership and the monetization of user data by tech companies further increase concerns about transparency. In light of these concerns, this study aims to review existing blockchain-based governance models and identify best-practice governance models focusing on corruption transparency, their characteristics, and components. The research will also examine the role of a token economy in addressing trusted third-party issues related to asset ownership management. Furthermore, we discuss the effect of smart contracts, blockchain, decentralized autonomous organizations (DAO), Web 3.0, and multifactor challenge set self-sovereign identity authentication (MFSSIA) as modern technologies to combat corruption and achieve transparency in the public sector. To achieve this, we conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) comprising peer-reviewed journals, proceedings, and book chapters published between 2012 and 2023. Using the SLR methodology, 45 primary and supporting studies have been selected for result extraction and analysis. Finally, we discovered seven blockchain-based governance models with their characteristics and primary components.
Methods: Systematic literature review following Kitchenham and Charters, using Google Scholar and Scopus. From 242 papers (2012â€“2023), 154 were reviewed; 45 primary and supporting studies were extracted and synthesized.
Results: The review identified seven blockchain-based governance models, with three positioned as anti-corruption solutions for the public sector. These models mainly target procurement, document verification, and e-voting, and emphasize transparency, accountability, and reduced intermediary reliance.
Conclusions: Blockchain, smart contracts, Web 3.0, DAOs, and MFSSIA can improve public-sector transparency and reduce corruption by minimizing physical interaction and intermediaries. Main limitations are reliance on published literature, possible publication bias, and insufficient exploration of scalability and token-economy ethics.

No new experiments or benchmark metrics are reported; the paper relies on review-based, qualitative evidence plus cited prototype/practical cases.

Consensus mechanisms mentioned include PoW, PoS, and DPoS; one token-economy example uses DPoS on Steem.

The stack is used to store, validate, and automate transactions, document flows, voting, and token management.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Public-sector governance and anti-corruption use cases: procurement, document verification, e-voting, participatory budgeting, land registration, notarization, identity verification, and public fund tracking. Data types include credentials, documents, ownership records, and tokenized assets.

Source: Defining blockchain governance principles: A comprehensive framework
Abstract: Blockchain eliminates the need for trusted third-party intermediaries in business by enabling decentralised architecture design in software applications. However, the vulnerabilities in on-chain autonomous decision-makings and cumbersome off-chain coordination lead to serious concerns about blockchain's ability to behave in a trustworthy and efficient way. Blockchain governance has received considerable attention to support the decision-making process during the use and evolution of blockchain. Nevertheless, the conventional governance frameworks do not apply to blockchain due to its distributed architecture and decentralised decision process. These inherent features lead to the absence of a clear source of authority in blockchain ecosystem. Currently, there is a lack of systematic guidance on the governance of blockchain. Therefore, in this paper, we present a comprehensive blockchain governance framework, which elucidates an integrated view of the degree of decentralisation, decision rights, incentives, accountability, ecosystem, and legal and ethical responsibilities. The above aspects are formulated as six high-level principles for blockchain governance. We demonstrate a qualitative analysis of the proposed framework, including case studies on five extant blockchain platforms, and comparison with existing blockchain governance frameworks. The results show that our proposed framework is feasible and applicable in a real-world context.
Methods: Systematic literature review of 37 papers from five databases, followed by a framework derivation and qualitative case studies of five blockchains (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Dash, Tezos, Hyperledger Fabric) plus comparison with nine existing governance frameworks.
Results: The framework identified six governance principles spanning decentralisation, incentives, decision rights, accountability, ecosystem, and legal/ethical responsibilities. Case studies showed the framework is feasible and applicable, and comparison revealed gaps in existing governance frameworks.
Conclusions: A comprehensive blockchain governance framework can guide real-world governance for blockchain and blockchain-based applications. Future work will develop a design-pattern catalogue and study architectural decisions for blockchain governance.

Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validated by a systematic literature review, qualitative analysis, five real-world case studies, and comparison against nine prior frameworks. Evidence is qualitative, with no quantitative performance metrics reported.

Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Dash use PoW; Tezos uses PoS; Hyperledger Fabric supports pluggable consensus, with Raft recommended, and distinguishes permissionless public, permissioned public, and permissioned private architectures.

The stack includes consensus and incentive mechanisms, smart contracts, APIs, testnets, GitHub source control, and in Fabric endorsed transactions, ordering service nodes, and Certificate Authorities.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Focuses on blockchain governance for blockchain platforms and blockchain-based applications, especially DeFi and enterprise DApps. Data concerns on-chain transactions, ledger history, smart contracts, private data, and application-level transaction handling.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Addresses access control, digital signatures, multi-signature, Merkle trees, Bloom filters, encryption, PKI/Certificate Authorities, and endorsement policies. Threats include smart-contract exploits, tampering, unauthorized access, privacy leakage, invalid blocks, scams, and data-removal/rollback needs.

The framework discusses regulators, audit trails, GDPR, antitrust policy, and institutional vs technical accountability across blockchain ecosystems.

The case studies cover Bitcoin, Ethereum, Dash, Tezos, and Hyperledger Fabric in real-world, document-based analysis.

Source: Blockchain-based framework for enhancing hazardous material traceability in seaports: opportunities and challenges in the maritime supply chain
Abstract: Maritime hazardous-material operations depend on timely, trusted, and auditable information exchange among port authorities, terminal operators, shipping lines, cargo owners, manufacturers, regulators, and emergency-response actors. In seaports, evidence concerning cargo identity, custody, documentation, storage conditions, sensor readings, mitigation actions, and regulatory closure is often dispersed across disconnected systems, delaying warning and weakening accountability. This study develops a permissioned blockchain-based framework that integrates IoT condition monitoring, cargo-specific event classification, selective off-chain/on-chain storage, encryption, role-based access, smart-contract alerts, and regulator-visible audit trails. The framework is evaluated through a deterministic, rule-based scenario involving a generic IMDG Class 3 container moving through a 90-minute port workflow. The evaluation specifies assumptions, event-processing and storage rules, a selected event log, a critical-alert payload, a constructed fragmented baseline, explicit performance metrics, and five stress conditions. Within this bounded scenario, the framework links all eight defined lifecycle elements, notifies all five designated stakeholder groups at critical escalation, retains seven event-level ledger entries instead of 19 raw sensor entries (a 63.2% reduction), detects an altered off-chain record through hash mismatch, and links all five required closure elements. These are scenario-level process results, not evidence of live latency, accident reduction, legal admissibility, or port-wide scalability. The study contributes a seaport-specific architecture and a transparent pre-pilot basis for prototype development, expert validation, and limited testing with approved operational data.
Methods: Conceptual framework development plus deterministic, rule-based simulation of a single IMDG Class 3 container over a 90-minute port workflow. The study uses synthetic data, a fragmented baseline comparison, and five stress conditions to verify internal process logic.
Results: Within the modeled scenario, the framework linked 8/8 lifecycle elements, notified 5/5 stakeholder groups, reduced ledger entries from 19 raw sensor records to 7 on-chain entries (63.2% reduction), detected an altered off-chain record via hash mismatch, and linked 5/5 closure elements.
Conclusions: The framework is a targeted evidence-and-coordination layer for hazardous-material traceability, not a generic visibility platform. The authors conclude that further controlled prototyping, expert review, load testing, and a limited pilot are needed before broader deployment.
Study Classification and Maturity: Design science / conceptual framework paper with simulation-based pre-pilot evaluation. Maturity is pre-pilot or prototype-ready, not operationally deployed.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Deterministic rule-based scenario evaluation using synthetic data, a constructed fragmented baseline, and five stress tests. Evidence is process-level and quantitative, not field-based or experimentally deployed.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Permissioned consortium blockchain architecture; Hyperledger Fabric is named as a suitable implementation option. The design uses smart contracts, off-chain/on-chain separation, encrypted sensitive events, hashes, custody records, acknowledgments, and closure evidence.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: Three-layer stack: data layer, blockchain layer, and application layer. It integrates IoT sensors, GPS, RFID, off-chain databases, APIs to port community/ERP/customs/TOS systems, dashboards, and role-based alerts.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Hazardous-material traceability in seaports for IMDG Class 3 container operations. Data include sensor readings, container identity, hazardous-material class, SDS reference, custody, inspection, deviation, response, and regulatory closure evidence.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses encryption, role-based access, cryptographic hashing, permissioned validation, and secure key-management practices. Addresses tampering, unauthorized access, privacy leakage, and altered off-chain records; smart-contract and node-failure risks are discussed as test targets.

The context is seaport hazardous-material operations; deployment is pre-pilot and limited-pilot oriented.

Source: Blockchain for citizens' participation in urban planning: The case of the city of Berlin. A value sensitive design approach
Abstract: The aim of the paper is to investigate how a blockchain-based platform for citizens' participation in urban planning should be developed adopting a Value Sensitive Design approach (VSD). VSD can be considered as an overarching methodological framework for new technologies development which takes into account moral and human values of all the direct and indirect stakeholders which might be impacted by the technology. By considering the perspectives of the different involved stakeholders, the paper specifically addresses the call for more research about blockchain-based services which adopts a human-centred approach instead of technocentric. The paper is based on the empirical analysis of a DApp called BBBlockchain which was specifically created with the purpose to improve citizens participation in urban planning decisions in two major residential development projects in Berlin, Germany. BBBlockchain is a proof of concept which is currently running on its own in-house test network but it can run on every EVM compatible blockchain. From the analysis of the information layer of participation, it can be argued that the most important values include transparency, inclusiveness and confidentiality.
Methods: Qualitative case study of BBBlockchain using Value Sensitive Design (VSD) with conceptual literature review and empirical thematic analysis. Data came from 10 semi-structured interviews, stakeholder meetings, platform content analysis, and a preliminary survey (n=25).
Results: Transparency, inclusiveness, and accountability emerged as the key values, but blockchain also created tension by increasing accountability and discouraging some stakeholders from sharing content. The platform improved traceability and reliability, yet information comprehensiveness and citizensâ€™ engagement remained limited.
Conclusions: VSD is presented as a suitable approach for developing blockchain-based participation platforms, but technology alone is insufficient without governance rules and human-centered design. The paper concludes that adoption depends on balancing transparency, confidentiality, and accountability within the urban-planning context.
Study Classification and Maturity: Empirical qualitative case study with conceptual VSD framing; proof-of-concept DApp in pilot testing. BBBlockchain was tested in two Berlin residential development projects and operated on an in-house test network/public PoA network.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation combined exploratory case study analysis, pilot testing, usability tests, interviews, stakeholder-meeting recordings, platform-content analysis, and a small survey. Evidence was both qualitative and limited quantitative (e.g., 37 entries, 25 survey respondents).
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: BBBlockchain is an Ethereum-based DApp built as a public permissionless system with smart contracts and an API-mediated interface. It later ran on an in-house public proof-of-authority network with three miner authorities and no central trusted third party.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: The stack includes Ethereum smart contracts, an API interface, an optional external-server GUI, and a mobile/desktop front end. Ethereum nodes mirror contract execution and hash-based integrity checks are shown to users; content can also be added via an editor interface and external monitoring tool (oracle).
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Urban planning participation in two Berlin residential development projects. The platform manages land-use plans, approval processes, contracts, and building information for information sharing, co-decision, and token issuance.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses hashing, immutability, cryptographic verification, and blockchain traceability to protect data integrity and detect manipulation. It addresses tampering, accountability, and secure documentation, but also notes the oracle problem and confidentiality risks.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: No formal interoperability standard such as LADM, INTERLIS, or INSPIRE is discussed. The paper only states that BBBlockchain can run on any EVM-compatible blockchain and later considered migration to Bitcoin RSK.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: Governance relies on rules of participation, stakeholder roles, and restrictions on what may be published, including privacy and confidentiality constraints. The paper notes unresolved legal support for responsibilities, dispute resolution, enforcement, and integration with existing urban-planning law.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Key barriers were technical complexity, low blockchain literacy, institutional resistance, accountability concerns, and legal/privacy constraints. Deployment was in Berlin, with the system moving from Rinkeby to an in-house public PoA network and tested in a pilot phase.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Main criteria were inclusiveness, transparency, accountability, information quality, and accessibility rather than throughput or latency. Reported gaps include weak evidence on participation effects, limited survey size (n=25), and unresolved issues of garbage inâ€“garbage out and blockchain-supported comprehension for non-experts.

Source: Transformations, transitions, or tall tales? A global review of the uptake and impact of NoSQL, blockchain, and big data analytics on the land administration sector
Abstract: Unstructured data, non-relational databases, distributed databases, and big data analytics potentially change the landscape for digital land data creation, use, management, and dissemination. The way land data is governed and the resultant impact on land tenure security delivery is open to substantial re-thinking. Drawing from international cases, this paper provides a state-of-the-art examination of prototypes and demonstrators from the global land sector. The aim is to deliver an insight into the opportunities, challenges, impacts, and future scenarios regarding the application of the emerging technologies. The paper finds that whilst uptake of non-relational and distributed databases is occurring, it remains largely at the level of proof-of-concept, demonstrator or pilot. Scaled uptake is occurring slower than anticipated, and to a lesser degree than in other sectors. However, the broader and longer-term impacts on the land sector remain difficult to judge. Meanwhile, emerging distributed analytical databases appear to be under-exploited or at least underexplored within the land sector. Overall, the examined technologies are seen to enable new operational approaches for conventional land sector transactions, and also entirely new land related services, digital products, and actors: the ways and means of holding, transferring, and securing land may become more nuanced, fractionalized, and/or automated. Whether these observed embryonic developments lead to sector transformation or orderly transition, is seen to be heavily reliant on the prevailing political, socio-cultural and institutional settings within a jurisdiction.
Methods: Systematic research synthesis of global land-sector literature, conference papers, grey literature, and two unpublished case studies (Land Layby, Brickx). The review used thematic analysis guided by an adapted LIS/database technologies framework.
Results: Uptake of NoSQL, blockchain/DLT, and big data tools remains mostly proof-of-concept, demonstrator, or pilot. RDBMS still dominate; distributed analytical databases and NewSQL are largely underused, while DLTs and fractional property platforms show emerging but limited operational use.
Conclusions: Emerging data technologies may enable new operational approaches and new land-related services, but broad sector impacts are still premature to judge. The authors recommend deeper study of legal, ethical, and institutional barriers and likely hybrid 1st/2nd/3rd generation LIS models.
Study Classification and Maturity: Global exploratory review/synthesis with case studies and thematic analysis. Highest maturity observed was mostly proof-of-concept, demonstrator, or pilot, with a few quasi-production or emerging operational cases.
Evaluation Method and Evidence: Validation is by literature synthesis plus document-based case study analysis, not experiments or simulations. Evidence is mainly qualitative, drawing on published works, reports, grey literature, and author experience, with examples from international cases.
Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain/DLT is discussed as a decentralized peer-to-peer node network that validates transactions and appends blocks. The main implemented example, Land Layby, planned Ethereum-based public ledger with permission levels and smart contracts; no formal consensus protocol is specified.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: The stack spans relational databases (PostgreSQL, STDM, SOLA), semi-structured formats (GML, LandXML, RDF), NoSQL systems (CouchDB, MongoDB, MarkLogic, Cassandra), DLTs, and big-data tools such as Hadoop/GeoSpark SQL. Integration is described via data transformation, middleware, and mirrored links to existing land registries, but implementation details are mostly conceptual.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land administration and land tenure security, including cadastres, land registries, land rights/RRRs, property transfer, and land-related analytics. Cases include digital land records, fractional property investment, and alternative registry concepts for Kenya and Australia.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Mechanisms include immutable ledgers, smart contracts, permissioned access, and transaction authentication by network nodes; the paper also mentions digital signatures only indirectly via blockchain validation. Threats discussed include fraud, corruption, tampering, privacy concerns, and conflicts between DLT and official registries.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: LADM/ISO 19152, GML, LandXML, RDF, ISO TC211, OGC, BIM, CityGML, LandInfra, and INSPIRE are discussed. Integration is mainly via schema transformation, exchange formats, middleware, and efforts to make LADM interoperable with other spatial standards.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The paper stresses legal recognition, identity authentication, regulatory compliance, and alignment with land transaction requirements. It highlights the need for government support, institutional cooperation, and unresolved conflicts between private DLT registries and official ministry registries.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Main barriers are institutional inertia, legal and political constraints, funding, lack of awareness, technical complexity, data population challenges, and conflicts over registry control. Deployment contexts include global cases, especially Kenya and Australia, with maturity ranging from conceptual to pilot and early quasi-production.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation criteria discussed include security, clarity, simplicity, timeliness, fairness, accessibility, cost, sustainability, scalability, and interoperability. Reported gaps are the lack of published large-scale land applications for NoSQL/NewSQL, minimal distributed analytics use, and too little evidence to assess broader impacts.

Source: The Land Administration Domain Model
Abstract: Societal drivers including poverty eradication, gender equality, indigenous recognition, adequate housing, sustainable agriculture, food security, climate change response, and good governance, influence contemporary land administration design. Equally, the opportunities provided by technological development also influence design approaches. The Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) attempts to align both: the data model provides a standardised global vocabulary for land administration. Abstract: The decision to refine the existing content and to extend the scope of Edition I of the ISO 19152:2012 Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) is a response to requests from the international Land Administration (LA) community. This response has to be formally organised in accordance with ISO guidelines. This begins with gathering feedback from ISO/TC 211 Member States on the need for updated and enhanced capabilities of the LADM. In addition, several proposals have been made to extend the scope of the LADM Edition I. After analysing the feedback received, it was proposed to develop the LADM Edition II as a multi-part standard: Part 1 â€” Generic conceptual model, Part 2 â€” Land registration, Part 3 â€” Marine georegulation, Part 4 â€” Valuation information, Part 5 â€” Spatial plan information and Part 6 â€” Implementation aspects. In other words, Edition I focuses on land tenure, while the design and development of Edition II is based on the inclusion of rights, restrictions and responsibilities (RRRs) concerning marine georegulation, valuation information, spatial plan information as well as LADM implementation. 3D representations are relevant for all parts. This paper focuses on the design of the new structure of the second edition of the LADM and on the (operational) capabilities of this new edition in relation to the LA issues in Parts (standards addressing a specific part of the scope) and Packages (groups of conceptually close classes), with a particular attention to the requirements and design related decisions taken in the revision process. The parts 1, 2, 4 and 5 are the parts in which the authors are currently involved. Part 1 will be a high-level umbrella standard; Part 2 is largely based on LADM Edition I and focuses on land registration, with an enhanced support on the surveying functionality, including new subclasses of spatial unit, and extended 3D spatial profiles. Part 3 harmonises the description of RRRs and aligns land concepts with marine aspects from the marine domain based on the International Hydrographic Organisation (IHO) S121 Maritime Limits and Boundaries Product Specification. Part 4 deals with valuation information used and produced in the context of land administration, while Part 5 deals with spatial planning information and includes the planned use of the land (zoning), resulting in RRRs. Lastly, Part 6 is planned to be about implementation of the LADM and will be developed in close collaboration with the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC).

Conclusions: LADM Edition II is more complete, harmonized, and closer to implementation than Edition I, with broader coverage of land administration/georegulation and stronger 3D support. ISO/TC 211 voting and validation were positive for Parts 1â€“5, while Part 6 remains planned.

Source: Application of blockchain smart contracts in smart tenancies: A Malaysian perspective
Abstract: The advancement in blockchain technology has enabled smart contracts to automate the execution of tenancy obligations, known as â€œsmart tenanciesâ€. The key findings are as follows: (1)(a) smart tenancies can and should be stamped when the user interface stipulates the information required for calculation of stamp duty; (1)(b) smart tenancies service provider have to comply with the Electronic Commerce Act 2006 to ensure that the system is reliable to attribute the electronic signatures to the contracting parties; (2) once the print-out of a smart tenancy is stamped, the tenant and landlord have an option to apply for endorsement of tenancy with the land registry under the National Land Code (Revised 2020); (3) the Legal Profession Act 1976 does not restrict the marketing, operation and maintenance of smart tenancies services to be done by law firms exclusively; and (4) there is no room for self-help eviction of a tenant in Malaysia, and the eviction process ought to be enforced with a court order.

Conclusions: Smart tenancies are legally workable in Malaysia with stamping, electronic-signature compliance, and post-stamping registry endorsement. Self-help eviction is not allowed; tenancy disputes should proceed through court order.

Abstract: The real estate sector is often presented as an exemplary field that benefits from practical blockchain applications. Conceptual blockchain literature was identified to propose blockchain benefits for the real estate sector in four categories: land administration, real estate transactions, tokenization, and real estate management. Although the conceptual and theoretical blockchain literature presents blockchain as a disruptive and transformative technology for the real estate sector, the empirical applications suggest that blockchain adoption materializes more in hybrid, smaller-scale settings, where blockchain is merely an add-on layer to existing systems. Overall, most of the conceptual blockchain benefits remain empirically unconfirmed. On the other hand, the empirical applications suggest that blockchain could, for example, increase efficiency, reduce time, and provide verifiability, transparency, and automation, even in smaller-scale, hybrid settings. Empirical applications were mostly hybrid, small-scale land administration cases; 12 of 26 had evaluations, and reported benefits included higher efficiency, verifiability, transparency, and sometimes reduced fraud and increased trust.

Abstract: Blockchain technology shows significant promise for addressing challenges within the agri-food supply chain. Abstract: Hybrid blockchain architectures combine centralized applications, like enterprise systems, with (public) blockchain to implement additional functionality, such as tamper-proof record keeping. The solution is motivated by a fintech use case, for which we also show the implementation of a prototype and an experimental evaluation of the latency and cost savings.

Source: Distributed Ledger Technology-based land transaction system with trusted nodes consensus mechanism
Abstract: Blockchain technology is an emerging solution to various financial applications that require a secure and tamper-proof transactions system. One such application is the land registry. Management of transactions for land registration is a tedious task. It is highly insecure and subject to forgery land records, Issues in verification, mediators, etc. This article presents a scalable and novel property/land registration framework based on blockchain technology. The transparent and immutable nature of blockchain technology makes it reliable for intrusive and fraudulent land registration activities. The framework uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), a Peer-to-Peer (P2P) swarm network. It allows the sharing and storing of data in an efficient, decentralized, and transparent manner. This article also proposes a Trusted Node Consensus Algorithm (TNCA) based on the miners' trust value that minimizes the computational overhead of broadcasting the new block. The proposed approach - trusted node consensus algorithm requires lesser time to add the block into the blockchain, and message exchange per consensus is 58.94% lesser than the traditional Proof-of-Work (PoW) approach and 26.44% lesser time than the existing load-balanced method.
Methods: Proposed blockchain-based property/land transaction framework using IPFS as a P2P swarm network and a trust value-based Trusted Node Consensus Algorithm (TNCA). Performance was evaluated by simulation with varying miners and blocks, comparing TNCA against PoW, PoS, DPoS, and a load-based trust approach.
Results: TNCA reduced message exchange by 58.94% versus PoW and execution time by 67.59% versus PoW, 61.65% versus PoS, and 47.99% versus DPoS. It also reduced execution time by 26.44% versus the load-trust-based approach.
Conclusions: The authors conclude the framework is scalable, secure, and suitable for real-time land/property registration. They note limitations including lack of a generic uniform blockchain architecture and increasing load from growing transactions, requiring efficient search algorithms.

Blockchain Platform, Consensus and Archi: Blockchain-based P2P swarm architecture built over IPFS with a government-owned, region-based registry structure. Consensus uses a Trusted Node Consensus Algorithm with trust-value-based leader selection and majority voting, replacing PoW.
System Architecture and Integration Stac: IPFS serves as the distributed storage and P2P layer, with regional web servers holding regional land databases and updated blockchain copies. A bootstrap server discovers peers and maintains active/inactive node lists; miners broadcast verified blocks to the network.
Data Application Domain &Use Case: Land/property registration and transfer in a government land registry. Data include buyer/seller identities, property details, land documents, map plans, ID proofs, witnesses, deeds, and previous block hashes.
Security Mechanisms and Threat Coverage: Uses digital signatures, cryptographic hashes, immutability, and trusted consensus to secure transactions. It targets forgery, tampering, fraudulent records, ambiguous titles, and unauthorized or invalid transaction approval.
Interoperability and Standards Integrati: Information Not Found: The full-text does not contain any reference to LADM, ISO 19152, INTERLIS, INSPIRE, GIS, or other cadastral standards integration.
Legal, Institutional and Governance Fram: The system is government-owned, with sub-registrar and registrar offices performing document verification and registration. The paper states the state sets policy and sub-regions implement it, but does not discuss legal validity or statutory recognition of blockchain records.
Barriers, Adoption and Deployment Contex: Targets state/union-territory land registry offices in a government-controlled setting. Main barriers cited are manual processing, paperwork, incorrect data, broker cost, fraud, scalability, and high computational overhead in PoW; deployment is proposed rather than field-tested.
Performance, Evaluation Criteria &Resear: Evaluation criteria are message exchange and execution time, with comparisons to PoW, PoS, DPoS, and a load-based trust approach. A stated gap is the lack of a generic uniform blockchain architecture and the need for efficient search algorithms as transaction volume grows.
